scope: Complete question/choices/explanation review of every Medium record marked unknown in the saved review queue, including the prior editorial revisions.

question.q: The posted price is held below equilibrium, but buyers wait in long lines. What policy most likely caused this?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A tax on sellers
An outward PPF shift
question.commonError: misses_waiting_as_shortage_rationing
question.feedback: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage, so nonprice rationing like waiting can appear.

question.q: A rent ceiling is set above the equilibrium rent. What is the likely result?
options: The ceiling is not binding and has no effect
The ceiling creates a shortage
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling shifts supply right
question.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind
question.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium does not prevent the market price from reaching equilibrium.

question.q: Why can a binding rent ceiling reduce the quality of rental housing?
options: Landlords have less incentive to maintain units when price cannot rise
Tenants always demand less housing at lower prices
Quantity supplied rises above quantity demanded
The ceiling is above equilibrium
question.commonError: misses_nonprice_effects_of_ceiling
question.feedback: A binding ceiling can create shortages and reduce incentives to maintain quality.

question.q: A government policy keeps apartment rents below equilibrium. Which outcome is most likely over time?
options: Shortages and nonprice rationing
Surpluses and unsold apartments
A rightward supply shift caused by lower rent
An increase in quantity supplied
question.commonError: misses_nonprice_rationing_under_ceiling
question.feedback: A binding rent ceiling creates shortages, so apartments may be rationed through waiting, search costs, or other nonprice methods.

question.q: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity demanded?
options: 250 units
150 units
200 units
300 units
question.commonError: reads_supply_curve_instead_of_demand_curve
question.feedback: At $20, the demand curve shows quantity demanded of 250 units.

question.q: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity supplied?
options: 150 units
250 units
200 units
100 units
question.commonError: reads_demand_curve_instead_of_supply_curve
question.feedback: At $20, the supply curve shows quantity supplied of 150 units.

question.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $40, what is the most likely result?
options: The price ceiling is not binding
A shortage of 100 units occurs
A surplus of 100 units occurs
The equilibrium quantity falls to 150
question.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind
question.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.

question.q: At the $1,000 rent ceiling, what shortage is shown?
options: 50 apartments
200 apartments
150 apartments
300 apartments
question.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
question.feedback: Read quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the $1,000 ceiling and subtract: 250 − 50 = 200 apartments.

question.q: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can be rented if transactions cannot exceed the number landlords offer?
options: 150 apartments
200 apartments
50 apartments
250 apartments
question.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
question.feedback: At $1,000, quantity supplied is only 50 apartments. Even though 250 are demanded, actual transactions cannot exceed the 50 units offered.

question.q: Equilibrium rent is $1,400. A ceiling is set at $1,550. What is the immediate market effect?
options: It creates a shortage because the ceiling is binding.
It creates a surplus because the ceiling is binding.
It has no immediate effect because the ceiling is above the equilibrium rent.
It creates a $150 tax wedge between buyers and sellers.
question.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind
question.feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium does not constrain the market price.

question.q: A government wants to make a good affordable, so it imposes a price ceiling. Which condition must hold for the policy to actually affect the market?
options: The ceiling must be below equilibrium price
The ceiling must be above equilibrium price
The ceiling must equal quantity demanded
The ceiling must be imposed on sellers only
question.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_affect_markets
question.feedback: A price ceiling only binds if it is below the equilibrium price.

question.q: A binding rent ceiling is imposed below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 1,200 apartments and quantity supplied is 850. What is the shortage?
options: 350 apartments
850 apartments
1,200 apartments
2,050 apartments
question.commonError: adds_qd_and_qs_instead_of_subtracting
question.feedback: Shortage is Qd - Qs: 1,200 - 850 = 350 apartments.

question.q: A rent ceiling is set below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 900 apartments and quantity supplied is 600. What occurs?
options: A shortage of 300 apartments
A surplus of 300 apartments
A shortage of 1,500 apartments
No effect because ceilings are minimum prices
question.commonError: adds_qd_and_qs_instead_of_subtracting
question.feedback: The shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 900 - 600 = 300.

question.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $20, what shortage results?
options: 100 units
50 units
150 units
400 units
question.commonError: adds_qd_and_qs_instead_of_subtracting
question.feedback: At $20, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150. The shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

question.q: A minimum wage is set below the equilibrium wage. What is the likely result?

It creates unemployment

question.q: What can result when a binding price floor is imposed in an agricultural market?
options: Unsold surplus output
A shortage of the crop
A lower legal price
A movement down the demand curve caused by lower price
question.commonError: confuses_floor_with_ceiling
question.feedback: A binding price floor keeps price above equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

question.q: How do a price floor above equilibrium and a price ceiling below equilibrium both interfere with market adjustment?
options: They prevent the market price from adjusting to equilibrium
They eliminate all gains from trade immediately
They make demand and supply irrelevant
They always increase the quantity traded
question.commonError: cannot_identify_why_binding_controls_matter
question.feedback: Binding price controls prevent price from moving to equilibrium, creating shortages or surpluses.

question.q: The graph shows a $40 price floor. Which statement correctly classifies the policy and identifies the competitive equilibrium price?
options: The floor is binding because it is above the $30 equilibrium price.
The floor is binding because it is above the $35 equilibrium price.
The floor is nonbinding, so the market clears at $30.
The floor is nonbinding, so the market clears at $35.
question.commonError: gets_binding_floor_direction_backwards
question.feedback: The demand and supply curves intersect at $30. The legal minimum of $40 is a price floor. It is above equilibrium, so it prevents the market from clearing at $30 and is binding.

question.q: The market begins where SL0 and DL intersect. A licensing reform lets more trained healthcare workers enter the occupation. At $20, how many workers are available before and after the change? Does this show a supply shift or movement along a curve?
options: Supply changes from 3,000 to 7,000 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 8,000 workers; this is movement along a fixed supply curve caused solely by wage.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 8,000 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 3,000 to 7,000 workers; this is movement along a fixed supply curve caused solely by wage.
question.commonError: Treats the wage as a labor-supply shifter rather than a cause of movement along labor supply.
question.feedback: At $20, SL0 gives 4,000 workers and SL1 gives 8,000. Easier entry expands the quantity available at each wage. A wage change by itself moves along a supply curve rather than relocating it.

$20 and 2,000 workers; firms’ demand limits employment.

question.feedback: The $20 floor is above the $15 equilibrium. At $20 firms demand 20 hundreds, so 2,000 are employed despite 6,000 willing workers. Actual trade is limited by the short side, labor demand.

question.q: How far is the legal minimum below the market-clearing wage? Does this minimum wage create a surplus of workers?
options: $10; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
$5; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
$10; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
$5; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
question.commonError: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
question.feedback: Equilibrium is $15 while the legal minimum is $10. Paying the market wage already complies with the floor. The $5 gap therefore creates neither a forced wage reduction nor policy-induced excess supply.

question.q: With equipment and floor space fixed, marginal output at an apple orchard falls from 16 to 11 crates as another worker joins. What does this imply about marginal and total output?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
Average product must equal marginal product
question.commonError: Confuses diminishing marginal product with falling total product or negative marginal product.
question.feedback: The added worker still contributes 11 crates, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 16 is diminishing marginal product.

question.q: A worker at a bakery adds 6 loaves per hour, each worth $8. The wage is $42 per hour. What should the competitive firm do?
options: Hire the worker because the value of the added output exceeds the wage
Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
question.commonError: Compares physical marginal product directly with a dollar wage instead of comparing VMP with labor cost.
question.feedback: The worker's VMP is $48 per hour (6 × $8). Because $48 exceeds $42, the added value is greater than labor cost.

question.q: A competitive car wash can hire another worker who would wash 3 additional cars per hour, selling for $15 each. Should it pay this worker $40 per hour?

question.commonError: Compares physical marginal product directly with a dollar wage instead of comparing VMP with labor cost.

question.q: A competitive landscaping firm’s next worker would complete 4 additional lawns per hour, selling for $14 each. Would hiring the worker for $60 per hour raise profit?

question.q: A bakery increases labor from 4 to 5 workers, and output rises from 120 to 138 loaves. What is the marginal product per additional worker?

question.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (138 − 120) ÷ (5 − 4) = 18 loaves per added worker.

question.q: A clinic hires more physicians, which makes each medical technician more productive. How are these inputs related in production?
options: Physicians and technicians are complements, raising technician demand
All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
question.commonError: Assumes productive inputs are always substitutes or always complements without using the stated relationship.
question.feedback: Physicians and technicians are complements, raising technician demand. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

question.commonError: Compares physical marginal product directly with a dollar wage instead of comparing VMP with labor cost.
question.feedback: The worker's VMP is $56 per hour (2 × $28). Because $56 exceeds $50, the added value is greater than labor cost.

question.q: The market wage for landscapers rises. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: A shift of labor demand
A shift of labor supply
Movement up the landscaper demand curve
No change in the firm's labor choice
question.commonError: Treats a wage change as a labor-demand shift or a productivity change as movement along the curve.
question.feedback: The wage is the price of labor, so changing it changes quantity of labor demanded along the existing curve.

question.q: A firm can use either paralegals or document-review software for the same task. How are these inputs related in production?
options: The scenario identifies software and paralegal labor as substitutes
All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
question.commonError: Assumes productive inputs are always substitutes or always complements without using the stated relationship.
question.feedback: The scenario identifies software and paralegal labor as substitutes. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

question.q: A new machine replaces manual cutting but makes finishing workers more productive. How does this affect demand for manual cutters and finishing workers?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
Demand can fall for cutting labor and rise for complementary finishing labor
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
question.commonError: Infers a cross-factor effect without identifying whether the inputs are complements or substitutes.
question.feedback: Demand can fall for cutting labor and rise for complementary finishing labor. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

question.q: The roofing crew still produces more after hiring, but the added output falls from 8 to 6 roof sections. Which conclusion follows?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
question.commonError: Confuses diminishing marginal product with falling total product or negative marginal product.
question.feedback: The added worker still contributes 6 roof sections, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 8 is diminishing marginal product.

question.q: An additional worker at a competitive packing plant would produce 10 more cases per hour, selling for $6 each. Should the plant hire the worker for $65 per hour?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire because any added revenue raises profit, regardless of the wage
Do not hire the worker because the value of the added output is below the wage
question.commonError: Compares physical marginal product directly with a dollar wage instead of comparing VMP with labor cost.
question.feedback: The worker's VMP is $60 per hour (10 × $6). Because $60 is below $65, the worker costs more than the added output value.

question.q: Homeowners cut spending on landscaping services. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: Movement along the original labor-demand curve
A shift of labor supply
No change in the firm's labor choice
A leftward shift of landscaper labor demand
question.commonError: Treats a wage change as a labor-demand shift or a productivity change as movement along the curve.
question.feedback: The product demand changes the value of labor at a given wage, so the labor-demand curve shifts.

question.q: Engineers become more effective when supported by skilled technicians. How are these inputs related in production?
options: All factors must be substitutes
The two labor types are complements in this production setting
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
question.commonError: Assumes productive inputs are always substitutes or always complements without using the stated relationship.
question.feedback: The two labor types are complements in this production setting. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

question.q: The wage for technicians rises with all demand determinants fixed. How does demand for labor respond?
options: The labor-demand curve shifts
Labor supply must shift in the same direction
Labor demand cannot respond to product markets
Quantity of technicians demanded falls along the existing curve
question.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
question.feedback: The wage changes quantity of labor demanded along the curve.

question.q: An engineering shortage delays every major building project. How does this affect demand for complementary construction inputs?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
Demand for complementary construction labor and equipment can decline
question.commonError: Infers a cross-factor effect without identifying whether the inputs are complements or substitutes.
question.feedback: Demand for complementary construction labor and equipment can decline. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

question.q: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces private investment. How does this affect the final increase in aggregate demand?
options: Larger because crowding out amplifies it
Smaller because crowding out offsets it
Zero because fiscal policy cannot affect aggregate demand
Negative because taxes always rise
question.commonError: Thinking the multiplier is never offset.
question.feedback: Crowding out weakens the final effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

question.q: Why can an initial increase in spending generate further rounds of spending?
options: One person’s spending becomes income that another person can spend.
Each purchase lowers banks’ reserve requirements.
Private spending automatically reduces government purchases.
Each purchase reduces the amount of money people want to hold.
question.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the initial spending increase
question.feedback: The multiplier works because spending becomes income, and some of that income gets spent again.

question.q: In the graph, what explains why the final shift in aggregate demand is larger than the initial shift?
options: The multiplier effect
Monetary neutrality
The Fisher effect
A reserve requirement
question.commonError: confusing the multiplier effect with monetary policy
question.feedback: The multiplier effect is the extra AD shift caused by income leading to additional consumption spending.

question.q: Fiscal expansion can raise interest rates. Which spending component can then fall, weakening the expansion?
options: Private investment.
Tax collections, which automatically fall to zero.
The price level, which immediately falls.
The money multiplier, which becomes infinite.
question.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens fiscal stimulus
question.feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

question.q: Which situation would make the multiplier effect larger?
options: A higher marginal propensity to consume
A lower marginal propensity to consume
More crowding out
A higher reserve requirement
question.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
question.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, which makes the multiplier larger.

question.q: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
options: Strong crowding out
A high marginal propensity to consume with no interest-rate effect
A large initial increase in government spending
A high willingness to consume extra income
question.commonError: ignoring offsetting effects from interest rates
question.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal stimulus by reducing private investment.

question.q: Government purchases and induced spending move demand from AD1 to AD3. If crowding out leaves demand at AD2, how much of the original expansion has been offset?
options: Part of it: final demand remains above AD1 but below AD3.
More than all of it: final demand lies below the original AD1.
None of it: the distance from AD2 to AD3 is additional induced spending.
All of it: reaching AD2 means spending has returned to its initial curve.
question.commonError: Thinking crowding out amplifies AD.
question.feedback: At a common price AD2 lies between AD1 and AD3. Crowding out reduces the gross expansion but does not reverse it. Identifying the offset requires distinguishing the original, gross and final demand positions.

question.q: In a simplified expenditure model, fiscal expansion would raise aggregate demand by $200 billion before crowding out. Crowding out offsets $60 billion, including its effects on further rounds of spending. What is the net increase in aggregate demand?
options: $140 billion
$260 billion
$200 billion
$60 billion
question.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
question.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 200 − 60 = $140 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

question.q: In the simple expenditure model, the marginal propensity to consume rises from 0.5 to 0.8. How does the government-purchases multiplier change?
options: 2 to 5
5 to 2
question.commonError: Using MPC itself as the multiplier.
question.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so it rises from 2 to 5.

question.q: Government purchases rise by $50 billion and the spending multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, what is the total increase in aggregate demand?
options: $50 billion
$100 billion
$150 billion
$200 billion
question.commonError: Using the spending change instead of multiplying it.
question.feedback: The total demand increase before crowding out is $50 billion × 3 = $150 billion.

question.q: The marginal propensity to consume is 0.6. If income rises by $1,000, how much does consumption rise?
question.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
question.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the change in income: 0.6 x $1,000 = $600.

question.q: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.6, what is the simple spending multiplier?
question.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
question.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.

question.q: The marginal propensity to consume is 0.8 and government purchases rise by $50 billion. What total increase in aggregate demand does the simple spending multiplier predict?
options: $250 billion
$40 billion
$62.5 billion
$50 billion
question.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
question.feedback: With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5. Total increase is 5 x $50 billion = $250 billion.

question.q: In a simplified expenditure model, fiscal expansion would raise aggregate demand by $300 billion before crowding out. Crowding out offsets $80 billion, including its effects on further rounds of spending. What is the net increase in aggregate demand?
options: $220 billion
$380 billion
$80 billion
$300 billion
question.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
question.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 300 − 80 = $220 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

question.q: The desired net aggregate demand increase is $330. Marginal propensity to consume is 0.5, and a total aggregate demand crowding-out offset of $110 is expected after induced effects. What purchases increase reaches the target?
options: $660; multiply the target by two, omitting the offset.
$110; subtract the offset before reversing the multiplier.
$220; divide target plus total offset by the multiplier.
$440; add the offset without reversing the multiplier.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “$440; add the offset but do not reverse the multiplier” in this fiscal multipliers and crowding out task.
question.feedback: 2ΔG−110=330, so ΔG=(330+110)/2=220. Reverse the net-effect equation; the offset is not an autonomous component to multiply again.

question.q: An increase in government purchases of $120 raises aggregate demand by $480 before crowding out in the simple model. What marginal propensity to consume does this imply, and does it determine how much aggregate demand will rise after crowding out?
options: The marginal propensity to consume is 0.25, equal to the share saved.
The marginal propensity to consume is 0.75; crowding out can still reduce the final increase.
The marginal propensity to consume is 4, equal to the spending multiplier.
The marginal propensity to consume is 0.75, so crowding out cannot change the final increase.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “MPC is 0.75 and therefore every realized net effect must equal the gross effect” in this fiscal multipliers and crowding out task.
question.feedback: The spending multiplier is 4 = 1/(1 − MPC), so MPC = 0.75. This gives the demand increase before crowding out. Later crowding out can reduce the final increase.

question.q: Two governments each increase purchases by $130. Economy A has a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8, and crowding out reduces its total increase in aggregate demand by $390. Economy B has a marginal propensity to consume of 0.5 and no crowding out. How do the final increases in aggregate demand compare?
options: Both increases are $260; crowding out offsets A’s larger multiplier.
A’s increase is larger at $650 because the higher propensity to consume always dominates.
B’s increase is zero because a lower propensity to consume prevents further spending.
A’s net effect is negative because its total crowding-out offset must be multiplied by five again.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A has the larger net effect $650; a larger MPC always wins” in this fiscal multipliers and crowding out task.
question.feedback: A: 5×130−390=260. B: 2×130=260. A larger increase before crowding out need not mean a larger increase afterward.

question.q: Fiscal expansion would add $100 to AD before crowding out. Higher rates reduce AD by a total $30 after induced investment effects. What net increase remains?
question.feedback: Subtract the already-total offset once: 100−30=70.
question.commonError: Adds crowding out to demand instead of subtracting it.

question.q: Use the aggregate-demand graph with a constant price level, P. How does output change when aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2?
options: Y1 to Y2
Y2 to Y1
Y2 to Y3
Y3 to Y1
question.commonError: Reading the graph backward.
question.feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

question.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Which curve shows the largest aggregate demand level?
options: AD1
AD2
AD3
P
question.commonError: Confusing curve position with label order.
question.feedback: AD3 is farthest to the right, so it shows the largest AD at price level P.

question.q: Which policy is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: Increasing government spending
Selling government bonds by the Fed
Raising reserve requirements
Increasing the discount rate
question.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with Fed policy
question.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

question.q: Which policy is contractionary fiscal policy?
options: Increasing taxes
Buying government bonds by the Fed
Lowering reserve requirements
Cutting the discount rate
question.commonError: confusing fiscal and monetary policy tools
question.feedback: Higher taxes are contractionary fiscal policy because they reduce disposable income and aggregate demand.

question.q: Why does a tax cut usually shift aggregate demand to the right?
options: Raises disposable income and consumption
Raises reserve requirements
Lowers the money multiplier directly
Forces banks to hold more reserves
question.commonError: thinking tax cuts work through bank reserves
question.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

question.q: Why does a cut in government purchases shift aggregate demand to the left?
options: Government spending is a component of aggregate demand
Money demand automatically rises
Banks stop creating money
Marginal propensity to consume becomes zero
question.commonError: forgetting that G is directly part of AD
question.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD, so reducing G shifts AD left.

question.q: Congress increases infrastructure spending during a recession. What is the direct effect on aggregate demand?
options: Shift aggregate demand right
Shift aggregate demand left
Reduce the money supply
Raise reserve requirements
question.commonError: treating fiscal stimulus like contractionary policy
question.feedback: Higher infrastructure spending raises G and shifts AD right.

question.q: The government raises taxes during an expansion. What is the likely effect on aggregate demand?
options: Aggregate demand shifts left
Aggregate demand shifts right
Aggregate demand becomes vertical
Money supply increases automatically
question.commonError: thinking tax increases raise consumption
question.feedback: Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

question.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, what is the net change in aggregate demand?
options: A $30 billion decrease.
No change.
A $30 billion increase.
A $130 billion increase.
question.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
question.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

question.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
options: $42 billion.
$184.6 billion.
$78 billion.
$120 billion.
question.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
question.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

question.q: Households save most of a temporary tax cut because they expect it to be reversed next year. How does its effect on aggregate demand compare with a tax cut that is mostly spent?
options: Smaller.
Necessarily leftward.
Identical.
Larger.
question.commonError: Ignoring household spending behavior.
question.feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

question.q: A $60 billion tax increase initially reduces consumption by $42 billion. What marginal propensity to consume does this imply?
question.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
question.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

question.q: An economy faces a positive AD shock of $240 billion. If policymakers use a tax increase that reduces disposable income by $100 billion and MPC is 0.8, what is the first-round consumption reduction?
options: $80 billion
$100 billion
$20 billion
$500 billion
question.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
question.feedback: The first-round consumption reduction is MPC times the disposable income change: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

question.q: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. How much of the rebate immediately increases consumption?
options: 50 percent of the rebate.
100 percent of the rebate.
75 percent of the rebate.
25 percent of the rebate.
question.commonError: Treating saving or debt repayment as immediate consumption.
question.feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

question.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
options: $80 billion
$20 billion
$100 billion
$125 billion
question.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
question.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is MPC times disposable income: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

question.q: The government pays $80 in transfers instead of buying goods and services. The marginal propensity to consume is 0.6. In a simple fixed-price model with no other changes, what happens to government purchases, initial consumption, and total aggregate demand?
options: Government purchases rise by $80, consumption initially stays unchanged, and aggregate demand rises by $200.
Government purchases stay unchanged, consumption initially falls by $48, and aggregate demand falls by $120.
Government purchases stay unchanged, consumption initially rises by $48, and aggregate demand rises by $120.
Government purchases, initial consumption, and aggregate demand all stay unchanged.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The transfer is neither G nor capable of affecting consumption, so AD is unchanged” in this fiscal policy and aggregate demand task.
question.feedback: Transfers are not government purchases, but recipients can spend part of them. Initial C=.6×transfer; multiplying by 1/(1−.6)=2.5 gives total 1.5×transfer.

question.q: Households expect a $90 tax increase to be temporary and cut consumption by less than the usual estimate. How should this smaller initial response be used when calculating the total effect on spending?
options: The budget identity proves consumption falls exactly by the full tax increase
Use the consumption response supported by the evidence before calculating the additional spending it induces
The tax increase must expand consumption because temporary taxes always reverse signs
The spending multiplier must be negative because the initial response is smaller
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The budget identity proves consumption falls exactly by the full tax increase” in this fiscal policy and aggregate demand task.
question.feedback: The multiplier calculation depends on how consumption initially responds. If expectations change that response, use the response supported by the evidence. A budget identity does not determine how much households change their spending.

question.q: In an economy with fixed prices, idle resources, and a marginal propensity to consume of 0.75, compare a $100 tax cut with a separate $100 increase in government purchases. How do their initial and total effects on aggregate demand differ?
options: The purchases plan initially adds $100 and ultimately $400; the tax cut initially adds $75 and ultimately $300
Both plans initially add $100 and ultimately $400; households spend the entire tax cut
The purchases plan adds only $100; the tax cut adds $400 because taxes have the larger multiplier
Both plans contract aggregate demand by $100; taxes and purchases have the same sign
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both plans initially add $100 and ultimately $400; households spend the entire tax cut” in this fiscal policy and aggregate demand task.
question.feedback: Purchases directly enter demand; only the MPC share of a tax cut initially becomes consumption. With multiplier 1/(1−.75)=4, the respective total effects are 4 G and 3×tax cut.

question.q: The government reduces purchases $20 during a recession. With spending multiplier 2 and no offsets, how does this affect the existing demand shortfall?
options: It widens the shortfall by $10
It has no effect because purchases are transfers
It widens the shortfall by $40
It narrows the shortfall by $40
question.feedback: The negative purchases impulse is multiplied:−20×2=−40. It reinforces a demand recession.
question.commonError: Treats a purchases cut as expansionary demand policy.

question.q: A $100 tax cut with MPC=.8 generates $80 of first-round consumption. An alternative is $90 of additional government purchases. At fixed prices, ignoring offsets and later induced spending rounds, which policy adds more to initial aggregate demand, and by how much?
options: The tax cut adds $10 more
Government purchases add $10 more
Government purchases add $90 more
The policies add the same amount
question.feedback: The repaired consumption result is $80. Direct government purchases add $90 to initial spending, so the purchase policy adds 90−80=$10 more. This compares initial effects, not full multipliers.
question.commonError: Uses the full tax cut as initial consumption instead of the supplied MPC-adjusted amount.

question.q: Expected inflation rises while the real interest rate stays unchanged. How will lenders adjust the nominal interest rate they require?
options: A higher nominal interest rate
A lower nominal interest rate
No repayment
A lower price level
question.commonError: thinking lenders ignore expected inflation
question.feedback: Lenders care about purchasing power, so higher expected inflation is built into higher nominal interest rates.

question.q: Two otherwise similar economies have the same long-run real interest rate, but expected inflation is 2 percent in one and 7 percent in the other. What should differ under the Fisher effect?
options: The second economy’s nominal interest rate should be about 5 percentage points higher.
The first economy’s nominal interest rate should be about 5 percentage points higher.
Both nominal interest rates must be identical because the real rates match.
The second economy’s real interest rate must be 5 percentage points higher.
question.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
question.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

question.q: Expected inflation falls from 6 percent to 2 percent while the long-run real interest rate remains 3 percent. What nominal-rate change is predicted?
options: The nominal rate rises from about 5 percent to about 9 percent.
The real rate falls from 3 percent to negative 1 percent automatically.
The nominal rate stays at 9 percent because only actual inflation matters.
The nominal rate falls from about 9 percent to about 5 percent.
question.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
question.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

question.q: A one-year loan is priced when inflation is expected to be 3 percent. Actual inflation later turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement separates the Fisher effect from the realized return?
options: The Fisher effect depends on actual inflation and ignores expectations.
Unexpected inflation raises both parties’ realized real returns.
Expected inflation helps set the nominal rate; actual inflation determines the realized real return.
The nominal contract rate automatically changes when actual inflation is observed.
question.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
question.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

question.q: Expected inflation rises 6 percentage points while the equilibrium real interest rate falls 2 percentage points. What happens to the nominal interest rate approximately?
options: It rises by about 4 percentage points because both components matter.
It rises by exactly 6 percentage points because the real rate cannot change.
It falls by about 8 percentage points because higher expected inflation lowers nominal rates.
It stays unchanged because the two components must offset completely.
question.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
question.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

question.q: Expected inflation falls sharply after a credible long-run policy change, but productive opportunities and saving behavior leave the real rate roughly unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Real interest rates must fall by exactly the same amount as expected inflation.
Nominal rates should stay fixed because only realized inflation affects contracts.
Nominal interest rates should fall as the inflation premium falls.
Nominal interest rates should rise because lower expected inflation raises the inflation premium.
question.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
question.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

question.q: A lender expected 4 percent inflation and charged 9 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 8 percent. What happened to the realized real return?
options: It was lower than expected
It was higher than expected
It was unchanged
It became nominal GDP
question.commonError: Ignoring unexpected inflation after a loan is written.
question.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real return to lenders.

question.q: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?
options: It stays unchanged because only expected inflation determines the nominal rate.
It falls because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.
It equals expected inflation because the real interest rate disappears in the long run.
It rises because the equilibrium real interest rate rises.
question.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
question.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

question.q: Using the Fisher approximation, the real interest rate stays at 3% while expected inflation rises from 4% to 9%. By how many percentage points does the nominal interest rate rise?
options: 3 points
4 points
5 points
9 points
question.commonError: Using the final inflation rate instead of the change.
question.feedback: Expected inflation rises by 5 percentage points, so the nominal rate rises by 5 points.

question.q: Using the Fisher approximation, expected inflation rises from 3% to 6% while the real interest rate stays at 2%. What is the new nominal interest rate?
options: 3 percent
5 percent
6 percent
8 percent
question.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
question.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

question.q: The nominal interest rate is 9% and expected inflation is 4%. What is the approximate expected real interest rate?
options: 5 percent
13 percent
4 percent
36 percent
question.commonError: adding inflation when solving for the real rate
question.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal rate minus expected inflation: 9 - 4 = 5 percent.

question.q: The real interest rate is 2% and expected inflation is 6%. What is the approximate nominal interest rate?
options: 8 percent
4 percent
3 percent
12 percent
question.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
question.feedback: Nominal interest rate is approximately real interest rate plus expected inflation: 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

question.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent and the real interest rate remains 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 2 percent.
question.commonError: forgetting to include the real interest rate in both periods
question.feedback: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 8 = 10.

question.q: For a $100 loan, expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% while the required expected real return falls from 4% to 3%. Under the Fisher approximation, which nominal-rate comparison is correct?
options: The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 8%; the real-rate decline partly offsets the inflation-expectation increase
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 9%; the real rate must be held fixed despite the supplied change
The nominal rate falls from 6% to 5%; subtract expected inflation from the required real return
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly” in this fisher effect task.
question.feedback: Initially i≈r+πe=4+2=6. Later i≈3+5=8. A one-for-one response to expected inflation requires a fixed real rate, which is not the case here.

question.q: A fixed-rate loan charges 7% nominal interest. Expected inflation is 3% when the loan is made, but actual inflation is 6%. How do the expected and realized real returns compare?
options: The expected real return was about 4% and the realized return is about 1%; the nominal rate stays at 7%.
The expected real return was about 1%, and the nominal contract rate automatically rises to 10%.
Both real returns are 4% because the nominal rate is fixed.
The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contract rate.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed” in this fisher effect task.
question.feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.

question.q: In a loan market financing $140 of projects, nominal rates fall 2 percentage points while the expected real rate is unchanged. Within the Fisher approximation, what inference follows and what remains unproved?
options: Expected inflation rose 2 points; actual future inflation must rise equally
Actual inflation already fell 2 points; no expectation assumption is needed
The real rate fell 2 points despite the stated fixed-real-rate condition
Expected inflation fell 2 points; actual future inflation need not equal that forecast
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Expected inflation rose 2 points; actual future inflation must rise equally” in this fisher effect task.
question.feedback: With Δr=0, Δi≈Δπe. A two-point nominal decline implies a two-point expectation decline in this model, but forecasts are not necessarily realized.

question.q: Using the Fisher approximation, expected inflation rises from 6% to 8% while the expected real rate remains 2%. What new nominal rate is consistent with both conditions?
question.feedback: Nominal≈real+expected inflation=2+8=10%, up from 8%.
question.commonError: Holds the nominal rate fixed despite higher expected inflation and a fixed real rate.
Changes nominal and expected inflation in opposite directions at a fixed real rate.
question.q: A contract quotes 8% nominal interest and expected inflation 6%. If a new contract has expected inflation 3% with the same expected real return, what nominal rate should it quote?

options: Workers balance speed against the expected cost of damage
Workers maximize speed because only rewards affect behavior
Damage must fall to zero for the incentives to exist
Every worker chooses the same speed regardless of risk
question.commonError: Considering one incentive while ignoring a simultaneous opposing incentive.
question.feedback: The speed bonus and damage consequence change different parts of the worker’s payoff.

question.q: A parking fine doubles, but patrols become rare. Why might violations change little?
options: The expected penalty may remain small because enforcement is unlikely
A larger statutory fine can never affect behavior when drivers know it exists
Drivers respond only to rewards, not penalties
Low enforcement guarantees more violations by every driver
question.commonError: Looking only at the posted penalty and ignoring enforcement probability.
question.feedback: Behavior responds to the expected consequence, which depends on both size and enforcement.

question.q: Two employees receive the same attendance bonus. One changes her schedule; the other has caregiving duties and cannot. What does this show?
options: The same incentive can produce different responses under different constraints
The bonus was not an incentive for either employee because their outcomes differed
A valid incentive must change everyone’s behavior
Constraints matter only when incentives are nonmonetary
question.commonError: Assuming identical payoffs generate identical responses.
question.feedback: The bonus changes payoffs, but constraints and alternatives shape each response.

question.q: A delivery app rewards drivers for accepting a high share of requests. Some drivers accept deliveries they are unlikely to complete and cancel later. What problem does this reveal?
options: The reward encourages drivers to improve their acceptance rating by taking requests they later cancel
The reward cannot be an incentive because cancellations rose after accepted jobs
Acceptance rate measures service quality perfectly
The response proves drivers ignored the metric
question.commonError: Evaluating only the rewarded metric and missing substitution.
question.feedback: Drivers improve acceptance statistics while shifting the problem into later cancellations.

question.q: A company offers either a $40 bonus or public recognition for completing training. Some workers value one more than the other. What follows?
options: Monetary and nonmonetary incentives can differ in strength across people
Only the cash option can change expected benefits
Recognition guarantees completion among all workers
Different preferences mean neither option is an incentive
question.commonError: Assuming all people rank monetary and nonmonetary incentives identically.
question.feedback: Both rewards can alter benefits, but their value depends on the decision-maker.

question.q: A gym charges a missed-appointment fee but waives it when members cancel a day ahead. Which decision does the rule most directly influence?
options: Whether members cancel early instead of simply not appearing
Whether every member continues the gym membership
Whether exercise produces health benefits
Whether members morally approve of cancellation rules
question.commonError: Confusing the targeted choice margin with broader outcomes or approval.
question.feedback: The avoidable fee makes advance cancellation more attractive relative to a no-show.

question.q: A city gives bus riders a $2 subsidy per ride. Ridership rises, but crowding increases and wait times get longer. What is the best interpretation?
options: The subsidy changed incentives and produced an unintended consequence
The subsidy eliminated scarcity
The subsidy created a price floor
The subsidy proves marginal analysis is irrelevant
question.commonError: misses_unintended_consequence_of_incentives
question.feedback: The subsidy encouraged more bus use, but the higher ridership created crowding and longer waits.

question.q: A farm subsidy pays per acre planted with one crop. Farmers expand acreage onto less suitable land. Which part is the incentive and which is the response?
options: Per-acre payment is the incentive; expansion onto marginal land is a response
Expanded acreage is the incentive; payment is the outcome
Crop suitability is the incentive; planting is moral approval
The subsidy is neither because planting was already possible
question.commonError: Interchanging a payoff change with the behavior it induces.
question.feedback: The payment changes the benefit of each planted acre; land expansion is a resulting choice.

question.q: A nonprofit grant rewards the number of people enrolled, not services completed. Enrollment rises and completion falls. Which measure is being optimized?
options: The funded enrollment count rather than the broader service objective
Completion because it is the organization’s stated mission
Both measures equally because they concern the same clients
Neither measure because nonprofits do not respond to funding
question.commonError: Assuming mission statements dominate the payoff attached to a measured target.
question.feedback: The grant rewards entry into the program, so effort shifts toward enrollment rather than completion.

question.q: A bonus tied only to sales volume causes excessive discounting. What happened?
options: Workers ignored the bonus and changed discounting for unrelated market reasons
Workers optimized the rewarded metric rather than total profit
The bonus eliminated every tradeoff involved in making sales
Sales volume became a public good shared equally by all firms
question.commonError: Evaluating the rewarded metric without examining its effect on total profit.
question.feedback: The bonus raises the payoff to volume even when discounts make some sales unprofitable.

question.q: A fee changes behavior for some people but not others. What is the best explanation?
options: The fee is not an incentive.
All people have identical marginal benefits.
People face different constraints, preferences, and alternatives.
Only laws create incentives.
question.commonError: Evaluating incentives without examining margins, metrics, or heterogeneity.
question.feedback: The same fee can change the relative attractiveness of an action by different amounts for different people. Someone with a close substitute may switch, while someone with few alternatives or a high benefit from the action may continue. An unchanged choice does not mean the fee created no incentive.

question.q: A policy subsidizes an action many people already planned to take. What limits additional impact?
options: Every payment creates an equal new action.
Subsidies cannot affect behavior.
The action has no opportunity cost.
Much of the money pays for actions already planned.
question.commonError: Evaluating incentives without examining margins, metrics, or heterogeneity.
question.feedback: People who would take the action without the subsidy can receive a payment without changing their behavior. Those payments are inframarginal: they support actions already planned rather than inducing additional ones. The policy’s additional impact depends on how many people change their choice because of the subsidy.

question.q: A call center rewards short calls and separately penalizes repeat complaints. How should agents respond?
options: Balance speed against the risk that poor service triggers repeat complaints
Make every call as short as possible because rewards dominate penalties
Ignore both rules unless all agents respond identically
Guarantee perfect service because two incentives are present
question.commonError: Ignoring one side of a multi-part incentive system.
question.feedback: Agents face a reward for speed and an expected cost for unresolved problems.

question.feedback: Training can raise productivity, and stronger demand for that skill raises its market return.

question.q: A household has $21,500 in measured money income. The poverty threshold that applies to it is $24,000. How is the household classified under this income-based rule?
options: Below the poverty threshold.
Above the poverty threshold.
Exactly at the poverty threshold.
Its wealth must also be known before this rule can be applied.
question.commonError: uses_wrong_income_measure_or_threshold
question.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $21,500, with the $24,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: Why is it misleading to compare a $5 wage in 1970 directly to a $15 wage today?
options: The purchasing power of money changes over time
Wages are not prices
Inflation only affects GDP, not wages
Nominal values are always real values
question.feedback: Dollar amounts from different years need to be adjusted for changes in the price level.

question.q: A pension has a full cost-of-living adjustment tied to the CPI. If measured inflation is 4 percent, what is the intended effect?
options: Raise the nominal payment about 4% to protect purchasing power.
Reduce the nominal payment about 4% to offset inflation.
Hold the nominal payment fixed so its real value automatically rises.
Convert the pension payment into a market interest rate.
question.commonError: Confusing nominal indexation with a reduction in benefits.
question.feedback: A CPI-linked adjustment raises the nominal amount to offset measured price growth.

question.q: A salary rises 6% while the relevant price index rises 4%. What happens to real purchasing power?
options: It rises modestly
It falls by 10%
It is exactly unchanged
It rises by the full 6%
question.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
question.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

question.q: A rent payment is indexed upward 3% when the relevant price index rises 3%. What is the intended real effect?
options: Raise the real rent by 6%
Cut the nominal rent by 3%
Convert rent into a real interest rate
Keep the payment’s purchasing power roughly constant
question.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
question.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

question.q: A nominal salary is unchanged while the consumer price level falls. What happens to its purchasing power?
options: It becomes an indexed tax threshold
It rises
It falls by definition
It remains unchanged in real terms
question.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
question.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.

question.q: A nominal wage rises 8% while CPI rises 5%. Using the exact ratio and rounding to one decimal place, how much does the real wage rise?
options: About 2.9%
Exactly 3.0%
About 13.4%
About 1.6%
question.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
question.feedback: Real wage growth=(1.08/1.05−1)×100≈2.8571%, or 2.9%. Subtracting rates gives only the 3% approximation.
question.roundingRule: Use (1.08 ÷ 1.05) − 1 and round to one decimal place.

question.q: A tax threshold is adjusted by only half of CPI inflation. What happens to its real value?
options: It rises faster than prices
It remains exactly constant
It becomes a nominal interest rate
It falls
question.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
question.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

question.q: A contract raises its nominal payment 3% each year while inflation is 6%. What happens to the real payment?
options: It declines
It rises about 9%
It remains constant because the payment increased
It equals the nominal interest rate
question.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
question.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A car cost $8,000 in the past when the CPI was 80. The equivalent current-dollar price is $28,000. What is the current CPI?
question.feedback: 28000 = 8000 x current CPI/80, so current CPI = 280.

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A current salary of $96,000 is equivalent to $60,000 in year-T dollars. If the current CPI is 240, what was the CPI in year T?

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A current income of $84,000 equals $60,000 in year-T dollars. If CPI today is 210, what was CPI in year T?
A scholarship rises 15% while CPI rises 10%. Using the exact ratio and rounding to one decimal place, what is its real increase?
options: About 4.5%
Exactly 5.0%
About 25.0% because the two nominal changes are added together
About 1.5%
question.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
question.feedback: Real scholarship growth=(1.15/1.10−1)×100≈4.5455%, or 4.5%. The nominal 15% gain is partly offset by the 10% price increase.
question.roundingRule: Use (1.15 ÷ 1.10) − 1 and round to one decimal place.

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A wage was $18,000 when the CPI was 90. The CPI is now 270. What is the wage in today's dollars?
question.feedback: Today's dollars = 18000 x 270/90 = 54000.

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A tuition bill was $4,000 when the CPI was 125. In today's dollars, it equals $6,400. What is today's CPI?
question.feedback: 6400 = 4000 x today's CPI/125, so today's CPI = 200.

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A salary is $72,000 today when the CPI is 240. What was its equivalent value in year-T dollars when the CPI was 160?

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A salary was $30,000 when the CPI was 150. The CPI is now 225. What is that salary in today's dollars?
question.feedback: Today's dollars = 30000 x 225/150 = 45000.

question.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
question.q: A movie ticket cost $4 when the CPI was 80. The CPI is now 240. What is the ticket price in today's dollars?
question.feedback: Today's dollars = 4 x 240/80 = 12.

question.q: A $190 monthly benefit is fully indexed to a 5% CPI rise, but its recipient's actual fixed basket rises 8%. Which conclusion distinguishes index protection from household purchasing power?
options: CPI-adjusted value falls 3%; household purchasing power is preserved
Both measures rise 13% because the index and basket changes add
CPI-adjusted value is preserved; purchasing power over this household basket falls about 2.8%
Both CPI-adjusted and household purchasing power are preserved because the contract is indexed
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “CPI-adjusted value falls 3%; household purchasing power is preserved” in this indexing and real values task.
question.feedback: The contract preserves value relative to CPI, not every household basket. For this basket the real factor is 1.05/1.08, or about a 2.78% decline.

question.q: A past monthly payment was $200 when CPI was 100. A current payment is $260 when CPI is 125. Which comparison uses common purchasing-power units?
options: The payments have equal purchasing power; both CPI and the payment increased
The current payment is $10 higher in current dollars; the past payment converts to $250
The current payment is $60 higher in real terms; compare unadjusted dollar amounts
The past payment is $10 higher in current dollars; deflate the past payment again
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The payments have equal purchasing power; both CPI and the payment increased” in this indexing and real values task.
question.feedback: The past payment in current dollars is 200×125/100 = 250. The current payment exceeds it by 10.

question.q: An indexed benefit of $210 is adjusted once a year. Prices rise while the next adjustment is six months away. Which change would reduce the delay without guaranteeing that the index matches every household’s spending?
options: Adjust payments more often; a mismatch with household spending can still affect purchasing power.
Adjust payments less often; the price index already matches every household’s spending.
Keep the original dollar payment fixed so that it follows current prices.
Use the GDP deflator because domestic output prices always match household spending.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Reset less frequently to reduce the lag; a CPI rule eliminates all household mismatch” in this indexing and real values task.
question.feedback: More frequent adjustment can shorten the timing gap. Even prompt CPI indexation cannot guarantee unchanged purchasing power for a different household consumption basket.

question.q: Why can heavy reliance on printing money become dangerous?
options: It can create rapid inflation and reduce money's value
It guarantees higher real GDP forever
It eliminates all tax burdens
It makes nominal variables real
question.commonError: Thinking printing money is costless financing.
question.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but it reduces the value of money and can create high inflation.

question.q: A government repeatedly prints money to pay its bills. Which risk is most directly connected to this policy?
options: Inflation tax and possible hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real output
Permanent monetary neutrality failure
A lower price level forever
question.commonError: thinking printing money creates real resources without inflation pressure
question.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but repeated reliance on it can create inflation or hyperinflation.

question.q: Why is the inflation tax called a tax even though Congress may not pass a tax law?
options: It reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.
It raises real GDP automatically.
It only applies to people who owe income taxes.
It directly increases the real wage.
question.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit and legislative
question.feedback: Inflation acts like a tax on money holders by reducing the purchasing power of their cash balances.

question.q: If prices are falling across the economy, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises.
It falls.
It becomes zero.
It becomes the nominal interest rate.
question.commonError: thinking falling prices reduce the purchasing power of money
question.feedback: Deflation means falling prices, so each dollar buys more. The value of money rises.

question.q: Inflation falls from 7 percent to 2 percent, but the overall price level is still rising. Which description is correct?
options: The economy is experiencing disinflation, not deflation.
The economy is experiencing deflation because inflation is lower.
The economy is experiencing hyperinflation because prices are still rising.
The price level must be falling by 5 percent.
question.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
question.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

question.q: A country prints money to cover deficits, prices rise rapidly, and people rush to spend cash before it loses value. Which idea is most central?
options: Inflation tax and falling money value
Crowding out and rising investment
Long-run aggregate supply growth and lower inflation
Commodity money and stable prices
question.commonError: Treating money printing as costless financing.
question.feedback: Printing money can finance spending through an inflation tax, reducing the value of money.

question.q: A country has no ability to borrow and keeps financing deficits by creating money. What is the likely risk if this continues?
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real GDP without inflation
Permanent deflation
A lower money supply
question.commonError: thinking money printing solves fiscal problems without inflation consequences
question.feedback: Persistent money creation to finance deficits can trigger high inflation or hyperinflation.

question.q: An economy enters unexpected deflation while households carry fixed nominal mortgage debt. What happens to the real debt burden, other things equal?
options: It rises because each repayment dollar has greater purchasing power.
It falls because lower prices make nominal debts shrink automatically.
It is unchanged because the price level cannot affect fixed nominal contracts.
It disappears because deflation forces lenders to cancel nominal debt.
question.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
question.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

question.q: If a government prints money to cover spending and the public starts expecting higher future inflation, what happens to nominal interest rates under the Fisher effect?
options: They rise as expected inflation rises.
They fall because money supply rose.
They stay fixed because real rates cannot change.
They become equal to the reserve ratio.
question.commonError: thinking more money always lowers every interest rate in every model and horizon
question.feedback: If money finance raises expected inflation, nominal interest rates tend to rise through the Fisher effect.

question.q: A heavily indebted economy experiences an unexpected 6 percent fall in the overall price level while nominal debts are fixed. Which balance-sheet effect is most likely?
options: Debtors receive an automatic reduction in the nominal face value of their debts.
Creditors lose because every repayment dollar is worth less in real terms.
The fall in the price level is disinflation and therefore cannot affect real debt burdens.
Debtors face a higher real repayment burden, which can weaken spending and financial positions.
question.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
question.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

question.q: If the price level falls from 125 to 120, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises because 1/P is larger.
It falls because 1/P is smaller.
It stays constant because P changed by less than 10.
It becomes equal to velocity.
question.commonError: thinking falling prices reduce the value of money
question.feedback: When the price level falls, each dollar buys more, so the value of money rises.

question.q: A household holds $100 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
question.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.

question.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 3%. A report calls this a fall in the price level and predicts a lower real burden of fixed nominal debt. Which correction is needed?
options: This is deflation: prices fall by 5%, and fixed nominal debt keeps losing real value.
Inflation is zero: prices and the real value of fixed nominal debt stay unchanged.
Inflation is accelerating: prices rise faster, and fixed nominal debt gains real value.
This is disinflation: prices still rise, and fixed nominal debt keeps losing real value.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Deflation: prices fall 5%; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
question.feedback: A positive inflation rate still raises the price level. A slower rise is disinflation, whereas deflation is a falling price level; fixed-debt effects also depend on the relevant price comparison.

question.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $140. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
question.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A bank expects a guaranteed bailout and therefore chooses a riskier portfolio. What causes the distortion?
options: The bank's hidden type before borrowing
Perfect screening
A lower opportunity cost of voting
Protection shifts part of the downside to others
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: When decision makers do not bear the full marginal loss, post-protection risk taking can rise.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: Drivers privately know their preexisting accident risk, which the insurer cannot observe. High-risk drivers are more likely to buy insurance, but no driver changes behavior after buying it. Which conclusion follows?
options: Every accident after purchase establishes moral hazard.
Insurance has necessarily reduced every driver’s care.
The pattern is adverse selection, not evidence of moral hazard.
The insurer has eliminated private information.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: Selection into coverage depends on privately known risk. Moral hazard would require a change in behavior caused by the contract.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: Insured drivers have more accidents than uninsured drivers. What additional comparison helps test whether insurance caused moral hazard?
options: Compare only the total number of drivers in each group.
Assume all drivers had identical risk before insurance.
Compare how otherwise similar drivers change care when coverage changes.
Treat each accident as direct evidence of less care.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: A raw difference may reflect preexisting risk. A credible comparison of behavior under different coverage helps identify the incentive effect.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An insurer reimburses all losses. It then adds a deductible that makes the insured bear part of each loss, holding information and all other terms fixed. Which incentive changes most directly?
options: The insured bears a smaller loss and therefore has less reason for care.
The insured has a stronger financial reason to prevent a loss.
The insurer learns every hidden characteristic before contracting.
The deductible guarantees no accident can occur.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: A deductible leaves some loss with the insured and can strengthen care incentives, without guaranteeing perfect care or revealing all types.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An insured driver maintains exactly the same level of care before and after coverage. An accident then occurs. Does that accident alone establish moral hazard?
options: Yes; every insured loss proves reduced care.
Yes; the insurer’s payment establishes hidden precontract risk.
No; moral hazard is impossible in insurance.
No; an accident alone does not show that insurance changed the driver’s behavior.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: A bad outcome can occur without a change in incentives or behavior. The stated unchanged care does not demonstrate moral hazard.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A driver conceals careless behavior after buying insurance. The insurer raises premiums for every customer. Why might that response fail to target the source of moral hazard?
options: Any higher premium makes all future actions observable.
A uniform premium necessarily eliminates hidden action.
The premium increase need not reward the individual driver for greater care.
Carelessness must have occurred before the insurance contract.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: An incentive contract must connect an individual’s action or outcome to a consequence. A uniform price rise alone may leave the relevant marginal incentive unchanged.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An insurer offers a high-deductible and a low-deductible plan so customers reveal risk through their choice. What mechanism is this?
options: Signaling: customers independently supply evidence of their risk.
Moral hazard: customers change their care after receiving coverage.
Adverse selection: the insurer attracts only lower-risk customers.
Screening: the insurer designs choices that help reveal customers’ risk.
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces different hidden types to self-select.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A lender requires collateral before approving a loan. What informational role can collateral play?
options: It insures the borrower against every loss
Borrowers’ willingness and ability to risk collateral can help the lender distinguish among them.
It creates moral hazard intentionally
It proves all borrowers have identical risk
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
