question.feedback: Contract terms can elicit private information when different risk types choose differently or face different costs.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A credential costs both worker types $2,000 and gives each a $5,000 wage premium. Can these payoffs alone separate the types?
options: No; both types gain by obtaining it.
Yes; only high-productivity workers gain.
Yes; neither worker type gains.
No; the credential must reduce wages.
question.commonError: ignores_type_specific_signaling_costs
question.feedback: Each type gains $3,000. Equal incentives to obtain the credential do not separate the types.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A credential has no effect on productive skill but is harder for low-productivity workers to earn. Could it still convey information?
options: Yes, if the different costs induce different choices by type.
No, because only training can affect employers’ beliefs.
Yes, because every worker must obtain it.
No, because signaling requires identical costs for both types.
question.commonError: ignores_type_specific_signaling_costs
question.feedback: A signal can reveal an existing characteristic without causing that characteristic; credibility depends on incentives to imitate.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A job applicant independently obtains a credible certificate before approaching employers. Employers did not require or design a menu of choices. Which information mechanism is described?
options: Screening by the employer
Moral hazard after employment
A benefits cliff
Signaling by the informed applicant
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: The informed side takes an observable action to communicate its type.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An informed seller voluntarily posts a warranty that is much more expensive for low-quality sellers to honor. Why can it convey quality?
options: All sellers face identical warranty costs and incentives.
Low-quality sellers may find imitation less profitable because expected warranty costs are higher.
Posting a warranty mechanically improves the physical product.
A warranty prevents buyers from learning about defects.
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: Different expected costs can make the observable warranty a credible signal rather than cheap talk.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: High-productivity workers gain $8,000 from a credential and pay $2,000 to earn it. Low-productivity workers gain $3,000 and pay $5,000. Which outcome is supported?
options: Only high-productivity workers choose the credential.
Both types choose the credential.
Only low-productivity workers choose the credential.
Neither type chooses the credential.
question.commonError: ignores_type_specific_signaling_costs
question.feedback: The high type has a positive net benefit of $6,000; the low type has a net cost of $2,000. These payoffs support separation.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A driver takes less care after obtaining broad insurance coverage. Which information problem does this illustrate?
options: Adverse selection before coverage
A credible quality signal
Moral hazard
Perfectly observed contracting
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: Coverage changes the incentive for an action taken after the contract; this is moral hazard.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: Behavior is perfectly monitored and a contract can condition payment on every action. What happens to hidden-action moral hazard?
options: It becomes adverse selection automatically
It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
It must increase
It makes insurance unnecessary in every case
question.commonError: confuses_observation_with_enforceable_incentives
question.feedback: Observable, contractible action allows terms to reward care or penalize risk, though monitoring itself may be costly.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: Two banks hold identical assets initially. Only one receives a credible promise that taxpayers will absorb large future losses. With other incentives fixed, which response is consistent with moral hazard?
options: The protected bank selects less risk because it bears all taxpayers’ losses.
Both banks must select identical risk because their initial assets match.
The unprotected bank becomes insured merely because another bank is protected.
The protected bank selects more risk because it bears less downside.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: The guarantee changes the protected bank’s marginal exposure to losses even though initial assets are equal.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A driver’s coverage expands while accident risk and driving conditions remain unchanged. Which response would be inconsistent with the claim that broader coverage reduced care in this case?
options: The driver stops paying for a useful safety precaution.
The driver begins leaving the vehicle unlocked.
The driver maintains exactly the same safety behavior.
The driver increases risky driving because losses are covered.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: Unchanged care does not support the specified behavioral mechanism. Coverage creates an incentive possibility, not proof that every person responds.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: Monitoring costs $8 per policy and is expected to reduce real accident losses by $5, with no other benefits or costs. Is monitoring justified by net resource savings in this example?
options: Yes; every reduction in moral hazard exceeds its cost.
No; it costs $3 more than the expected loss reduction.
Yes; the net saving is $13.
No; the reduction in losses is a transfer rather than a resource benefit.
question.commonError: ignores_monitoring_resource_cost
question.feedback: The resource gain is $5 and the cost is $8, giving net savings of −$3.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: Why can a credential reveal productivity when it is more costly for low-productivity workers to obtain?
options: Different net benefits can lead the two types to choose differently.
The credential must physically raise every worker’s productivity.
All workers must find it equally attractive to obtain.
Employers must observe productivity before seeing the credential.
question.commonError: ignores_type_specific_signaling_costs
question.feedback: A cost difference can support separation if high-productivity workers want the credential and low-productivity workers do not.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An employer offers two contracts so applicants with different productivity choose different terms. The applicants know their own productivity, but the employer does not. Who is using information to distinguish among applicants, and how?
options: The applicants use screening by accepting the employer’s terms.
The employer signals each applicant’s productivity by offering a job.
The applicants reveal moral hazard simply by choosing different contracts.
The employer uses screening by designing the contract choices.
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: Screening is initiated by the less-informed side through offers that reveal private information via choices.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A bank offers borrowers a choice between a low-interest loan with collateral and a high-interest loan without collateral. Borrowers privately know their repayment risk. Which action constitutes screening?
options: A borrower’s unsolicited public reputation campaign
The bank’s design of the contract menu
The bank’s payment after a default
A borrower’s change in effort after the loan
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: The uninformed bank designs alternatives intended to reveal risk through borrowers’ choices.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A credential raises productive skill equally for all workers. Does that benefit alone establish that the credential separates workers by their prior productivity?
options: No; improving everyone’s skills does not by itself reveal their earlier productivity.
Yes; all training is necessarily a separating signal.
Yes; equal skill gains imply different credential costs.
No; credentials can never both teach and signal.
question.commonError: ignores_type_specific_signaling_costs
question.feedback: Human-capital formation and signaling are distinct mechanisms. Evidence of one does not, by itself, demonstrate the other.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An insurer offers a high-deductible and a low-deductible plan so customers reveal risk through their choice. What mechanism is this?
options: Signaling: customers independently supply evidence of their risk.
Moral hazard: customers change their care after receiving coverage.
Adverse selection: the insurer attracts only lower-risk customers.
Screening: the insurer designs choices that help reveal customers’ risk.
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces different hidden types to self-select.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A bank expects a guaranteed bailout and therefore chooses a riskier portfolio. What causes the distortion?
options: The bank's hidden type before borrowing
Perfect screening
A lower opportunity cost of voting
Protection shifts part of the downside to others
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: When decision makers do not bear the full marginal loss, post-protection risk taking can rise.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A deductible reduces claims, but some customers also stop buying insurance. Which observation directly supports a reduction in moral hazard?
options: Customers who remain insured take more care.
Only low-risk customers leave the insurance pool.
The insurer collects fewer premiums.
The number of insured customers falls.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: Moral hazard concerns behavior after coverage. Changes in who purchases coverage concern selection and do not by themselves establish greater care.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An insurer adds a deductible, but a separate employer plan reimburses that deductible in full. What happens to its incentive for the customer to prevent losses?
options: Reimbursement weakens the incentive created by the deductible.
Reimbursement makes the customer bear more of each loss.
Reimbursement reveals the customer’s inherited risk.
Reimbursement necessarily eliminates all accidents.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: If another party fully repays the deductible, the customer does not bear that marginal loss and the intended incentive is weakened.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A customer can avoid a $100 loss by spending $10 on care. Full insurance repays the loss. If the policy instead leaves the first $20 of the loss uninsured, how does the private incentive change?
options: Avoiding the deductible can make the $10 precaution worthwhile.
The customer still bears none of the preventable loss.
Care becomes worthwhile only if it costs more than $20.
The deductible changes the physical loss to $20.
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: Without care the customer now bears $20; spending $10 to avoid it is privately worthwhile. The physical loss remains $100.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: Why can a deductible reduce moral hazard?
options: It reveals every customer's risk type
The customer pays part of a loss and has more reason to prevent it.
It guarantees that no accident occurs
It makes coverage a public good
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: Cost sharing preserves some incentive to take care after coverage begins.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: An insurer offers plans with different deductibles so applicants reveal risk through their choices. What mechanism is this?
options: Signaling: customers independently supply evidence of their risk.
Screening: the insurer designs choices that help reveal customers’ risk.
Moral hazard: customers change their care after receiving coverage.
Adverse selection: the insurer attracts only lower-risk customers.
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces hidden types to self-select.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: If an insurer can observe every safety action and enforce contract terms that reward or penalize those actions, what happens to hidden-action moral hazard?
options: It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
It automatically becomes adverse selection
It must increase
It makes every insurance contract unnecessary
question.commonError: confuses_hidden_action_with_hidden_type
question.feedback: When enforceable contract terms reward or penalize observed safety actions, they can reduce the hidden-action problem.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy

question.q: A job applicant obtains a certificate before applying. An employer separately offers trial contracts to help distinguish applicants’ abilities. Which action is signaling?
options: The applicant’s certificate
The employer’s contract menu
Both actions are signaling by the informed side.
Neither action can convey information.
question.commonError: reverses_informed_and_uninformed_initiator
question.feedback: The informed applicant initiates the certificate signal. The uninformed employer initiates the screening menu.

question.q: An economist shows a PPF shifting outward after years of investment in capital and technology. What is the best interpretation?
options: The economy's productive capacity has increased
The economy moved inside the PPF because resources are idle
The CPI basket became fixed
A tax wedge disappeared
question.commonError: confuses_movement_along_ppf_with_outward_shift
question.feedback: An outward PPF shift means the economy can produce more because resources, technology, or productivity improved.

question.q: A minimum wage is raised above the equilibrium wage for low-skill labor. What is the expected market result?
options: A shortage of labor, meaning firms cannot find enough workers
No change because price floors never bind
An automatic increase in productivity
A surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire
question.commonError: thinks_higher_wage_always_increases_employment
question.feedback: A binding minimum wage is a price floor. It raises the wage above equilibrium and can create a surplus of labor.

question.q: At $10 per hour, firms hire 1,000 workers and 1,000 workers want jobs. At a $15 minimum wage, firms want 800 workers and 1,200 workers want jobs. What is the labor surplus?
options: 400 workers
200 workers
800 workers
1,200 workers
question.commonError: subtracts_new_employment_from_original_employment_only
question.feedback: The surplus is workers wanting jobs minus workers firms want to hire: 1,200 - 800 = 400.

question.q: A tax is imposed on sellers. Buyers pay a higher price, sellers receive a lower price, and fewer units are sold. What concept ties these effects together?
options: A price floor that creates a labor surplus
A tax wedge that shrinks the market
Substitution bias in the CPI
Discouraged-worker measurement
question.commonError: thinks_tax_only_affects_the_side_legally_paying_it
question.feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, reducing the quantity sold.

question.q: A tax is legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers. What does tax-incidence analysis imply?
options: Buyers always bear 100% of the burden
Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
Sellers always bear 100% of the burden
The tax disappears from the market
question.commonError: confuses_statutory_incidence_with_economic_incidence
question.feedback: Tax incidence depends on market responses, not simply on whether the law says buyers or sellers pay the tax.

question.q: Demand is less elastic than supply. Which side bears more of a per-unit tax?
options: Sellers bear more because buyers can easily leave
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because taxes do not affect prices
Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change
question.commonError: assigns_burden_to_more_elastic_side
question.feedback: The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden because it has fewer good alternatives.

question.q: Gasoline prices rise after a supply disruption. A city responds with a binding price ceiling. What is the most likely result?
options: A surplus because suppliers produce more at the lower price
No effect because ceilings above equilibrium are always binding
A shortage because the legal price is held below the market-clearing price
Higher productivity because gasoline is cheaper
question.commonError: thinks_lower_legal_price_eliminates_scarcity
question.feedback: A binding price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

question.q: A storm reduces supply while demand stays the same. Before any price control, what happens in the market?
options: Equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises
Both price and quantity rise
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
Both price and quantity fall
question.commonError: confuses_supply_decrease_with_quantity_supplied_decrease
question.feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising equilibrium price and lowering equilibrium quantity.

question.q: A binding price ceiling holds the posted price below equilibrium. What happens to the underlying scarcity?
options: Scarcity disappears when prices are legally capped
All consumers get more of the good
Shortages cause waiting, side markets, favoritism, or lower quality
The CPI cannot measure any price change
question.commonError: assumes_price_controls_remove_tradeoffs
question.feedback: A ceiling can hold down the legal money price, but scarcity still appears through shortages and nonprice rationing.

question.q: Assume competitive markets in a small country that takes the world price as given. Trade is unrestricted, transport costs are zero, and domestic demand and supply are unchanged. Demer becomes a net importer of tablets. Relative to its no-trade equilibrium price, where must the world price lie?
options: Below the no-trade price.
Above the no-trade price.
Exactly at the no-trade price.
Its position cannot be inferred from net imports.
question.commonError: reverses_world_price_comparison
question.feedback: Net imports mean domestic demand exceeds domestic supply at the world price. With ordinary demand and supply, that gap occurs below the autarky equilibrium price.

question.q: Assume competitive markets in a small country that takes the world price as given. Trade is unrestricted, transport costs are zero, and domestic demand and supply are unchanged. Estara’s no-trade wool-blanket price is $53, and the world price is $30. Relative to autarky, what happens to domestic production and consumption?
options: Production rises; consumption falls.
Production falls; consumption rises.
Both production and consumption rise.
Both production and consumption fall.
question.commonError: reverses_world_price_comparison
question.feedback: Opening to the lower world price moves domestic producers down supply and consumers down demand: domestic production falls, consumption rises, and imports fill the gap.

question.q: Assume competitive markets in a small country that takes the world price as given. Trade is unrestricted, transport costs are zero, and domestic demand and supply are unchanged. At the world price, Faron’s firms produce 90 batches of tiles and its residents consume 60. What is the trade position?
options: Imports of 30 batches.
Exports of 60 batches.
Imports of 150 batches.
Exports of 30 batches.
question.commonError: reverses_import_export_quantity_gap
question.feedback: Domestic production exceeds domestic consumption by 90 - 60 = 30 batches. Those excess batches are exported.

question.q: Assume competitive markets in a small country that takes the world price as given. Trade is unrestricted, transport costs are zero, and domestic demand and supply are unchanged. Galena exports medical gloves at a world price of $58. What does this imply about its no-trade equilibrium price?
options: It must have been above $58.
It must have equaled $58.
It must have been below $58.
It could have been either above or below $58.
question.commonError: reverses_world_price_comparison
question.feedback: Exports occur when the world price is above autarky: domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. Therefore the no-trade price was below $58.

question.q: Assume competitive markets in two small countries that take the world price as given. Trade is unrestricted, transport costs are zero, and domestic demand and supply are unchanged. Haven’s no-trade garden-tool price is $60 and Ilyria’s is $35. Both face a world price of $44. Which prediction follows?
options: Haven imports and Ilyria exports.
Both countries import.
Haven exports and Ilyria imports.
Both countries export.
question.commonError: reverses_world_price_comparison
question.feedback: Compare each domestic no-trade price with the same world price: $44 < $60 makes Haven an importer; $44 > $35 makes Ilyria an exporter. Comparing the two countries’ prices only to one another is insufficient.

question.q: Assume competitive markets in a small country that takes the world price as given. Trade is unrestricted, transport costs are zero, and domestic demand and supply are unchanged. Juno’s no-trade olive-oil price is $62. The world price first is $38, then rises to $70. Which change in trade position follows?
options: Exporter at both world prices.
Importer at $38, exporter at $70.
Exporter at $38, importer at $70.
Importer at both world prices.
question.commonError: reverses_world_price_comparison
question.feedback: At $38 below autarky, domestic demand exceeds supply and Juno imports. At $70 above autarky, domestic supply exceeds demand and Juno exports. The position must be reassessed when the world price crosses $62.

question.q: Under a voluntary export restraint, foreign firms receive free rights to supply 45 units. Buyers pay $27 while the unchanged world price is $23. Who receives the $180 scarcity rent?
options: The importing government as tariff revenue
Domestic producers in addition to their producer surplus
Domestic consumers as a price rebate
The foreign firms holding the export rights
question.commonError: assigns_quota_rents_to_government_automatically
question.feedback: The price wedge is $4 and 45 units cross the border: $180. The foreign holders of the free rights receive the rents; the importing treasury collects no tariff.

question.q: Use the trade graph. Compared with free trade at a world price of $4, by how many units does the tariff reduce imports?
options: 50 thousand
100 thousand
150 thousand
200 thousand
question.commonError: misreads_trade_graph
question.feedback: Free-trade imports are 250 − 50 = 200 thousand; after the tariff they are 100 thousand.

question.q: Use the trade graph. At the domestic price of $6 created by the quota, how much do domestic producers supply?
options: 75 thousand
175 thousand
150 thousand
200 thousand
question.commonError: misreads_trade_graph
question.feedback: The $6 line intersects supply at Q = 150 thousand.

question.q: A policy analyst says “trade is beneficial, so nobody can be harmed by opening the market.” What is wrong with the statement?
options: Only exporters can gain from trade
Consumer and producer surplus never change with trade
Net gains do not imply every group gains
Trade can never raise total surplus
question.commonError: fails_net_welfare_or_distribution_reasoning
question.feedback: The standard result is aggregate: winners can gain more than losers lose.

question.q: In an importing market, which pair is most consistent with opening to free trade at a lower world price?
options: Both consumer and producer surplus must rise by the same amount
Consumer surplus rises; producer surplus falls
Consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises
Both consumer and producer surplus must fall
question.commonError: fails_net_welfare_or_distribution_reasoning
question.feedback: Lower prices benefit domestic buyers and hurt domestic sellers in an importing market.

question.q: In an exporting market, which pair is most consistent with opening to free trade at a higher world price?
options: Consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises
Consumer surplus rises; producer surplus falls
Both sides lose equally
Consumer surplus and producer surplus cannot change
question.commonError: fails_net_welfare_or_distribution_reasoning
question.feedback: Higher domestic prices hurt buyers but benefit sellers in an exporting market.

question.q: Why does a small-country tariff reduce total surplus even though it creates government revenue?
options: Producer surplus always falls under a tariff
The world price rises by the full tariff
Some lost consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss rather than a transfer
Government revenue is never part of national surplus
question.commonError: treats_tariff_revenue_as_full_welfare_loss
question.feedback: Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.

question.q: A quota allows 30 imported units. The domestic price is $18 and the world price is $14. What is total quota rent?
question.commonError: miscompares_tariff_and_quota

question.q: A tariff and quota produce the same domestic price and import quantity. What determines whether their national welfare effects are identical?
options: Whether producers earn any surplus
Who receives the quota rents
Whether domestic consumers exist
Whether the world price is positive
question.commonError: miscompares_tariff_and_quota
question.feedback: A tariff creates government revenue; a quota can create equivalent rents that may go to domestic or foreign license holders.

question.q: A binding quota is tightened. In the standard import model, which combination is most likely?
options: Domestic price rises and imports fall
Domestic price falls and imports rise
Domestic price and imports both remain fixed
Domestic price falls and exports rise
question.commonError: miscompares_tariff_and_quota
question.feedback: A tighter quantity limit restricts import supply further and pushes the domestic price upward.

question.q: Refer to the quota-rent graph. What is the value of rectangle R?
question.commonError: assigns_quota_rents_to_government_automatically
question.feedback: The domestic-world price gap is $10 across 20 imported units.

question.q: Opening to trade raises consumer surplus by $780 and lowers producer surplus by $460. With no other effects, what is the change in total surplus?
question.commonError: equates_group_loss_with_total_loss
question.feedback: Total surplus rises by $780 − $460 = $320.

question.q: Opening to trade raises producer surplus by $900 and lowers consumer surplus by $540. With no other effects, what is the change in total surplus?
question.commonError: equates_group_loss_with_total_loss
question.feedback: Total surplus rises by $900 − $540 = $360.

question.q: Use the import graph. At a world price of $30, what is consumer surplus?
question.commonError: ignores_consumer_price_and_quantity_changes
question.feedback: At Pw = $30, consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

question.q: Use the import graph. At a world price of $30, what is producer surplus?
question.commonError: ignores_producer_price_and_quantity_changes
question.feedback: At Pw = $30, producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: ½ × 10 × 10 = $50.

question.q: Use the export graph. At a world price of $70, what is consumer surplus?
question.commonError: ignores_consumer_price_and_quantity_changes
question.feedback: At Pw = $70, consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 10 × 10 = $50.

question.q: Use the export graph. At a world price of $70, what is producer surplus?
question.commonError: ignores_producer_price_and_quantity_changes
question.feedback: At Pw = $70, producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

question.q: Total surplus is $900 without trade and $1,300 with free trade. How large are the gains from trade?
question.commonError: assumes_every_person_must_gain
question.feedback: Gains from trade equal the increase in total surplus: $1,300 − $900 = $400.

question.q: Which is a transfer rather than a net loss?
options: A mutually beneficial trade prevented by policy
High-cost production replacing imports
Consumption valued above world cost that no longer occurs
A shift of surplus from consumers to producers
question.commonError: counts_transfers_as_social_losses
question.feedback: A shift of surplus from consumers to producers is a transfer between domestic groups. Prevented mutually beneficial trades and inefficient production are net social losses.

question.q: Why do import gains exceed producer losses in the standard model?
options: Lower-cost sourcing and added consumption create extra surplus
Producer losses are excluded
Imports raise domestic price
Domestic production expands
question.commonError: assumes_every_person_must_gain
question.feedback: With imports, lower-cost foreign supply replaces some higher-cost domestic production and the lower price creates additional consumption gains. Together those gains exceed the producer-surplus loss.

question.q: Why do export gains exceed consumer losses in the standard model?
options: Consumer losses are excluded
Higher-value foreign sales and added production create extra surplus
Exports lower domestic price
Domestic production contracts
question.commonError: assumes_every_person_must_gain
question.feedback: With exports, additional domestic production is sold where the world price exceeds marginal cost, and those production gains exceed the consumer-surplus loss from the higher domestic price.

question.q: Trade raises total surplus but lowers income in one region. What does this show about efficiency and distribution?
options: Trade has no efficiency gain
Equity is identical to total surplus
Efficiency and equity can point to different concerns
Imports must be banned
question.commonError: equates_efficiency_with_fairness
question.feedback: Trade can increase total surplus while imposing concentrated losses on particular regions or groups, so efficiency and equity are separate questions.

question.q: A report finds that gains from trade are large enough to compensate those who lose. What does this establish about compensation?
options: Losers are automatically paid
No one loses
The government must impose a quota
Winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible
question.commonError: equates_efficiency_with_fairness
question.feedback: If total surplus rises, the winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible, but compensation occurs only if an actual transfer or policy is implemented.

question.q: In an import market, domestic price falls from $50 to $30. Which group loses?
options: Domestic producers
Domestic consumers
Foreign consumers only
The government automatically
question.commonError: confuses_total_gain_with_universal_gain
question.feedback: A lower import price reduces the price domestic producers receive and the quantity they sell, so domestic producers lose surplus.

question.q: In an export market, domestic price rises from $50 to $70. Which group loses?
options: Domestic producers
Domestic consumers
Foreign producers only
The government automatically
question.commonError: confuses_total_gain_with_universal_gain
question.feedback: A higher export price raises the price domestic consumers pay and reduces the quantity they buy, so domestic consumers lose surplus.

question.q: Which measure is needed for national gains from trade?
options: Change in import quantity alone
Change in producer revenue alone
Change in total domestic consumer plus producer surplus
Change in the physical trade balance alone
question.commonError: equates_group_loss_with_total_loss
question.feedback: National gains from trade are measured by the change in total domestic surplus: consumer surplus plus producer surplus.

question.q: Why can trade raise total surplus even when some people lose?
options: Individual losses are ignored
Prices do not matter
Only firms count
Total surplus sums gains and losses across groups
question.commonError: assumes_every_person_must_gain
question.feedback: Aggregate gains require total gains to exceed total losses; they do not require every person or group to gain.

question.q: At the world price, domestic buyers demand 50 units and domestic producers supply 10. How is the 40-unit gap filled?
options: Imports
Exports
Tariff revenue
Producer surplus
question.commonError: misreads_world_price_or_trade_gap
question.feedback: At the world price, domestic quantity demanded exceeds domestic quantity supplied by 40 units. That excess demand is filled by imports.

question.q: At the world price, domestic producers supply 50 units and domestic buyers demand 10. What happens to the 40-unit difference?
options: Imports
Exports
Quota rent
Consumer surplus
question.commonError: misreads_world_price_or_trade_gap
question.feedback: At the world price, domestic quantity supplied exceeds domestic quantity demanded by 40 units. That excess supply is exported.

question.q: Refer to the graph. Which quantity combination is correct after the tariff?
options: Domestic firms supply 50 thousand units, buyers demand 250 thousand, and imports are 200 thousand.
Domestic firms supply 200 thousand units, buyers demand 100 thousand, and exports are 100 thousand.
Domestic supply and demand are both 150 thousand units, so there are no imports.
Domestic firms supply 100 thousand units, buyers demand 200 thousand, and imports are 100 thousand.
question.commonError: misreads_trade_graph
question.feedback: At the tariff-inclusive price of $6, supply is 100 thousand and demand is 200 thousand, leaving 100 thousand imports.

question.q: An economy has national saving of $640 billion and domestic investment of $500 billion. What is NCO?
options: $1.14 trillion
$140 billion
−$140 billion
$500 billion
question.commonError: Adds saving and investment instead of subtracting investment from saving to obtain NCO.
question.feedback: From S = I + NCO, NCO = $640 billion − $500 billion = $140 billion.

question.q: A country records NCO of −$60 billion. What must its net exports equal?
options: −$60 billion
$60 billion
An amount that cannot be inferred
question.commonError: Reverses the sign of exports minus imports or of the identity NX=NCO.
question.feedback: NX and NCO are equal in the accounts, so negative NCO implies an equal trade deficit.

question.q: Domestic residents buy $240 billion of foreign assets while foreigners buy $310 billion of domestic assets. What is NCO?
options: $70 billion
$240 billion
$550 billion
−$70 billion
question.commonError: Reverses resident purchases of foreign assets minus foreign purchases of domestic assets.
question.feedback: NCO = $240 billion − $310 billion = −$70 billion, indicating net capital inflow.

question.q: A household buys a $2,000 imported computer with no other economic change. What does GDP accounting do?
options: Investment rises by $2,000 and GDP rises by $2,000
Net exports rise by $2,000 while consumption is unchanged
Consumption rises by $2,000 and imports rise by $2,000, leaving GDP unchanged
GDP falls by $2,000 because imports are subtracted
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Investment rises by $2,000 and GDP rises by $2,000” in this international transactions and identities task.
question.feedback: The purchase enters consumption, while the import subtraction removes the foreign-produced computer from domestic GDP.

question.q: If national saving is less than domestic investment, which combination is consistent with the identities?
options: Zero net capital outflow and a trade deficit
Negative net capital outflow and a trade deficit
Positive net capital outflow and a trade surplus
Positive net capital outflow and balanced trade
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Zero NCO and a trade deficit” in this international transactions and identities task.
question.feedback: S − I equals NCO, so S below I makes NCO negative; NX = NCO makes net exports negative as well.

question.q: A country has a $90 billion trade surplus and domestic investment of $260 billion. What national saving is consistent with the accounts?
options: $170 billion
$260 billion
$440 billion
$350 billion
question.commonError: Subtracts a trade surplus from investment instead of using national saving = investment + net exports.
question.feedback: NX = NCO = $90 billion, and S = I + NCO = $260 billion + $90 billion = $350 billion.

question.q: National saving is $300 billion and investment is $360 billion. Which external balance follows?
options: Net capital outflow and net exports are $60 billion
Net capital outflow is −$60 billion and net exports is $60 billion
Both balances are $660 billion
Net capital outflow and net exports are −$60 billion
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “NCO is −$60 billion and NX is $60 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
question.feedback: S − I = −$60 billion, and the identity makes both NCO and NX equal to that amount.

question.q: A domestic airline buys a newly produced aircraft from France. How does the purchase enter domestic GDP accounting?
options: It enters consumption but not imports
It directly reduces domestic output
It raises investment and imports by the same amount
It lowers investment and raises exports
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It enters consumption but not imports” in this international transactions and identities task.
question.feedback: The aircraft is business investment, but its foreign production is removed through the import term.

question.q: Trade is balanced. Under the standard open-economy accounting identities, what must be true of net capital outflow?
options: Net capital outflow equals domestic investment
Net capital outflow equals zero
Net capital outflow is positive
Net capital outflow is negative
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “NCO equals domestic investment” in this international transactions and identities task.
question.feedback: Balanced trade means NX = 0, and NX = NCO requires NCO = 0.

question.q: A student computes net exports as imports minus exports. Which correction fixes the sign?
options: Use saving plus investment
Subtract imports from exports
Add imports to exports
Subtract exports from imports
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Use saving plus investment” in this international transactions and identities task.
question.feedback: Net exports are X − M, so a larger import value makes NX smaller, not larger.

question.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
question.q: In a competitive labor market, why can a minimum wage above equilibrium create unemployment?
options: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity of labor demanded
Quantity of labor demanded exceeds quantity supplied
All workers leave the labor force
Firms hire more low-skill workers
question.feedback: A wage floor above equilibrium creates a surplus of labor.

question.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
question.q: How can unemployment insurance improve worker outcomes even if it lengthens unemployment spells?
options: It supports income while workers seek better matches
It eliminates structural mismatch immediately
It forces all firms to hire
It lowers the labor force to zero
question.feedback: Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.

question.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
question.q: A union negotiates wages above the competitive equilibrium. What is the likely effect in that labor market?
options: More workers want jobs than firms want to hire
Firms hire every worker who wants a job
Labor demand shifts to infinity
The unemployment rate is impossible to calculate
question.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor in that market.

question.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
question.q: According to efficiency-wage theory, why might a firm choose to pay wages above the market-clearing level?
options: Improve effort, retention, or worker quality
Guarantee zero unemployment
Eliminate all inflation
Make GDP equal CPI
question.feedback: Efficiency wages can make workers more productive or reduce costly turnover.

question.q: How do a union wage and an efficiency wage differ most directly?
options: A union wage is bargained collectively; an efficiency wage is voluntarily chosen by the firm
A union wage is always below equilibrium; an efficiency wage is always legally mandated
A union wage affects only prices; an efficiency wage affects only GDP accounting
They are identical policies imposed by government in every labor market
question.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
question.feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

question.q: A state improves job-search assistance while leaving unemployment benefits unchanged. Which outcome is most directly targeted?
options: Higher cyclical unemployment through weaker aggregate demand
A larger labor surplus from a binding minimum wage
A permanent increase in structural mismatch
Shorter frictional unemployment spells through faster matching
question.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
question.feedback: Job-search assistance improves worker-firm matching, so it can shorten normal search spells and reduce frictional unemployment.

question.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
question.q: A union contract raises wages above the competitive equilibrium. Which workers are most likely hurt?
options: Workers no longer hired at the higher union wage
All union workers who keep their jobs
Only retired workers
Only consumers of imported goods
question.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can reduce labor demanded, hurting workers who cannot get hired.

question.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
question.q: A union wage raises pay for employed members but reduces hiring by firms. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
options: Insiders gain while some outsiders lose job opportunities
All workers must benefit equally
The unemployment rate must fall to zero
The policy only affects CPI
question.feedback: Union wage gains can help employed members but reduce opportunities for workers not hired.

question.q: Above-market wages improve effort among 290 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
options: Whether retained employees should count as unemployed when wages exceed equilibrium.
Whether higher-paid workers should be excluded from the unemployment-rate denominator.
Whether identical technology alone guarantees that the effects offset.
Whether higher productivity and lower turnover outweigh higher labor costs and reduced hiring.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium” in this labor market institutions task.
question.feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

question.q: A competitive labor market initially clears at $15 with a legal minimum of $12. Labor demand then falls so that the new market-clearing wage would be $10. The minimum stays $12; at that wage firms demand 90 workers and 120 offer labor. What changes under the competitive wage-floor model?
options: The minimum stays nonbinding; employment is 120 and there is no labor surplus
The minimum changes from binding to nonbinding; employment is 90 and the labor surplus is 30
The minimum changes from nonbinding to binding; employment is 90 and the labor surplus is 30
The minimum changes from nonbinding to binding; employment is 120 and the labor surplus is 90
question.commonError: Keeps the initial nonbinding diagnosis after the equilibrium wage changes.
question.feedback: Initially $12 is below equilibrium and does not bind. After equilibrium falls to $10, the unchanged $12 floor binds. Firms hire the 90 workers demanded at that wage; 120−90=30 workers are the excess supply of labor.

question.q: A firm claims higher pay is profitable because it cuts turnover costs. What comparison tests that claim rather than assuming any wage premium pays for itself?
options: Compare posted wages across firms alone; a higher wage establishes higher profit.
Compare added wage expense with reduced turnover costs and any productivity gain.
Compare the wage with the legal minimum alone; retention costs cannot affect profit.
Compare headcounts alone; wage expense and worker productivity do not affect profit.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Compare the wage with the legal minimum alone; retention costs cannot affect profit.
question.feedback: The efficiency-wage claim is behavioral, not an accounting identity. The firm must weigh the extra wage bill against lower hiring/training costs from quits and any productivity benefit; a premium alone does not prove profitability.

question.commonError: Treats all willing workers as employed despite firms’ lower demand at the efficiency wage.
question.q: A labor market would clear at $18. Firms instead maintain a $22 efficiency wage to reduce costly quits. At $22, 120 workers offer labor and firms want to hire 90. In this simple model, what employment and labor surplus result while firms maintain that wage?
options: 120 employed; no workers in excess supply
90 employed; no workers in excess supply
90 employed; 30 workers in excess supply
120 employed; 30 workers in excess supply
question.feedback: At the maintained wage, firms hire the 90 workers demanded. Labor supplied exceeds labor demanded by 120−90=30. The turnover incentive can explain maintaining the high wage without eliminating the associated excess supply.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: Why can GDP rise while well-being does not clearly improve?
options: GDP fails to record any final goods sold in legal markets
Every production increase automatically reduces leisure and environmental quality
Higher GDP guarantees equal gains for households across the income distribution
GDP may ignore pollution, leisure loss, and unequal distribution
question.feedback: GDP is useful, but it misses important quality-of-life factors.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: Which statement is the strongest evaluation of GDP as a welfare measure?
options: GDP is complete whenever nominal prices remain unchanged
GDP measures only leisure, safety, and environmental quality
GDP is useful but misses nonmarket quality-of-life factors
GDP is useless because it excludes all current market production
question.feedback: GDP is useful but incomplete as a measure of well-being.

question.q: A software update greatly improves usefulness while its market price is unchanged. What difficulty can arise?
options: GDP may not fully capture the quality improvement
Real GDP must fall because price is unchanged
The update counts only as a transfer
GDP already measures every consumer benefit exactly
question.commonError: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
question.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

question.q: A factory expands output while causing more pollution. What is the careful conclusion?
options: GDP and welfare must rise by the same percentage
Welfare must fall because production increased
Pollution is subtracted automatically from nominal GDP
GDP rises, while the net welfare effect remains uncertain
question.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
question.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

question.q: A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals. What can happen?
options: GDP is unchanged because meals are identical
Real output must double
GDP rises because more activity is purchased in markets
GDP falls because restaurant work is intermediate
question.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
question.feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

question.q: Production is unchanged, but workplace injuries fall after a safety improvement. What does GDP alone miss?
options: A transfer counted in government purchases
A welfare gain from greater safety
A decline in all final output
A required increase in imports
question.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
question.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: A country cuts pollution regulations, output rises, but air quality worsens and illness increases. What does this show about GDP?
options: GDP must fall whenever pollution or illness increases after production
GDP automatically subtracts every environmental and health cost from output
Higher measured production proves that every resident became better off
GDP may rise even when broader well-being does not clearly improve
question.feedback: GDP counts production but does not fully capture environmental damage or health costs.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: Two countries have equal GDP per person, but one has more leisure, cleaner air, and lower crime. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: GDP per person misses some important parts of well-being
The cleaner country must have lower real GDP
GDP perfectly ranks living standards
Crime and leisure are already fully included in GDP
question.feedback: GDP per person is useful but incomplete because it misses non-market quality-of-life factors.

question.q: Two countries have the same real GDP per person, but one has longer life expectancy, safer streets, and cleaner water. What follows?
options: Equal measured output does not imply equal well-being
Both countries must have equal welfare
The safer country must have lower real GDP
Health and safety are fully included in the GDP average
question.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
question.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: Country A has higher GDP per person than Country B, but Country B has cleaner air, more leisure, and longer life expectancy. What should an economist conclude?
options: GDP per person is useful but incomplete for comparing well-being
Country A must have higher well-being in every respect
Country B must have higher GDP once adjusted correctly
GDP ignores all market output
question.feedback: GDP per person helps compare material output but misses some important well-being measures.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding activity raises GDP. Why is this not necessarily an improvement in well-being?
options: GDP excludes all construction completed after a natural disaster
Destroyed homes are recorded as current business investment spending
Rebuilding makes the original household losses irrelevant to welfare
GDP counts rebuilding, not the destruction’s welfare loss
question.feedback: GDP can rise from rebuilding even though society is replacing destroyed assets.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: A country increases GDP by requiring longer work hours and reducing vacation time. What GDP limitation does this expose?
options: GDP omits lost leisure
GDP excludes wages
GDP cannot count final goods
GDP only counts imports
question.feedback: GDP measures production but does not fully value leisure.

question.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
question.q: A country has GDP of $2T and population of 20M. Another has GDP of $4T and population of 80M. Which has higher GDP per person?
options: The first country, with $100,000 per person versus $50,000
The second country, because total GDP is larger
They are equal because both are measured in trillions
It cannot be determined without imports
question.feedback: GDP per person is $2T/20M = $100,000 and $4T/80M = $50,000.

question.q: Real GDP per person rises 21% while leisure falls and air quality deteriorates. What can be concluded about output per person and well-being?
options: Output per person increased, but the net welfare change requires valuing the omitted losses
Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage
Output per person decreased because environmental damage is automatically deducted from GDP
Output per person is unknown because GDP cannot be measured when leisure changes
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage” in this limits of gdp task.
question.feedback: Real GDP per person measures average production, not a complete welfare index. Leisure and environmental quality can offset some or all benefits; their values are not supplied.

question.q: Two countries have the same real GDP per person of $21,200. One has greater inequality and poorer health. What can be concluded about output and well-being?
options: Every resident has the same income, so the health differences cannot affect well-being.
The less equal country must have lower real GDP per person despite the stated figures.
The averages reveal nothing about either output or well-being.
Average measured output is equal, but inequality and health may imply different levels of well-being.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Every resident has equal income; different health outcomes therefore cannot change the ranking” in this limits of gdp task.
question.feedback: Equal GDP per person establishes equality of average measured production, not individual incomes or a complete welfare ranking. Distribution and health are separate evidence.

question.q: A storm destroys existing homes. Rebuilding produces $23 million of current construction, while families lose housing services during repairs. Which GDP-versus-welfare comparison is correct?
options: Rebuilding is excluded because it replaces old assets; neither GDP nor welfare changes
Destruction is automatically subtracted from GDP by the replacement value; GDP equals the net welfare effect
Rebuilding adds to current GDP; loss of existing wealth and services prevents treating it as a net welfare gain
Destruction and rebuilding both add to current GDP; their sum measures the welfare gain
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Rebuilding is excluded because it replaces old assets; neither GDP nor welfare changes” in this limits of gdp task.
question.feedback: Current reconstruction is production. Destruction of existing assets is a wealth loss, not automatically a negative final purchase; lost services also matter for welfare.

question.feedback: The central bank fixes the money supply in this model, so money supply is vertical.

options: D
A
E
G
question.commonError: Tracking only money demand or money supply.
question.feedback: MD2 and MS2 intersect at point d.

options: e
d
g
a

question.feedback: MD1 and MS1 intersect at point e.

question.q: Compare original point B with simultaneous-shift point C. What happens to quantity of money and the nominal interest rate?
options: Quantity rises from 75 to 100 while the interest rate falls from 3 percent to 1 percent
Quantity stays at 75 while the interest rate rises from 3 percent to 6 percent
Quantity rises from 75 to 100 while the interest rate rises from 3 percent to 4 percent
Quantity falls from 100 to 75 while the interest rate falls from 4 percent to 3 percent
question.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
question.feedback: The increase in money supply raises equilibrium quantity, while the simultaneous increase in money demand is strong enough to leave the interest rate one point higher than at B.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

question.q: A rise in real income shifts money demand right. If the Fed holds money supply fixed, what happens next?
options: Interest rates rise.
Interest rates fall.
Money supply rises automatically.
Investment rises because borrowing is cheaper.
question.commonError: thinking higher income lowers transaction demand for money
question.feedback: Higher income increases money demand. With fixed money supply, the interest rate rises.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

question.q: Transaction demand for money increases at every rate in an economy with money supply 100. The central bank wants to hold the interest rate fixed in the standard liquidity-preference model. Which response and curve distinction are correct?
options: Leave supply fixed because higher demand is only movement along the original curve
Shift money demand back by redefining the unchanged nominal supply as a demand curve
Raise money supply enough to meet the added demand at that rate; the demand curve still shifted
Reduce money supply to match the higher demand; the interest rate then stays fixed
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Leave supply fixed because higher demand is only movement along the original curve” in this liquidity preference and money market task.
question.feedback: At the old rate, higher money demand creates excess demand. Increasing supply to meet it can keep the rate unchanged; a fixed observed rate does not prove no demand shift.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

question.q: Real income rises and the price level falls while nominal money supply is fixed. Interest rates stay unchanged. A report says neither change affected money demand. Which correction follows?
options: Both effects reduced demand; an unchanged rate proves the supply curve slopes downward.
Opposing demand effects can offset; an unchanged rate does not prove each effect was zero.
Both effects must be zero; an unchanged rate identifies each separate demand response.
Nominal supply must have risen; offsetting money-demand effects are impossible.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Both effects must be zero; an unchanged rate identifies each separate demand response.
question.feedback: Income and prices affect nominal money demand in opposing directions here. Their effects may balance at the unchanged rate even though each has a nonzero effect; one observed equilibrium does not identify both separate contributions.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

question.q: At the current interest rate, desired money holdings exceed fixed supply by 120. Which portfolio adjustment and rate direction restore equilibrium in the standard model?
options: People try to sell bonds for money, lowering bond prices and raising the interest rate
People try to buy bonds with unwanted money, raising bond prices and lowering the interest rate
The central bank must create money automatically; the interest rate cannot adjust
Bond prices and interest rates rise together until money demand is unchanged
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “People try to buy bonds with unwanted money, raising bond prices and lowering the interest rate” in this liquidity preference and money market task.
question.feedback: Excess money demand motivates asset sales. Lower bond prices correspond to higher yields, which reduce money demand toward fixed supply. Individual attempts cannot change aggregate money supply by themselves.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

question.q: Income rises and money demand increases, with money supply fixed. If investment is interest-sensitive, what follow-on pressure results?
options: Higher interest raises investment
Investment is unchanged by assumption whenever income changes
Higher interest reduces investment
Lower interest raises investment
question.feedback: Greater money demand raises the equilibrium rate; the higher financing cost reduces interest-sensitive investment.
question.commonError: Reverses the interest-rate-to-investment link.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

question.commonError: Confuses demand for money with demand for interest-bearing bonds.
question.q: Money demand rises at fixed supply. A firm borrows at the resulting market interest rate. Relative to before the shift, what happens to its financing cost?
options: It falls as the equilibrium interest rate rises
It falls because demand for money means demand for bonds rises
It stays fixed because money demand cannot affect rates
It rises as the equilibrium interest rate rises
question.feedback: With a fixed quantity of money, higher demand raises its opportunity cost, the interest rate faced by borrowers.

question.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
question.q: Country A grows at 1% per year and Country B grows at 4% per year. What is the most likely long-run result?
options: The income gap can become much larger over time
Both countries must end with the same income
Country A must always become richer
Growth rates do not affect living standards
question.feedback: Small growth-rate differences compound into large long-run income differences.

question.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
question.q: Which comparison best captures differences in living standards across countries?
options: Real GDP per person
Nominal interest rates only
The number of banks
The unemployment rate alone
question.feedback: Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards.

question.q: A country’s real GDP grows by 4% while its population grows by 1%. Approximately how much does real GDP per person grow?
options: 1 percent.
4 percent.
3 percent.
5 percent.
question.commonError: Using total GDP growth without adjusting for population.
question.feedback: Approximate real GDP per person growth is 4% − 1% = 3%.

question.q: A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged. What is the most careful interpretation?
options: Productivity must rise because total output increased after workers supplied more hours.
Living standards must fall because any increase in work hours necessarily reduces output.
Real GDP per person cannot change when total hours worked change but output per hour does not.
Real GDP may rise, but productivity is unchanged and lost leisure can limit the welfare gain.
question.commonError: Equating more total labor input with higher productivity and complete welfare improvement.
question.feedback: More hours can raise output without raising output per hour, and GDP does not fully value lost leisure.

question.q: Why can a country with lower initial income eventually catch a richer country?
options: A persistently higher growth rate can compound enough to close the initial income gap.
Lower initial income automatically guarantees convergence even without faster growth.
Nominal GDP always grows faster in poorer countries because their prices are lower.
Population growth alone raises real output per person without any productivity change.
question.commonError: Assuming starting income permanently fixes a country’s relative position.
question.feedback: Sustained differences in growth rates compound over time and can outweigh an initial income gap.

question.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
question.q: Which country likely has the higher living standard, holding other quality-of-life factors aside?
options: Country A with real GDP of $1T and population of 10M
Country B with real GDP of $2T and population of 80M
Country C with nominal GDP of $3T but unknown prices
Country D with higher inflation
question.feedback: Country A has real GDP per person of $100,000; Country B has $25,000.

question.q: A country’s real GDP per person rises 3 percent, but most of the gain goes to a small share of households. What can be concluded?
options: Every household’s real income must have risen by exactly 3 percent.
Real GDP per person must have fallen because the distribution changed.
Average output per person rose, but the typical household may have gained less.
The price level must have increased by the same 3 percent.
question.commonError: Treating an average as a description of every household’s experience.
question.feedback: Real GDP per person is an average and does not reveal how income or output gains are distributed.

question.q: A country’s real GDP grows 3 percent while its population grows 4 percent. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
options: It rises about 7 percent.
It rises about 1 percent.
It remains unchanged.
It falls about 1 percent.
question.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth instead of subtracting it.
question.feedback: Approximate per-person growth equals real GDP growth minus population growth: 3% − 4% = −1%.

question.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
question.q: A country grows real GDP by 6% while population grows by 2%. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
options: It rises by about 4%
It rises by 8%
It falls by 4%
It is unchanged
question.feedback: Real GDP per person grows roughly by real GDP growth minus population growth, or about 4%.

question.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
question.q: A country with rapid population growth sees total real GDP rise but real GDP per person stay flat. What is the best interpretation?
options: Output is rising, but not faster than population
Living standards must be rising quickly
Productivity must have doubled
Inflation explains all growth
question.feedback: Living standards are better captured by output per person, not total output alone.

question.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
question.q: Using the Rule of 70, Country X growing at 3.5% doubles in about how many years, and Country Y growing at 1.75% doubles in about how many years?
options: 20 years and 40 years
10 years and 20 years
35 years and 70 years
40 years and 20 years

question.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
question.q: If real GDP per person rises from $20,000 to $26,000, what is the percentage increase?

question.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
question.q: Using the Rule of 70, about how long does income take to double if it grows by 5% each year?
options: 7 years
14 years
35 years
70 years
question.feedback: 70 divided by 5 equals about 14 years.

question.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
question.q: Using the Rule of 70, about how long does income take to double if it grows by 1% each year?
options: 1 year
10 years
35 years
70 years
question.feedback: 70 divided by 1 equals about 70 years.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%” in this living standards and growth task.
question.q: Real GDP is initially $150 billion. It grows 6%, while population grows 8%. Which statement reconciles aggregate growth and average output?
options: Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%
Per-person output rises 14% because output and population growth add
Aggregate output falls because population growth exceeds GDP growth
Aggregate real output rises, but real GDP per person falls about 1.9%
question.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.06/1.08−1≈−1.85%. A larger economy can have lower average output if population grows faster.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A's higher initial level means its percentage growth must exceed B's” in this living standards and growth task.
question.q: Country A starts with real GDP per person of $40,160 and grows by 2% annually. Country B starts at half that level and grows by 7%. Using the Rule of 70, why is it incorrect to conclude that B catches A in ten years?
options: B doubles in ten years; A's starting level establishes catch-up then.
A doubles in ten years; B doubles in thirty-five, preventing catch-up.
B doubles in ten years; A also grows, delaying catch-up.
B doubles in five years; doubling its growth rate halves catch-up time.
question.feedback: 70/7≈10 years doubles B's starting level; 70/2≈35 years doubles A's. A is a moving target, so B reaching A's initial level is not the same as reaching A's contemporaneous level.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Use equal totals as proof of equal average living standards” in this living standards and growth task.
question.q: Two countries each report $170 billion GDP. One has twice the population and a 20% higher price level. The GDP figures are nominal. Which comparison is justified before a living-standard ranking?
options: Use equal nominal totals to infer equal real output per person.
Adjust for prices and population before comparing real output per person.
Adjust for population alone; nominal price differences do not affect the comparison.
Adjust for prices alone; population differences do not affect per-person output.
question.feedback: A nominal aggregate combines scale and prices. A per-person real comparison must remove both; even real GDP per person remains incomplete welfare evidence.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Every person's real income rises 10% because the average rises 10%” in this living standards and growth task.
question.q: Real GDP per person rises from $180 to $198, but gains accrue mainly to a small group. Which inference distinguishes an average from individual outcomes?
options: Average real output rises 10%; the typical person's gain requires distributional evidence
Every person's real income rises 10% because the average rises 10%
No real output grew because not everyone gained equally
Average real output falls if the largest gains go to high-income people
question.feedback: The aggregate per-capita ratio rises 10%, but that does not identify every person's income or the median. Distribution is additional evidence, not part of the arithmetic average.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both policies create identical future paths because each mentions a 4% change” in this living standards and growth task.
question.q: A country with initial real GDP per person $190 sustains 4% growth instead of 2%. Another policy raises the level once by 4% but leaves later growth at 2%. Which comparison recognizes the long-run distinction?
options: Sustained growth changes only the level; the level increase shortens subsequent doubling time.
Both shorten subsequent doubling time equally; each policy specifies the same 4% figure.
Neither changes the future path; percentage changes affect nominal measures rather than output.
Sustained growth compounds faster; the level increase leaves subsequent doubling time unchanged.
question.feedback: A growth-rate change repeatedly changes the path, whereas a one-time level gain shifts the starting point. Under Rule of 70, sustained 4% growth implies roughly 17.5-year doubling versus 35 at 2%.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Per-person output rises 14% because output and population growth add” in this living standards and growth task.
question.q: Real GDP is initially $200 billion. It grows 6%, while population grows 8%. Which statement reconciles aggregate growth and average output?
options: Per-person output rises 14% because output and population growth add
Aggregate output falls because population growth exceeds GDP growth
Aggregate real output rises, but real GDP per person falls about 1.9%
Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%
question.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.06/1.08−1≈−1.85%. A larger economy can have lower average output if population grows faster.

question.q: Two countries each report $120 billion GDP. One has twice the population and a 20% higher price level. The GDP figures are nominal. Which comparison is justified before a living-standard ranking?
options: Use equal nominal totals to infer equal real output per person.
Adjust for prices and population before comparing real output per person.
Adjust for population alone; nominal price differences do not affect the comparison.
Adjust for prices alone; population differences do not affect per-person output.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Use equal totals as proof of equal average living standards” in this living standards and growth task.
question.feedback: A nominal aggregate combines scale and prices. A per-person real comparison must remove both; even real GDP per person remains incomplete welfare evidence.

question.commonError: Holds per-person GDP fixed when population changes.
question.q: Real GDP is $3 trillion and population 100 million. If population rises to 120 million with real GDP unchanged, what is new real GDP per person?
question.feedback: Divide 3 trillion by 120 million to get 25,000. More people share unchanged real output.

question.commonError: Makes doubling time proportional to the growth rate.
question.q: Using the Rule of 70, compare a 2% annual growth rate with 4%. What happens to approximate doubling time?
options: It rises from 17.5 to 35 years
It falls from 70 to 35 years
It stays 35 years because both rates are positive
It falls from 35 to 17.5 years
question.feedback: 70/2=35; 70/4=17.5. Doubling the growth rate halves approximate doubling time.

question.q: In the loanable-funds model, why does firms' desired investment form the demand for funds?
options: Investment projects create demand for finance, and higher real borrowing costs make fewer projects worthwhile.
Households supply funds for firms, so investment is the supply schedule for loanable funds.
The central bank fixes investment at each rate, so desired borrowing is independent of financing costs.
Higher real borrowing costs make every investment project more profitable, increasing desired borrowing.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “S0, the upward-sloping red curve” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Firms seek finance for investment projects. A higher real interest rate raises financing costs, making fewer projects worthwhile and reducing desired borrowing along the investment-demand schedule.

question.q: Refer to the graph above. What does point A establish about planned saving and investment?
options: Saving exceeds investment by 140
Investment exceeds saving by 8 percent
Both quantities are zero at equilibrium
Their aggregate quantities are equal at 140
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Saving exceeds investment by 140” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Point A is the S0-D0 intersection, so the two planned quantities are equal at 140 units.
