question.q: Which variable acts as the price coordinating saving and investment in the loanable-funds market?
options: The quantity of loanable funds.
The real interest rate.
The government budget balance.
The stock of productive capital.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal axis” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: The real interest rate is the return to supplying funds and the real cost of borrowing. Changes in that price affect saving supplied and investment demanded.

question.q: What creates demand in the loanable-funds market?
options: Desired investment spending
Current household consumption
The stock of federal debt
Net tax revenue alone
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Current household consumption” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Firms and households demand funds to finance investment projects whose expected returns justify borrowing.

question.q: What adjustment is expected when the real interest rate is above equilibrium?
options: Excess supply puts downward pressure on the rate
Excess demand puts upward pressure on the rate
Investment demand shifts right automatically
Public saving becomes negative
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Excess demand puts upward pressure on the rate” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Above equilibrium, savers offer more funds than investors want, creating downward pressure on the real interest rate.

question.q: A lower real interest rate by itself causes what change in investment?
options: A rightward shift of investment demand
A movement down along investment demand
A leftward shift of the supply of loanable funds
A movement up along the supply of loanable funds
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A rightward shift of investment demand” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: A rate change changes the quantity of investment demanded along the existing curve; it does not shift that curve.

question.q: New technology raises expected returns on capital at every real interest rate. What changes?
options: There is only movement along investment demand
The supply of loanable funds shifts left
The quantity axis shifts
Investment demand shifts right
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “There is only movement along investment demand” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Higher project profitability is a non-interest determinant of investment demand, so the entire curve shifts right.

question.q: Businesses become pessimistic about future sales. What is the correct diagrammatic treatment?
options: Investment demand moves downward along itself
The supply of loanable funds shifts right
Investment demand shifts left
The supply of loanable funds moves upward along itself
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Investment demand moves downward along itself” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Weaker expected sales reduce project profitability at each real rate, shifting investment demand left.

question.q: The quantity of saving rises after the rate increases, with preferences unchanged. What occurred?
options: A shift in the supply of loanable funds
An shift in the demand for loanable funds
Movement along the saving curve
A change in public saving
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A saving-supply shift” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: With no non-interest determinant changing, the rate increase explains a larger quantity supplied along the same curve.

question.q: Refer to the graph above. At a real interest rate above 8 percent, which comparison does the graph imply?
options: Investment demanded exceeds saving supplied
Saving supplied exceeds investment demanded
Saving and investment remain equal
Both curves shift to the right
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Investment demanded exceeds saving supplied” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Above A, the upward S0 curve lies to the right of D0, so the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.

question.q: The real interest rate rises from 8% to 10% along unchanged curves for the supply of loanable funds and investment demand. How do the quantities supplied and demanded respond?
options: Saving supplied rises and investment demanded falls.
Saving supplied falls and investment demanded rises.
Both quantities rise because the same interest rate applies to savers and borrowers.
Both schedules shift right because the real interest rate changes.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Less saving supplied and more investment demanded” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: A higher real rate encourages saving and makes fewer investment projects worthwhile. These are movements along the fixed schedules, not shifts of the schedules themselves.

question.q: The real interest rate is above equilibrium with loanable-funds curves unchanged. Which adjustment moves the market back toward equilibrium?
options: Excess investment demand pushes the rate up, increasing the imbalance
Excess saving pushes the rate down toward equilibrium
The supply of loanable funds shifts left until all planned investment disappears
Investment demand shifts right because the high rate makes more projects profitable
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Excess investment demand pushes the rate up, increasing the imbalance” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Above equilibrium, the quantity of funds supplied exceeds the quantity demanded. Downward pressure on the rate causes movements along both curves until planned saving and investment are equal.

question.q: A student labels desired investment as the supply of loanable funds. What correction is needed?
options: Investment is supply; consumption is demand
Both investment and saving are demand
Both investment and saving are supply
Investment is demand; national saving is supply
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Investment is supply; consumption is demand” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Borrowers demand funds to finance desired investment, while national saving provides the funds supplied.

question.q: If only the real interest rate rises, does the saving curve shift?
options: No, quantity saved rises along the curve
Yes, the supply of loanable funds shifts right
Yes, the supply of loanable funds shifts left
No, quantity saved must fall
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Yes, saving supply shifts right” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: A change in the market price causes movement along the saving curve, not a shift.

question.q: Households save more at each interest rate. In the loanable-funds market, with investment demand unchanged, which equilibrium change follows?
options: Supply shifts right, lowering interest and raising investment
Demand shifts right, raising interest and investment
Supply shifts left, raising interest and lowering investment
Demand shifts left, lowering interest and investment
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Demand shifts right, raising interest and investment” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
question.feedback: Saving supplies loanable funds. A rightward supply shift lowers their price (interest) and raises the equilibrium quantity invested.

question.q: Refer to the graph above. How does the equilibrium change from A to B?
options: The rate rises and quantity falls
Both rate and quantity rise
Both rate and quantity fall
The rate falls and quantity rises
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The rate rises and quantity falls” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: The graph moves from A (80, 8 percent) to B (120, 6 percent).

options: 8 percent

7 percent
10 percent
question.commonError: Uses a rate at a different location instead of reading the specified equilibrium intersection.
question.feedback: The left-shifted S1 curve intersects D0 at B on the 8 percent level.

options: Households become less willing to save

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real interest rate falls by itself” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: Less saving at every rate shifts the supply curve left, matching S0 to S1.

question.q: A tax incentive encourages households to save more for retirement. What happens in the market for loanable funds?
options: Supply shifts left, raising the rate and lowering quantity
Demand shifts right, raising both outcomes
Demand shifts left, lowering both outcomes
Supply shifts right, lowering the rate and raising quantity
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Supply shifts left, raising the rate and lowering quantity” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: Greater saving increases supply at each rate; the new equilibrium has a lower real rate and more funds.

question.q: A rise in the supply of loanable funds lowers the equilibrium real rate. How does investment respond?
options: Investment demand shifts left
Investment rises along its demand curve
Investment demand shifts right
Investment falls along demand
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Investment demand shifts left” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: The saving shock shifts supply; the lower rate increases the quantity of investment demanded along unchanged demand.

question.q: The market begins at A on D0 and S0. Investment demand shifts to D1 while S0 stays fixed. How does equilibrium change, and what induces savers to provide the new quantity?
options: The rate rises from 5% to 6% and quantity rises from 80 to 100; the higher return induces movement along S0.
The rate rises from 5% to 7% and quantity rises from 80 to 120 because the rate increase shifts S0 right.
The rate rises from 5% to 7% and quantity rises from 80 to 120; the higher return induces movement along S0.
Quantity rises from 80 to 120 while the rate falls, because stronger investment demand reduces borrowing costs.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both the rate and quantity fall” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: The graph shows A at 80/5 and B at 120/7. Investment demand shifts right, and the higher real rate encourages additional saving along the unchanged supply schedule.

It remains at 6%.
It falls below 6%.
It cannot be determined from the graph.

question.q: The supply of loanable funds and investment demand both increase. What must happen to equilibrium quantity?
options: It falls
It remains fixed
Its direction is always ambiguous
It rises
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It falls” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: Both shifts raise the equilibrium quantity; their competing effects make the real-rate direction depend on relative sizes.

question.q: The supply of loanable funds falls while investment demand rises. What happens to the equilibrium real interest rate?
options: It falls
It remains unchanged
It rises
It cannot be determined
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It falls” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: Both the leftward supply shift and the rightward demand shift put upward pressure on the equilibrium real interest rate, while their quantity effects oppose one another.

question.q: Which event could explain the movement from A to B with the other determinants unchanged?
options: A deterioration in the government budget lowers national saving at each real interest rate.
An improvement in the government budget raises national saving at each real interest rate.
An investment tax credit raises desired investment at each real interest rate.
Reduced expected project profitability lowers desired investment at each real interest rate.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Households become more willing to save at every real rate” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: The graph shows saving supply moving right from S0 to S1 while D0 stays fixed. A budget improvement can increase public and national saving. Investment incentives instead change demand for funds.

options: Investment demand shifts right
Investment demand shifts left
The supply of loanable funds shifts left
The supply of loanable funds shifts right
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Investment demand shifts right” in this loanable funds shifts task.
question.feedback: National saving is the supply of loanable funds, so an increase shifts that curve right.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output

question.q: A hurricane destroys factories and transport infrastructure. Which long-run effect is most likely?
options: Long-run aggregate supply shifts left because productive capacity falls.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because inputs are scarcer.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts right because rebuilding spending rises.
Only aggregate demand shifts right.
question.commonError: Focusing on reconstruction spending while ignoring lost capacity.
question.feedback: Destroyed capital reduces the economy’s potential output.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output

question.q: A disaster destroys capital and reduces potential output from its initial level of 30. Rebuilding raises aggregate demand. Why does the extra spending not establish that productive capacity has recovered?
options: Higher aggregate demand immediately restores all the capital lost in the disaster.
Capital destruction affects only demand, leaving productive capacity unchanged.
The two shocks must exactly offset their effects on both prices and output.
Demand can raise short-run output while the lost capital still limits productive capacity.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Higher AD shifts LRAS right immediately and must more than reverse the capital loss” in this long run aggregate supply and potential output task.
question.feedback: Demand and productive capacity are different schedules. Spending can use or strain remaining resources; restoration of capital or productivity requires separate evidence.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output

question.q: Technology raises potential output from 100 to 110. If actual output stays 100, what output gap exists relative to the new long-run aggregate supply?
options: A 110-unit recessionary gap
A 10-unit recessionary gap
A 10-unit inflationary gap
No gap because actual output did not change
question.feedback: The benchmark rose:actual 100−potential 110=−10. A capacity gain can open a shortfall if demand does not keep pace.
question.commonError: Uses the old potential-output benchmark after a capacity change.

question.q: A lasting foreign economic boom raises net exports and pushes domestic output above potential. With no policy response, how do expected prices and short-run aggregate supply adjust over time?
options: Rise and shift short-run aggregate supply left
Fall and shift short-run aggregate supply right
Stay fixed forever
Shift aggregate demand farther right
question.commonError: Thinking output stays above potential forever.
question.feedback: When output is above potential, pressures raise expected prices and shift SRAS left over time.

question.q: A lasting fall in aggregate demand pushes output below unchanged potential. With no policy response, how does the economy tend to adjust over time?
options: Falling expected prices and short-run aggregate supply shifting right
Rising expected prices and short-run aggregate supply shifting left
Long-run aggregate supply shifting left permanently
Aggregate demand becoming horizontal
question.commonError: Missing self-correction through expectations.
question.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, shifting SRAS right.

question.q: An increase in demand that remains in place pushes production above potential. Policymakers do nothing, and wage contracts are gradually renegotiated as workers and firms revise price expectations upward. Which change is most consistent with self-correction?
options: Rising wages and input costs shift short-run aggregate supply left; aggregate demand stays unchanged.
Aggregate demand shifts left automatically as soon as wages rise.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts right because the economy briefly produced above potential.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because firms respond to the higher price level by cutting costs.
question.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
question.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

question.q: Which statement best describes the macro outcome shown by the move from A to B?
options: Recession with accelerating inflation pressure.
Demand-pull inflation with no long-run growth.
Long-run growth with lower price pressure.
No change in either output or the price level.
question.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
question.feedback: Higher LRAS and SRAS support more output alongside a lower price level.
question.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with AD0, SRAS0, SRAS1, vertical LRAS0 and LRAS1, and intersections A and B.
question.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. Blue AD0 slopes downward. Red SRAS0 slopes upward; dashed SRAS1 lies below and right of SRAS0. LRAS0 is vertical at GDP 100 and dashed LRAS1 is vertical to its right at GDP 115. A, the AD0-SRAS0-LRAS0 intersection, is at (100,125). B, the AD0-SRAS1-LRAS1 intersection, is at (115,110). Dashed guides connect A and B to the axes.

question.q: After a fall in demand, output is 20 below potential. Aggregate demand and productive capacity stay unchanged, while wages and price expectations gradually adjust. Which adjustment closes the gap under these assumptions?
options: Higher wages shift short-run aggregate supply left, increasing output at unchanged demand.
Lower wages shift short-run aggregate supply right, returning output to unchanged potential.
Aggregate demand shifts right automatically, without any wage adjustment.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts left to meet actual output, despite unchanged productive capacity.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Higher expected prices shift SRAS left; that raises output at the fixed AD” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.
question.feedback: Under the stated adjustment model, lower cost/price expectations improve short-run supply and bring output toward potential. This is conditional on flexibility over time and no new demand/capacity shock.

question.q: After a fall in demand, output is 60 below potential. Aggregate demand and productive capacity stay unchanged, while wages and price expectations gradually adjust. Which adjustment closes the gap under these assumptions?
options: Higher wages shift short-run aggregate supply left, increasing output at unchanged demand.
Aggregate demand shifts right automatically, without any wage adjustment.
Lower wages shift short-run aggregate supply right, returning output to unchanged potential.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts left to meet actual output, despite unchanged productive capacity.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “LRAS shifts left to the recession output; unchanged resources force capacity to fall” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.
question.feedback: Under the stated adjustment model, lower cost/price expectations improve short-run supply and bring output toward potential. This is conditional on flexibility over time and no new demand/capacity shock.

question.q: Output is below unchanged potential, but nominal wages are fixed by contracts for one year. Officials predict an immediate recovery caused solely by lower wages. What is wrong with this forecast?
options: The timing is reasonable, but lower wages would contract short-run supply.
The direction is reasonable, but the stated contracts prevent this wage adjustment from occurring immediately.
The forecast fails because returning to potential requires lower productive capacity.
The forecast is valid because fixed wage contracts have no effect on the timing of cost adjustment.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Neither is appropriate because returning to Y1 requires LRAS to move left” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.
question.feedback: Lower wages could reduce costs and expand short-run supply, but the stipulated contracts prevent that wage channel from operating immediately. The expected direction does not establish the timing.

question.q: Output is above potential, but wage adjustment is slow. A proposed demand stimulus would arrive before self-correction. How would that stimulus initially affect the existing gap, other conditions equal?
options: It would permanently raise long-run aggregate supply by the size of the stimulus
It would enlarge the positive output gap
It would directly lower expected wages and close the gap
It would reduce aggregate demand and close the gap
question.feedback: Extra demand at an already above-potential starting point pushes activity further above capacity before wage adjustment.
question.commonError: Applies recession stimulus to an inflationary output gap.

question.q: Refer to the long-run Phillips curve graph. Which pair of points are long-run equilibria?
options: A and d
B and c
A and b
C and d
question.commonError: Treating all SRPC points as long-run equilibria.
question.feedback: Points b and c lie on the vertical LRPC at U2.

question.q: What natural rate of unemployment is shown by the LRPC?
options: 3 percent
6 percent
5 percent
10 percent
question.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
question.feedback: The vertical LRPC is drawn at 5 percent unemployment, so that is the natural rate.

question.q: What does this long-run Phillips curve imply about a policy that permanently maintains higher inflation?
options: Long-run unemployment remains 5%; higher sustained inflation does not buy a permanent unemployment reduction.
Long-run unemployment remains 2.5%; higher sustained inflation does not buy a permanent unemployment reduction.
Long-run unemployment starts at 5% but falls permanently as policy moves upward along long-run Phillips curve.
Unemployment remains 5% at every short-run point because long-run Phillips curve also fixes the slope of short-run Phillips curve.
question.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
question.feedback: LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5%. Once expectations adjust, a higher sustained inflation rate changes the inflation coordinate rather than the natural unemployment rate. Short-run deviations can still occur.

question.q: Demand expansion temporarily pushes unemployment below natural. After expected inflation adjusts, where does unemployment tend to go?
options: To zero regardless of labor institutions
Above natural forever with no inflation change
Back toward the natural rate
Permanently farther below the natural rate
question.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
question.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

question.q: Job-matching technology improves and lowers structural unemployment. What Phillips-curve change can follow?
options: The long-run Phillips curve becomes downward sloping
The long-run Phillips curve shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy moves left along the same long-run Phillips curve
The short-run Phillips curve must shift upward at every point
question.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
question.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

question.q: A rise in long-term mismatch raises the natural rate. What happens to the LRPC?
options: It shifts right
It shifts left
It rotates to horizontal
It stays fixed at the old natural rate
question.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
question.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

question.q: Why can many inflation rates appear on the same vertical LRPC?
options: Inflation is unable to change nominal wages
Every point has zero expected inflation
Aggregate demand fixes the natural rate
Long-run unemployment equals natural after expectations adjust
question.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
question.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

question.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects high inflation with unemployment at the natural rate?
options: a
b
c
d
question.commonError: Confusing short-run and long-run points.
question.feedback: Point b lies on the LRPC at U2 and inflation I2.
question.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
question.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

question.q: In the standard expectations-augmented Phillips model with no supply-shock offset, actual inflation equals expected inflation. What does the equation imply about unemployment?
options: At the natural rate
Below the natural rate
Above the natural rate
Equal to zero
question.commonError: Missing the role of inflation surprises.
question.feedback: With no inflation surprise, unemployment equals the natural rate. The no-offset assumption matters: an independent supply shock can also affect the relationship.

question.q: What does the diagram imply about the natural unemployment rate when short-run Phillips curve changes from SRPC0 to SRPC1?
options: It remains 5%; shifting the short-run inflation relationship does not itself change the long-run unemployment benchmark.
It remains 6%; shifting the short-run inflation relationship does not itself change the long-run unemployment benchmark.
It becomes 6% because point B always determines the natural rate, even off long-run Phillips curve.
It remains 5%, so unemployment cannot deviate from 5% anywhere on either short-run curve.
question.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
question.feedback: LRPC stays vertical at 5%. Point B is a short-run observation at 6% unemployment, not a new natural-rate marker. Short-run and long-run unemployment need not coincide.
question.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.

Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

question.q: Which description of point A is correct?
options: A is only on SRPC0 and remains below the natural unemployment rate.
A is only on long-run Phillips curve and remains above the natural unemployment rate.
A is on both SRPC0 and long-run Phillips curve at the natural rate
A is the location where SRPC0 turns into a vertical Phillips curve.
question.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
question.feedback: Point A is where the short-run curve crosses the long-run curve, so unemployment equals the natural rate there.
question.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
question.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

question.q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?
options: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.
question.commonError: Inferring a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from cross-country inflation differences.
question.feedback: The vertical LRPC allows different steady inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Unemployment stays permanently lower because the downward SRPC is also the long-run policy menu” in this long run phillips curve task.
question.q: A government seeks permanently lower unemployment by repeatedly surprising workers with higher inflation. Expected inflation eventually adapts, and labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run assessment is justified?
options: Unemployment stays permanently lower because the downward short-run Phillips curve is also the long-run policy menu
The natural rate rises one-for-one with each price-level increase by definition
The price level must return to its original value when unemployment returns to natural
Unemployment returns toward its natural rate at higher inflation; a lasting reduction needs changed real labor-market conditions
question.feedback: With expectations adjusting and the natural rate unchanged, the long-run curve is vertical. Repeated monetary surprises do not establish a permanently lower unemployment benchmark.

question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both must move LRPC right because lower unemployment requires higher inflation” in this long run phillips curve task.
question.q: Compare a demand boom that temporarily lowers unemployment with a reform that reduces structural unemployment. Which can change the natural unemployment rate?
options: The demand boom permanently lowers the natural rate; the reform affects only inflation.
Neither can change the natural rate because it is determined by the price level.
The structural reform can lower the natural rate; the demand boom alone changes actual unemployment around that benchmark.
Both must raise the natural rate because lower unemployment requires higher inflation.
question.feedback: Demand surprises can move actual unemployment temporarily below natural unemployment. A persistent reduction in structural unemployment can lower the natural rate itself and shift the long-run Phillips curve left.

question.q: A labor-market reform lowers natural unemployment while a monetary expansion raises inflation. How could a report mistakenly credit monetary expansion for a permanent unemployment gain?
options: By distinguishing the reform's effect on the natural rate of unemployment from the monetary policy's nominal effect.
By checking whether expectations have caught up before interpreting the unemployment observation.
By comparing labor-market structure before and after the reform rather than using inflation alone.
By attributing the reform's change in the natural rate of unemployment to the simultaneous demand expansion.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: By distinguishing the reform's benchmark change from the monetary policy's nominal effect.
question.feedback: Simultaneous events do not identify a single cause. A real matching or skill reform can lower natural unemployment; demand expansion alone does not establish that structural change. The comparison must separate the two mechanisms.

question.q: Demand expansion raises inflation persistently, and expectations eventually catch up. If natural unemployment is 5%, which long-run pair is possible?
options: Higher inflation with unemployment permanently below 5% solely from the surprise
Lower inflation with unemployment permanently above 5% solely from the surprise
Unchanged inflation with unemployment fixed at zero
Higher inflation with unemployment back at 5%
question.feedback: Full adjustment eliminates the initial unemployment surprise. The long-run rate stays natural while demand policy can leave higher inflation.
question.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from persistent demand inflation.

question.q: Job matching permanently improves and natural unemployment falls from 5% to 4%. What happens to the LRPC?
options: It becomes horizontal at 4% inflation
It shifts left to 4% unemployment
It shifts right to 6% unemployment
It remains at 5% and only actual inflation changes
question.commonError: Treats a changed natural rate as movement along a fixed LRPC.
question.feedback: LRPC is located at natural unemployment. A lower natural rate shifts the vertical benchmark left.

question.q: A persistent labor-market change raises natural unemployment from 4% to 5%. Policymakers maintain 6% inflation, which eventually becomes fully expected. What long-run point follows in the natural-rate model?
options: 5% unemployment and 6% inflation, on an long-run Phillips curve to the right of the old one
4% unemployment and 6% inflation, on the old long-run Phillips curve because higher inflation restores employment
5% unemployment and 4% inflation, because the old unemployment rate fixes long-run inflation
6% unemployment and 5% inflation, because the inflation and natural-rate coordinates exchange places
question.commonError: Assumes fully anticipated higher inflation can restore the former natural unemployment rate.
question.feedback: The new natural rate puts the vertical LRPC at 5% unemployment. Once 6% inflation is fully anticipated it does not keep unemployment below that benchmark, so the long-run point is (u=5%, inflation=6%).

question.q: The fourth unit provides a marginal benefit of $18 and has a marginal cost of $14. Should it be produced or consumed?
options: Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
Rejected because any positive marginal cost makes the unit undesirable
Accepted only if no sunk costs were incurred earlier
Rejected unless average benefit also rises.
question.commonError: Using total or average values instead of the next unit.
question.feedback: The fourth unit adds $4 in net benefit.

question.q: A firm has spent a nonrefundable $50,000 developing a product. Finishing it will cost another $12,000 and is expected to bring in $18,000. What should the firm do?
options: Cancel because total spending would reach $62,000
Finish so the original $50,000 is not wasted
Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
Ignore the $18,000 expected revenue because it is uncertain.
question.commonError: Including sunk development spending in the marginal comparison.
question.feedback: The $50,000 is unrecoverable; the relevant comparison is $18,000 versus $12,000.

question.q: Staying open an extra hour would bring a museum $900 in admissions revenue and add $1,100 in staffing and utility costs. What does marginal analysis recommend?
options: Stay open because total daily revenue is high
Stay open to recover fixed building costs
Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
Close only if average cost rises.
question.commonError: Using totals or fixed costs rather than incremental values.
question.feedback: The extra hour reduces net benefit by $200.

question.q: A factory’s average cost is $14, while producing unit 101 raises total cost from $1,400 to $1,418. Which cost is relevant to the unit-101 decision?
options: The $18 marginal cost of unit 101
The $14 average cost of existing output
The $1,418 total cost after production
The $1,400 cost already incurred
question.commonError: Using average or total cost instead of the added cost.
question.feedback: Unit 101 changes total cost by $18; that increment is its marginal cost.

question.q: A student values the grade benefit of another hour of study at 9 points and its fatigue cost at 6 points. What is the net marginal benefit?
options: 3 points.
15 points.
6 points.
9 points.
question.commonError: Adding benefit and cost or reporting only one side.
question.feedback: Net marginal benefit equals 9 minus 6.

question.q: A warehouse’s average handling cost is $9 per box. The next box costs $13 to handle and brings in $15 after all other variable costs. What should the warehouse do?
options: Handle it because $15 exceeds the $13 marginal cost
Reject it because marginal cost exceeds average cost
Handle it only if average cost falls below $9
Reject it because total handling cost rises
question.commonError: Using average cost instead of the next box’s cost.
question.feedback: The box adds $2 in profit even though its marginal cost exceeds average cost.

question.q: A firm can run up to four ads. Their marginal benefits are $90, $70, $45, and $20; each ad costs $50. How many ads should run?
options: Two ads
One ad
Three ads
Four ads
question.commonError: Stopping early or continuing after MB falls below MC.
question.feedback: Only the first two ads have marginal benefit at least $50.

question.q: A project has an unrecoverable $8,000 design cost. Finishing costs $3,000 and yields $4,200; cancellation costs $400. Which comparison is relevant?
options: Finish for a $1,200 future gain versus paying $400 to cancel
Compare the full $11,000 spending with $4,200 revenue
Finish only to recover the $8,000 design cost
Cancel because any remaining cost is harmful
question.commonError: Including sunk design cost or ignoring the cancellation alternative.
question.feedback: The future choices are a $1,200 net gain from finishing or a $400 cancellation cost.

question.q: A platform can add one feature now for $80,000. It yields $95,000 in direct benefit but delays a security upgrade worth $25,000. What is the feature’s net marginal effect?
question.commonError: Ignoring the displaced incremental alternative.
question.feedback: $95,000 minus $80,000 direct cost minus $25,000 opportunity cost equals -$10,000.

question.q: Adding one more flight would bring in $80,000 in revenue, incur $54,000 in operating costs, and impose $18,000 in expected delay costs on other flights. What is its net marginal benefit?
question.commonError: Ignoring congestion cost or adding benefit and costs.

question.q: A police department considers one more patrol. Crime reduction is valued at $120,000, added payroll is $75,000, and the officers would forgo training worth $38,000. What is net marginal benefit?
question.commonError: Ignoring forgone training or adding values.

question.q: The next unit has marginal benefit $24 and marginal cost $19. What should happen?
options: Continue only because past costs are sunk.
Stop because cost is positive.
Stop unless average benefit rises.
Produce or consume the next unit.
question.commonError: Rejecting a unit whenever it has any cost.
question.feedback: The next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

question.q: A fee has already been paid, but its refund terms have not yet been checked. When should it affect the current decision?
options: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
Only when total benefits are positive.
Always, because past spending must be recovered.
Never, even if a refund remains available.
question.commonError: Using a blanket rule without checking whether the cost is truly sunk.
question.feedback: Check whether the current choice changes how much of the fee can be recovered. A refund available under one choice but not another is relevant; a payment that cannot be recovered or changed is sunk. Having paid the fee does not by itself establish that it is irrelevant, and a desire to recover past spending is not a marginal benefit.

question.q: A school considers one more tutoring session. Total benefit would rise from 72 to 80 points and total cost from 48 to 54 points. Which values should be compared?
options: Marginal benefit 8 and marginal cost 6
Total benefit 80 and total cost 54
Average benefit 76 and average cost 51
Prior benefit 72 and prior cost 48
question.commonError: Comparing totals or averages instead of their changes.
question.feedback: The additional session adds 8 benefit points and 6 cost points.

question.q: A firm’s average profit is positive. The next order adds $180 in revenue and $205 in avoidable cost. What should it do?
options: Reject the order because its marginal contribution is negative
Accept because average profit across all prior orders remains positive
Accept because total revenue will rise
Reject only if fixed cost also rises
question.commonError: Using positive average profit instead of the next order’s margin.
question.feedback: The order reduces profit by $25.

question.q: Total benefit rises from 300 to 336 with one more unit; total cost rises from 210 to 242. What should happen?
options: Add the unit because MB 36 exceeds MC 32
Stop because total cost rises by 32
Add only if average benefit increases
Stop because total cost remains positive
question.commonError: Using totals or treating any added cost as disqualifying.
question.feedback: The next unit adds 4 in net benefit.

question.q: A market price is too low. Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
options: Price should rise
Price should fall
Supply should vanish
Demand must be zero
question.commonError: gets_shortage_price_pressure_backwards
question.feedback: A shortage creates upward pressure on price as buyers compete for limited goods.

question.q: A market price is too high. Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
options: Price should fall
Price should rise
Demand shifts right in response to unsold inventory
Supply shifts left before price can adjust
question.commonError: gets_surplus_price_pressure_backwards
question.feedback: A surplus creates downward pressure on price as sellers compete to sell the extra output.

question.q: A hurricane destroys part of the orange crop. What is the likely result in the orange market?
options: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Quantity demanded rises because supply fell
question.commonError: confuses_supply_shock_with_demand_increase
question.feedback: A crop loss reduces supply, which raises price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

question.q: A new health report says blueberries are especially beneficial. What likely happens in the blueberry market?
options: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
Quantity supplied falls because demand rose
question.commonError: confuses_demand_shift_with_supply_shift
question.feedback: A favorable taste or information change increases demand, raising price and quantity.

question.q: Refer to the graph. A production improvement shifts supply from S1 to S2 while demand remains D1. Which explanation connects the curve shift to the new equilibrium?
options: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls and quantity rises
Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price and quantity rise
Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price falls and quantity rises
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, so price rises and quantity falls
question.commonError: gets_supply_shift_effect_backwards
question.feedback: The production improvement shifts supply right to S2. Along unchanged D1, the intersection moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.

question.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. If demand shifts from D1 to D2 while supply remains at S2, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
question.commonError: gets_demand_shift_effect_backwards
question.feedback: Moving from D1 with S2 to D2 with S2 raises equilibrium price from P1 to P2 and raises equilibrium quantity from Q2 to Q3.

question.q: Refer to the graph. What can be concluded about the move from D to B?
options: Price falls; quantity rises in the drawing
Price and quantity both remain unchanged
Quantity falls; the price direction is ambiguous
Price rises; quantity is unchanged in the drawing

question.q: Inventories are accumulating because sellers are offering more units than buyers want at the current price. What market condition exists?
options: A situation where quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
A situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A point outside the PPF
A legal maximum price
question.commonError: reverses_surplus_and_shortage
question.feedback: A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.

question.q: At the current price, buyers want 180 units and sellers offer 120 units. What exists, and what pressure follows?
options: A shortage; price tends to rise
A surplus; price tends to fall
A shortage; price tends to fall
A surplus; price tends to rise
question.commonError: reverses_shortage_and_price_pressure
question.feedback: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward.

question.q: A market price is above equilibrium. Which result is most likely in an unregulated market?
options: A surplus creates downward pressure on price
A shortage creates upward pressure on price
Unsold inventories shift demand right
Seller competition shifts supply left
question.commonError: gets_surplus_price_pressure_backwards
question.feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus, and sellers respond by lowering price.

question.q: What distinguishes an external cost from an ordinary private cost?
options: It is always paid as a tax
It is any expense a seller records
An external cost falls on a third party outside the transaction
It exists only for public goods
question.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
question.feedback: External effects reach people outside the exchange. Costs already paid by the buyer or seller are private; an external cost is omitted from their exchange and therefore from the market price.

question.q: An externality can be harmful or beneficial, and it can arise from production or consumption. Why must these two distinctions be considered separately?
options: Sign and channel are always the same
Only production creates positive spillovers
Only consumption creates negative spillovers
Whether others gain or lose differs from which activity causes the effect.
question.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
question.feedback: Sign and source are separate dimensions. A positive or negative sign identifies the effect on third parties, whereas production or consumption identifies the activity that generates it.

question.q: A firm's research helps other firms imitate a process. Which comparison of private and social benefits fits this case?
options: Social benefit of production exceeds the producer's private benefit
Social cost of consumption exceeds private cost
Private benefit of consumption exceeds social benefit
The effect is negative because rivals benefit
question.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
question.feedback: Knowledge spillovers can make social production returns exceed private returns. Because imitators receive gains without compensating the innovator, private production incentives can be weaker than the total social return.

question.q: Buyers receive all benefits and sellers bear all costs of a trade. What externality evidence is present?
options: A negative production externality
None from those facts alone
A positive consumption externality
Both positive and negative externalities
question.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
question.feedback: An externality requires a third-party effect. Benefits and costs confined to the transacting parties are already private; evidence of a spillover requires an effect on someone else.

question.q: A factory ignores a constant marginal pollution cost. Relative to efficient quantity, what does the market tend to produce?
options: Too little output
The efficient output automatically
Too much output
Zero output in every case
question.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
question.feedback: Ignoring external cost makes private marginal cost too low. The factory compares MPB with MPC and omits pollution damage, so MPC lies below MSC and the private intersection occurs at too much output.

question.q: Consumers ignore harms their purchases impose on bystanders. What is the usual quantity result?
options: Underconsumption
No quantity distortion
A shortage caused by a price ceiling
Overconsumption
question.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
question.feedback: Private marginal benefit exceeds social marginal benefit. When consumers omit harm to bystanders, MPB lies above MSB and the market chooses units whose social benefit is below their social cost.

question.q: Plants have different abatement costs, but a regulator orders equal cuts. What concern arises?
options: The same aggregate reduction may cost more than necessary
The policy changes a negative externality into a positive one
Equal cuts guarantee equal marginal costs
The rule automatically creates tax revenue
question.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
question.feedback: Uniform cuts can ignore marginal-cost differences. Equal cuts ignore differences in marginal abatement cost, so the target could be reached with less total cost by shifting reductions toward lower-cost plants.

question.q: A safety rule bans disposal of toxic waste in a river. What is its intended mechanism?
options: Subsidize river disposal
Prevent the harmful action rather than price each unit
Create a tradable cap automatically
Guarantee compensation to every resident
question.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
question.feedback: A prohibition directly restricts the action. A ban is a direct quantity restriction: it prevents the damaging behavior instead of charging a price for each unit of harm.

question.q: How does an emissions standard differ from a corrective tax?
options: A standard fixes a legal quantity constraint; a tax sets a price on harm
A standard creates revenue while a tax never does
A tax fixes emissions with certainty
They are identical whenever enforced
question.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
question.feedback: Quantity and price instruments use different control variables. A standard determines an allowed quantity, while a corrective tax changes the marginal private price; those instruments need not produce identical certainty or revenue.

question.q: Why might a performance standard be preferred to mandated technology?
options: It removes monitoring needs
It can let firms choose how to meet the required outcome
It guarantees zero compliance cost
It turns the externality into a public good
question.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
question.feedback: Performance standards preserve some compliance flexibility. Firms retain freedom to select the least-cost method, although regulators still must define, monitor, and enforce the performance outcome.

question.q: A corrective tax equals marginal external cost at efficient output. What does it accomplish?
options: It makes the decision-maker face the omitted social cost
It guarantees sellers bear the legal tax
It eliminates distributional effects
It makes revenue equal DWL
question.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
question.feedback: The tax internalizes marginal external cost. At the efficient quantity, adding the tax to the private margin closes the gap between private and social cost and removes the incentive to choose harmful excess units.

question.q: Why is tax revenue not the same as deadweight loss?
options: Revenue is always larger than social costs
Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is forgone net social surplus
Deadweight loss is a producer transfer
They are identical with downward demand
question.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
question.feedback: Transfers and efficiency losses differ. Tax revenue changes who holds purchasing power, while deadweight loss measures mutually beneficial surplus that disappears because quantity is inefficient.

question.q: Why can a positive production externality make output too low?
options: MPC exceeds every buyer's willingness to pay
Producers do not receive the full social benefit they create
Consumers impose an external cost
MSC is always above MPC
question.commonError: Reversing social and private curves or predicting overproduction instead of underproduction.
question.feedback: Omitted external benefits weaken private incentives. For a positive production externality, MSC lies below MPC because some production benefit reaches third parties rather than the producer.

question.q: Why is subsidy expenditure not proof that a positive-externality policy raises welfare?
options: Every subsidy payment is a deadweight loss.
Spending determines externality sign
A subsidy cannot change quantity
Correction benefits must be compared with resource and financing costs
question.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
question.feedback: Fiscal cost and net social benefit are distinct. Government spending is a fiscal cost, not a direct measure of welfare; policy evaluation must compare the external benefit gained with real resource and financing costs.

question.q: Reducing the next ton of emissions costs Firm A $20 and Firm B $70. Emissions permits trade for $45 per ton. How can trading encourage the firms to reduce emissions at lower cost?
options: B abates more because its cost is higher
A abates more and can sell permits; B buys permits and abates less
Both must abate equally
Trading loosens the cap
question.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
question.feedback: The lower-cost reducer abates when cost is below permit price. Firm A's $20 abatement cost is below the $45 permit price, while Firm B's $70 cost is above it, so trade assigns more reduction to the lower-cost source.

question.q: What happens to the emissions cap when two firms trade an existing permit?
options: It rises by one unit
It falls by one unit
The cap is unchanged
It becomes voluntary
question.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
question.feedback: Trading reallocates an existing right. A trade transfers permission to emit from one firm to another; it neither creates nor retires a permit and therefore leaves aggregate emissions unchanged.

question.q: A paper mill buys downstream fishing rights and cuts pollution because its pollution now reduces its own fishing income. What is illustrated?
options: The mill now bears the fishing losses itself, giving it an incentive to reduce the spillover.
A binding price ceiling
A government permit cap
Guaranteed correction through norms
question.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
question.feedback: Common ownership brings the external cost into private calculation. Combining ownership makes the mill bear both production gains and fishery losses, bringing a previously external cost into the same private decision.

40 hours; voluntary payments necessarily capture every nonpayer’s benefit.
20 hours; voluntary payments necessarily capture every nonpayer’s benefit.
question.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
question.feedback: Private Benefit meets MC at 40 hours; MSB meets MC at 80. Between them MSB exceeds cost. Nonexcludability allows nonpayers to benefit, so observed private contributions can understate the relevant social marginal benefit.

question.q: An unencrypted radio signal reaches every receiver in its broadcast area. Why is it nonexcludable?
options: Listening uses up the signal
The station faces no production cost
The station cannot feasibly block individual nonpayers from receiving it
Government owns every receiver
question.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
question.feedback: With an open broadcast, individual nonpayers cannot feasibly be denied reception, which makes consumption nonexcludable.

question.q: A private park requires a membership card at its only entrance. Which conclusion follows?
options: The park is nonexcludable because nature is shared
The park is excludable because nonmembers can be turned away
The park is rival only because it charges
The park must be a private good even when empty
question.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
question.feedback: A controlled entrance makes denial of access feasible. Excludability alone does not determine rivalry or the final four-way classification.

question.q: A news site removes its paywall and permits unlimited anonymous reading. Which dimension changes?
options: It becomes more rival
It becomes legally prohibited
It becomes a common resource because information is depleted
It becomes less excludable
question.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
question.feedback: Removing the paywall makes it difficult to deny content to nonpayers; it does not make digital information rival.

question.q: A city posts hurricane maps online without login restrictions. Which statement about consumption is correct?
options: The maps are rival because many people download them
The maps are nonexcludable under the stated access policy
The maps are excludable because the city created them
The maps are private goods because servers cost money
question.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
question.feedback: Open access means users cannot be denied based on payment. Production cost and public ownership do not determine excludability.

question.q: Thousands of households receive the same uncrowded radio signal. Why is reception nonrival?
options: Another listener does not reduce the signal available to others
The station can charge every listener
Stations do not compete
Broadcast equipment has no cost
question.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
question.feedback: Nonrivalry means adding a listener does not diminish the signal or reception available to existing listeners.

question.q: An extra download of a digital report does not slow the server or delete anyone's copy. Which characteristic is present?
options: Nonexcludability
Rivalry among publishers
Nonrivalry
Resource depletion
question.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
question.feedback: The extra download leaves the report fully available to others, so consumption is nonrival under the stated capacity conditions.

question.q: Why can observed donations understate demand for a pure public good?
options: Public goods have no social benefit
Donations always exceed marginal cost
Rival consumption forces people to donate twice
Noncontributors may still benefit, weakening incentives to reveal willingness to pay
question.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
question.feedback: Voluntary payments reveal only contributed private willingness to pay. Free riders can enjoy the good while withholding part of their valuation.

question.q: How can free riding lead to too little mosquito control?
options: Each treated household uses up the protection
Voluntary contributions can fall below the total social willingness to pay
Private payments necessarily exceed MSB
Mosquito control becomes a common resource
question.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
question.feedback: Area-wide treatment benefits noncontributors, so private contributions may not capture all social benefit and provision can stop below the efficient level.

question.q: A public safety website is funded by voluntary gifts. Many users assume enough other people will donate. What is the likely result?
options: The website becomes rival
Every user reveals full willingness to pay
The efficient quantity must be zero
Contributions may be too low relative to the site's social benefit
question.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
question.feedback: When each user relies on others to fund a nonexcludable service, aggregate contributions can be insufficient even when users collectively value it highly.

question.q: If exclusion technology becomes effective for a formerly open broadcast, what happens to the free-rider problem?
options: It intensifies because payment becomes easier
It is unchanged because excludability never matters
It can weaken because access can be conditioned on payment
It turns automatically into common-resource overuse
question.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
question.feedback: When nonpayers can be denied access, receiving the benefit depends more directly on payment, reducing the incentive to free ride.

question.q: Which observation would be strongest evidence of free riding in a clean-air alert service?

The service has a positive operating cost
Two firms offer weather forecasts
question.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
question.feedback: Use by noncontributors shows people obtaining the nonexcludable benefit without helping finance it.

question.q: For a pure public good with no exclusion or alternative revenue, why may a profit-seeking firm provide too little?

Its marginal cost must be zero
Every customer consumes a different quantity
Public goods cannot be produced with labor
question.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
question.feedback: Nonexcludability makes it difficult to charge all beneficiaries, so revenue reflects less than the good's total social benefit.

question.q: A company funds free weather alerts with advertising. Why can provision occur despite open access?

question.q: A business association signs a contract to finance district-wide security patrols. What problem does the contract address?

It coordinates payment for a benefit that reaches many businesses
It guarantees zero enforcement cost
It removes every nonmember from the district
question.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.

Subscriptions eliminate marginal cost
Subscribers stop sharing a common quantity

question.feedback: A subscription lets the provider deny access to nonmembers, making revenue collection feasible while consumption can remain nonrival over the relevant range.

question.q: How can free riding bias a survey used to value a proposed public good?

question.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
question.feedback: People who expect to receive the good regardless of payment may report low values to reduce their expected cost share.

Total benefit equals government spending
question.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
question.feedback: Observed gifts reflect contributed private payments, not necessarily the full value received by contributors and free riders.

question.q: What quantity of vapes is socially efficient? Which marginal benefit and cost must be equal?
options: 160 thousand vapes; MSB and MPC meet, equating social marginal benefit and cost.
140 thousand vapes; equality of private benefit and private cost is sufficient even with an unpriced spillover.
140 thousand vapes; MSB and MPC meet, equating social marginal benefit and cost.
160 thousand vapes; equality of private benefit and private cost is sufficient even with an unpriced spillover.
question.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
question.feedback: MPB–MPC Q = 180; MSB–MPC Q = 140; at Q = 140, MPB = $12 and MSB = $8. At 140, the relevant social marginal curves meet. Moving toward this quantity adds units with social benefit above cost or removes units with cost above benefit. Private equality alone omits the spillover.

MPB is a straight line from (0, $19) to (240, $7). MPC is a straight line from (0, $1) to (240, $13). MSB is a straight line from (0, $15) to (240, $3), parallel to MPB. A red dot marks the MPB-MPC intersection at (180, $10); a green dot marks the MSB-MPC intersection at (140, $8). Dashed guides project those dots to the axes. A purple vertical bracket near Q = 140 spans the MSB-MPC value $8 to the MPB value $12.

question.q: What quantity of gardens is socially efficient? Which marginal benefit and cost must be equal?
options: 170 gardens; MSC and MPB meet, equating social marginal benefit and cost.
150 gardens; equality of private benefit and private cost is sufficient even with an unpriced spillover.
170 gardens; equality of private benefit and private cost is sufficient even with an unpriced spillover.
150 gardens; MSC and MPB meet, equating social marginal benefit and cost.
question.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
question.feedback: MPC–MPB Q = 100; MSC–MPB Q = 150; at Q = 150, MPC = $15 and MSC = $10. At 150, the relevant social marginal curves meet. Moving toward this quantity adds units with social benefit above cost or removes units with cost above benefit. Private equality alone omits the spillover.

question.q: What daily quantity of transit rides is socially efficient? Which marginal benefit and cost must be equal?
options: 200 thousand rides per day; MSB and MPC meet, equating social marginal benefit and cost.
220 thousand rides per day; MSB and MPC meet, equating social marginal benefit and cost.
200 thousand rides per day; equality of private benefit and private cost is sufficient even with an unpriced spillover.
220 thousand rides per day; equality of private benefit and private cost is sufficient even with an unpriced spillover.
question.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
question.feedback: MPB–MPC Q = 150; MSB–MPC Q = 200; at Q = 200, MSB = $6 and MPB = $4. At 200, the relevant social marginal curves meet. Moving toward this quantity adds units with social benefit above cost or removes units with cost above benefit. Private equality alone omits the spillover.

question.q: A council can afford 20, 30 or 40 miles of protection. Which target in the graph maximizes net social benefit, and what is the economic reason?
options: 40 miles; stop adding protection when marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
30 miles; any affordable target is equally efficient regardless of marginal benefits and costs.
30 miles; stop adding protection when marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
40 miles; any affordable target is equally efficient regardless of marginal benefits and costs.
question.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
question.feedback: MSB meets MC at 30 miles. The units between 20 and 30 add positive net benefits, while units beyond 30 cost more than their added benefit. Affordability permits a choice; it does not establish efficiency.
question.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
question.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

question.q: At 40 radio hours, how much marginal benefit would be missed by counting only Group A? Why should Group B’s benefit also be included?
options: $2,000; Group B also benefits from the same marginal hour.
$1,000; Group B consumes a separate hour that must be added to the quantity.
$1,000; Group B also benefits from the same marginal hour.
$2,000; Group B consumes a separate hour that must be added to the quantity.
question.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
question.feedback: At Q = 40, Group B’s MB is 10 hundreds, or $1,000. Omitting B misses a benefit of the same nonrival hour; it does not omit a separate unit of programming.
question.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
question.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

question.q: Which case is a negative externality?
options: Noise from a venue reducing nearby residents’ well-being.
A buyer paying the posted price.
A student receiving private tutoring that affects only the student and tutor.
A firm lowering its own cost.
question.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
question.feedback: Noise that reduces nearby residents’ well-being imposes a cost on third parties outside the transaction, so it is a negative externality.

question.q: Why might a public good be underprovided privately?
options: Use by one person prevents all others from using it.
People can benefit without paying, weakening voluntary funding.
Exclusion is effortless.
Every consumer reveals exact willingness to pay.
question.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
question.feedback: When nonpayers can benefit from the good, individuals have an incentive to free ride, so voluntary private funding can be below the efficient level.

question.q: What is the standard efficiency concern with market power?
options: Every firm earns zero accounting profit.
All prices fall below marginal cost.
Output may be restricted below the level where buyer value exceeds production cost.
Products become nonrival when one firm sets the market price.
question.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
question.feedback: Market power can restrict output below the efficient quantity, leaving mutually beneficial trades unrealized and creating deadweight loss.

question.q: Refer to the graph. At the efficient emergency-siren quantity, what marginal benefit and marginal cost are shown?
options: $10,000 per siren
$20,000 per siren
$30,000 per siren
$40,000 per siren
question.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
question.feedback: At 40 sirens, the graph shows 20 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so MSB and MC both equal $20,000 per siren.
question.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
question.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

question.q: Which number of sirens and decision rule maximize net social benefits in the graph?
options: 40; stop where marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
60; stop where marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
40; expand until total benefit falls to zero.
60; expand until total benefit falls to zero.
question.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
question.feedback: MSB intersects MC at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren. Further sirens have cost above their added benefit even though total benefit remains positive. The decision rule is marginal.
question.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
question.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

question.q: A student says free riding means 'people are bad.' What is the more precise economic explanation?
options: Public goods eliminate incentives
Free riding requires theft
Nonrivalry means only one person benefits
Nonexcludability allows a person to benefit without bearing the contribution cost
question.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
question.feedback: The mechanism is an incentive created by nonexcludability: an individual can receive the benefit while shifting payment to others.

question.q: What is the precise private-provision concern for a pure nonexcludable public good?
options: Private firms are legally barred from production
Market revenue may fall short of the social value created
Marginal social benefit is always zero
Every unit is overused like a common resource
question.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
question.feedback: When beneficiaries can receive the good without paying, the provider cannot capture all willingness to pay, so profitable output may be below efficient provision.

question.q: A study examines how a minimum wage affects employment in one local industry. Is this primarily microeconomic or macroeconomic analysis?
options: Macroeconomic analysis because wages use money.
Neither because policy is involved.
Microeconomic analysis.
Macroeconomic analysis because employment is always aggregate.
question.commonError: Using the topic word rather than the level of analysis.
question.feedback: The focus is a specific market and group of firms and workers.

question.q: A report studies how household saving decisions collectively affect national investment. Which statement is best?
options: It is purely micro because households are mentioned.
It is purely macro because individual choices do not matter.
It cannot be economic analysis.
It links microeconomic behavior to a macroeconomic outcome.
question.commonError: Treating micro and macro as unrelated silos.
question.feedback: Macroeconomic aggregates emerge from many individual decisions and institutions.

question.q: A tax credit changes purchases in the electric-bicycle market. Why can the analysis be microeconomic?
options: It focuses on buyers and sellers in one market
It may change tax revenue
It uses a national currency
It was enacted by a government
question.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
question.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

question.q: A central bank action is studied through its effect on national spending and inflation. Why is this macroeconomic?
options: Interest rates cannot be studied by microeconomics
The outcomes are economy-wide aggregates
Central banks never affect individual markets
Any government institution defines the field
question.commonError: Calling a large organization macro even when the question concerns one decision-maker.
question.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment.

question.q: A study follows household saving and then asks how total saving affects national investment. What levels appear?
options: Two unrelated micro questions
Only macro because households disappear
Individual choices and an aggregate outcome
Only micro because saving begins at home
question.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
question.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

question.q: A retailer has 20,000 stores, but a study asks how that one firm sets delivery fees. What matters for classification?
options: The number of employees alone
Whether fees are quoted in dollars
Whether the retailer operates nationally
The unit of analysis, not the firm’s size
question.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
question.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

question.q: A researcher studies how a new tax affects the market for soda. Another researcher studies how inflation affects all consumers. Which pairing is correct?
options: Soda tax is microeconomics; inflation is macroeconomics
Soda tax is macroeconomics; inflation is microeconomics
Both are only microeconomics
Both are only macroeconomics
question.commonError: classifies_any_tax_as_macro
question.feedback: A specific product market is microeconomics. Economy-wide inflation is macroeconomics.

question.q: A central bank raises interest rates. Which question is most macroeconomic?
options: How will one bank price a particular loan?
How will one household refinance a mortgage?
How will the policy affect inflation and total output?
How will one firm choose a supplier?
question.commonError: Classifying by institution rather than outcome level.
question.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide inflation and output effects.
