question.q: A city changes zoning rules for one housing market. Is analysis of this change primarily microeconomic or macroeconomic?
options: Automatically macroeconomic because a city acted
Not economics because the rule is local
Macroeconomic because housing has prices
Primarily microeconomic despite government involvement
question.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
question.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

question.q: A large corporation changes one product’s price. Why is size not decisive?
options: Product prices are macro indicators, even if the evidence covers only one industry
Classification follows the question’s unit of analysis
Corporations cannot be studied microeconomically
Large firms are national aggregates
question.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
question.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

question.q: Which question about interest rates is most macroeconomic?
options: How one firm finances equipment
How one borrower chooses a loan
How rates affect total spending and inflation
How one bank prices a mortgage
question.commonError: Calling a large organization macro even when the question concerns one decision-maker.
question.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment.

question.q: Two models answer different questions about the same market. How should an economist choose between them?
options: Always choose the more complicated model.
Use whichever gives the preferred answer.
Use the model whose mechanisms and assumptions fit the question.
Assume one model must be universally correct.
question.commonError: Treating model complexity as the sole quality criterion.
question.feedback: Model choice depends on purpose, relevant mechanisms, and evidence.

question.q: A simple model omits a factor that is small in one setting but large in another. What follows?
options: Any omission makes the model worthless.
The factor must be irrelevant everywhere.
The model becomes a definition rather than an explanation.
The model may work in the first setting and fail in the second.
question.commonError: Applying a model without checking context.
question.feedback: The importance of an omitted factor depends on the situation.

question.q: A wage model assumes workers can change jobs easily, but licenses block movement. What should the analyst do?
options: Reject every wage model regardless of its purpose
Treat licensing as a value judgment rather than evidence
Revise the application because the mobility assumption fails
Keep the prediction because assumptions never affect results
question.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
question.feedback: Licensing blocks the assumed job mobility, so the analyst should revise the assumption or limit the model’s application.

question.q: A household model predicts spending from income, but families also face new credit limits. Why might the prediction change?
options: Adding any factor guarantees a perfect prediction
An omitted constraint became important in this setting
Income no longer matters in any household decision
The original relationship became a definition
question.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
question.feedback: New credit limits add a binding constraint, so income alone no longer predicts the household’s feasible spending response.

question.q: One inflation model studies demand pressure; another studies supply disruptions. Which should be used after an energy shock?
options: The model containing the relevant supply mechanism
The model with the most equations on the page
Whichever model predicts the preferred policy
Average the two models without checking their assumptions.
question.commonError: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
question.feedback: An energy shock operates through supply costs, making the supply-disruption model the more relevant mechanism.

question.q: Adding dozens of variables improves historical fit but makes the mechanism impossible to interpret. What tradeoff appears?
options: Fit improved while explanatory clarity declined
Complexity proved the mechanism was causal
Interpretation no longer matters for policy
Every omitted variable has been eliminated
question.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
question.feedback: The added variables improve fit but reduce interpretability, creating a prediction-versus-mechanism tradeoff.

question.q: A restaurant-demand model assumes nearby competitors stay open, but two close. What should happen to the forecast?
options: Reconsider it because a held-constant condition changed
Keep it because assumptions do not affect forecasts
Reject all demand models as permanently useless
Treat competitor closures as a moral judgment
question.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
question.feedback: Competitor closures violate the forecast’s fixed-competition assumption and may shift demand toward the restaurant.

question.q: One model explains short-run layoffs; another explains long-run hiring. How should a firm choose?
options: Always select the model with more variables and equations
Average both answers without checking assumptions
Use whichever model supports its preferred plan
Match the model to the time horizon and question
question.commonError: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
question.feedback: The firm should match model horizon to its decision: the layoff model for short-run adjustment and the hiring model for long-run planning.

question.q: A model predicts well in rural areas but not dense cities. What is the first question to ask?
options: Would adding any variable guarantee success
Are city outcomes outside economic analysis
Do its assumptions fit both settings equally well
Must every rural observation be discarded
question.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
question.feedback: The first review is whether density changes a key mechanism or assumption that held in rural markets.

question.q: Banks choose to hold more excess reserves instead of making loans. How does this affect deposit creation?
options: Stronger because lending rises
Weaker because lending falls
Unchanged because reserves do not matter
Infinite because deposits disappear
question.commonError: Ignoring bank behavior in monetary control.
question.feedback: When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.

question.q: Why is the simple money multiplier only a rough prediction in the real world?
options: Banks may hold excess reserves and people may hold currency.
The Fed cannot affect reserves in any way.
Deposits are not part of the money supply.
Banks always lend exactly zero.
question.commonError: thinking the simple multiplier always predicts the exact result
question.feedback: The simple multiplier assumes banks lend all excess reserves and the public holds no currency; excess reserves and currency holdings make actual money creation smaller.

question.q: Households hold more currency and fewer bank deposits. How does this affect banks’ ability to support lending?
options: Fewer deposits available to support loans
More deposits available to support loans
No reserve requirement
A larger required reserve ratio automatically
question.commonError: thinking currency holdings do not affect bank lending
question.feedback: When people hold more currency, fewer funds sit in deposits, which limits bank lending and money creation.

question.q: A bank holds excess reserves during a financial panic. What happens to deposit creation compared with the simple multiplier prediction?
options: Deposit creation is weaker.
Deposit creation is stronger.
Deposit creation is exactly unchanged.
Deposit creation becomes unrelated to reserves.
question.commonError: ignoring bank behavior in money creation
question.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

question.q: Which situation makes the Fed's control over the money supply less precise?
options: Banks change how much they want to lend.
The Fed exists as a central bank.
Money has three functions.
Prices are quoted in dollars.
question.commonError: thinking central bank control is mechanically perfect
question.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but bank lending decisions affect the final amount of money created.

question.q: The central bank supplies ample reserves and banks are willing to lend, but households and firms become reluctant to borrow. What happens to deposit creation relative to the simple multiplier maximum?
options: Weak loan demand can keep deposit creation below the simple-multiplier maximum
It must equal the maximum because reserve supply alone determines every loan
It must exceed the maximum because unborrowed reserves count twice
It becomes fiscal policy because borrowers are not requesting loans
question.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
question.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

question.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold the new reserves instead of lending them. What happens to the money multiplier process?
options: It weakens despite higher reserves
It strengthens despite no lending
It becomes unrelated to banks
It eliminates currency from M1
question.commonError: Assuming Fed purchases always create full deposit expansion.
question.feedback: Fed purchases raise reserves, but deposit expansion is weaker if banks do not lend those reserves.

question.q: A student says, 'The Fed can perfectly control the money supply because it controls reserves.' What is the best correction?
options: Bank reserves and public currency choices affect final money creation.
The Fed cannot influence reserves at all.
Banks cannot create money in a fractional reserve system.
Currency held by the public always increases deposits.
question.commonError: assuming Fed control over reserves equals perfect control over money supply
question.feedback: The Fed has powerful tools, but final money creation depends partly on banks and the public.

question.q: If the Fed injects reserves but banks choose not to lend them, why might the money supply grow less than expected?
options: The reserves remain idle instead of supporting new deposits.
The reserve requirement must have become 100 percent by law.
The public must have stopped using money entirely.
The Fed's bond purchase automatically reduced deposits.
question.commonError: assuming injected reserves are always fully multiplied
question.feedback: Reserves only multiply into deposits if banks lend and borrowers redeposit. If banks sit on reserves, the multiplier weakens.

question.q: Why can a higher interest rate on reserves tighten monetary policy?
options: Makes holding reserves more attractive relative to lending
Forces households to hold more commodity money
Automatically lowers all taxes
Makes money demand zero
question.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending incentives
question.feedback: If reserves pay more, banks may prefer holding reserves over making loans, which can restrain money creation.

question.q: In a hypothetical banking system, banks initially hold exactly their required reserves. The reserve ratio stays at 10%. Banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The public deposits $50 million in currency it previously held. Including this initial deposit, what is the maximum total increase in deposits?
options: $500 million
$50 million
$45 million
$5 million
question.commonError: thinking currency deposited into banks cannot support money creation
question.feedback: Moving currency into deposits gives banks reserves to support lending. With a multiplier of 10, $50 million can support up to $500 million in deposits. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

question.q: In a hypothetical banking system, banks initially hold exactly their required reserves. The reserve ratio stays at 15%. Banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The public deposits $30 million in currency it previously held. Including this initial deposit, what is the maximum total increase in deposits?
options: $200 million
$30 million
$25.5 million
$4.5 million
question.commonError: calculating only the first-round loan instead of total deposit expansion
question.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.15 = 6.666..., so $30 million can support about $200 million in total deposits. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

question.q: A bank has $1,000,000 in assets and $80,000 in capital. Its assets lose $40,000 in value while its liabilities stay unchanged. What is its remaining capital?
question.commonError: Thinking losses reduce liabilities first.
question.feedback: Losses reduce bank capital. $80,000 - $40,000 = $40,000.

question.q: Banks receive $280 in reserves but face few creditworthy loan applications. A proposal assumes more reserves alone will create a fixed proportional lending boom. Which missing link matters?
options: Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.
Reserves already represent loan applications; the injection establishes adequate credit demand.
Banks need willing, qualified borrowers as well as reserve capacity.
Loans require equal reductions in existing deposits; weak demand preserves deposits.
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Every reserve dollar is a loan request, so demand is already guaranteed” in this monetary control limits task.
question.feedback: Having liquidity is different from finding loans acceptable to both lender and borrower. Reserve supply alone does not establish demand, risk-adjusted profitability or capital headroom.

question.q: Households withdraw $300 from checking into currency while the total of M1 initially stays constant. In a bank-reserve model, which change can still weaken later deposit expansion?
options: M1 must fall initially because currency held by households is outside money
Banks lose reserves and deposits; unchanged initial M1 does not imply unchanged bank lending capacity
Banks gain reserves and deposits; currency withdrawals expand the redepositing base
Bank capital automatically rises by the currency withdrawal, raising lending capacity
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “M1 must fall initially because currency held by households is outside money” in this monetary control limits task.
question.feedback: Checking falls while public currency rises, initially preserving M1. The banking system loses reserves and a deposit liability; less reserve availability can constrain later deposit creation despite unchanged initial money.

question.q: Two otherwise comparable banking systems receive $320 in reserves. In A, banks lend available funds and payments are redeposited. In B, banks hold additional reserves and customers retain more currency. Which comparison is supported?
options: A can support a larger deposit expansion; the simple multiplier is less descriptive of B's behavior
B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending
Both expansions must be equal because the required reserve ratio alone determines actual lending
A's expansion must be zero because redepositing cancels every loan
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending” in this monetary control limits task.
question.feedback: Extra reserve holdings and currency retention reduce successive lending/redepositing rounds. The same reserve injection and formal required ratio need not produce the same actual multiplier.

question.q: A reserve injection could support $1,000 of deposits in the simple maximum model. Banks instead retain additional excess reserves. Relative to that maximum, how much deposit creation would you expect?
options: No reserves remaining because deposits remove reserves from the system
Less deposit creation, other conditions equal
More deposit creation because excess reserves are loans
Exactly $1,000 regardless of lending decisions
question.feedback: Additional reserve retention leaves less available for repeated lending and deposit expansion than the restrictive simple maximum assumes.
question.commonError: Treats the simple multiplier maximum as guaranteed actual expansion.
Substitutes the simple theoretical multiplier for the observed ratio.
question.q: A $100 reserve injection is followed by $400 in additional deposits. The simple model with rr=10% predicts $1,000. Which observed multiplier should be used to describe this episode?
options: 10, because the legal ratio fixes actual expansion
0.25, because reserves are divided by deposits
40, because both quantities must be expressed as percentages
4, below the simple maximum 10
question.feedback: Observed deposit expansion per reserve dollar=400/100=4. Leakages or other lending constraints can leave it below 10.

question.q: All nominal prices and wages double while relative prices and real activity stay unchanged. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
A supply shock
A liquidity trap
question.commonError: Missing the real versus nominal distinction.
question.feedback: Monetary neutrality says nominal variables can change while real variables remain unchanged in the long run.

question.q: All nominal prices double while relative prices and real activity stay unchanged. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
The multiplier effect
Liquidity preference
question.commonError: thinking changes in nominal prices automatically change relative prices
question.feedback: Monetary neutrality says money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

question.q: Which statement is consistent with the classical dichotomy?
options: Money growth can raise nominal wages while long-run real wages stay unchanged.
Money growth changes only real variables and never nominal variables.
Nominal and real variables are always identical.
The price level is a real variable.
question.commonError: thinking nominal and real variables move identically
question.feedback: Under the classical dichotomy, money affects nominal variables, while real variables are determined by real factors in the long run.

question.q: A nominal wage rises from $15 to $30 while the price level doubles. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays the same.
It doubles.
It falls by half.
It becomes zero.
question.commonError: thinking a higher nominal wage always means a higher real wage
question.feedback: If nominal wages and the price level both double, the real wage is unchanged.

question.q: After a sustained monetary expansion, the long-run price level is higher and nominal wages are higher by roughly the same proportion. What happens to the real wage if productivity is unchanged?
options: It can return to about its previous level.
It rises with the nominal wage even though prices rise proportionately.
It falls to zero because money growth raises prices.
It becomes equal to the rate of money-supply growth.
question.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
question.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

question.q: If every nominal price and nominal wage doubles, why might employment and output be unchanged in the long run?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged.
Workers receive twice as many physical goods per hour.
Money demand must fall to zero.
The reserve requirement doubles automatically.
question.commonError: thinking nominal doubling changes real incentives by itself
question.feedback: If all nominal values double together, real wages and relative prices do not change, so real decisions need not change.

question.q: A country doubles its money supply and, in the long run, all dollar prices double. What happens to the value of money?
options: It falls by half.
It doubles.
It stays unchanged.
It becomes equal to real GDP.
question.commonError: thinking money supply doubling doubles the value of money
question.feedback: If the price level doubles, the value of money, 1/P, falls by half.

question.q: A central bank doubles the money supply, output is unchanged, and all nominal wages and prices double. Which claim is strongest?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged
Real wages double with nominal wages
Relative prices double with prices
Output must double with money
question.commonError: Confusing nominal doubling with real doubling.
question.feedback: If wages and prices double together, real wages and relative prices remain unchanged.

question.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 6 percent while the price level rises 9 percent. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls by about 3 percent
It rises by about 3 percent
It rises by about 15 percent
It stays unchanged
question.commonError: Treating nominal wage growth as real wage growth.
question.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so 6 - 9 = -3 percent.

question.q: Nominal wages rise 12 percent while the price level rises 8 percent. Approximately what happens to the real wage?
options: It rises by about 4 percent.
It falls by about 4 percent.
It rises by about 20 percent.
It is unchanged.
question.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
question.feedback: Real wage growth is roughly nominal wage growth minus inflation: 12 percent - 8 percent = 4 percent.

question.q: If nominal GDP rises 10 percent while real GDP rises 4 percent, what happened to the price level approximately?
options: It rose about 6 percent.
It rose about 14 percent.
It fell about 6 percent.
It stayed fixed.
question.commonError: adding real growth to nominal growth instead of subtracting
question.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price level growth is about 10 - 4 = 6 percent.

question.q: A student says nominal wages rose 8 percent, so workers are better off. Inflation was 11 percent. How did workers' real wages change?
options: Real wages fell because prices rose faster than nominal wages.
Real wages rose because nominal wages increased above zero.
Real wages were unchanged because all inflation is neutral immediately.
Real wages doubled because nominal wages are measured in dollars.
question.commonError: Confusing nominal wage growth with real wage growth.
question.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so workers lost purchasing power.

question.q: A worker earns $20 per hour, and a unit of output costs $5. What is the worker’s real wage?
options: 4 units of output per hour
$25 per hour
100 units of output per hour
0.25 units of output per hour
question.commonError: multiplying wage by price level instead of dividing
question.feedback: Real wage equals nominal wage divided by price level: 20 / 5 = 4 units of output per hour.

question.q: Pizza rises from $10 to $20 while soda rises from $2 to $4. How does the price of pizza measured in sodas change?
options: Is unchanged
Doubles
Falls by half
Becomes zero
question.commonError: thinking nominal price increases always change relative prices
question.feedback: Pizza was 5 sodas before and 5 sodas after. The relative price is unchanged.

question.q: A worker initially earns $100 while the consumption-price index is 100. In a long-run monetary-neutrality comparison, nominal wages and all prices double while real technology and resources are unchanged. Which conclusion respects both nominal and real measures?
options: Nominal pay doubles while the real wage and long-run productive capacity can remain unchanged
The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double
Productive capacity doubles because a larger money stock is itself more real capital
Nominal pay is unchanged because neutrality freezes every monetary variable
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double” in this monetary neutrality task.
question.feedback: A real wage is nominal wage divided by prices; doubling both preserves the ratio. Long-run neutrality permits nominal changes without corresponding changes in real productive capacity.

question.q: A one-time increase in money causes temporary output above potential. Over time wages and expected prices adjust. Which comparison avoids confusing long-run neutrality with immediate neutrality?
options: Short-run output stays at potential; long-run neutrality also rules out temporary real effects.
Short-run output rises; long-run potential rises equally despite unchanged productive resources.
Short-run output rises; long-run neutrality requires prices to return to their original level.
Short-run output can rise; long-run output returns to potential at higher prices.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Short-run output stays at potential; long-run neutrality also rules out temporary real effects.
question.feedback: Sticky wages/prices allow short-run real effects. Longer-run adjustment can return output to potential while nominal prices stay higher; neutrality does not require no transitional effect.

question.q: Nominal wages rise 6%, while prices rise 4%. A claim that these changes demonstrate complete monetary neutrality is made. Which assessment follows from the real-wage evidence?
options: The real wage rises 10%; nominal wage and price growth should be added
The real wage falls about 1.9%; the price factor belongs in the numerator
The real wage rises about 1.9%; these unequal proportional changes do not by themselves demonstrate unchanged real wages
The real wage is unchanged because any simultaneous nominal wage and price rise is neutral
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real wage rises 10%; nominal wage and price growth should be added” in this monetary neutrality task.
question.feedback: The real-wage factor is 1.06/1.04≈1.01923. Equal proportional nominal changes would leave the ratio unchanged; these are not equal. The calculation alone also does not identify what caused the changes.

question.q: All nominal prices double in a long-run neutrality comparison. A worker’s nominal wage also doubles from $20 to $40. What happens to the real wage?
options: It rises by $20 of purchasing power
It is unchanged
It doubles
It halves
question.feedback: Real wage=W/P. Doubling numerator and denominator leaves the ratio unchanged.
question.commonError: Treats a nominal wage rise as a real gain when prices rise proportionately.
Counts a proportional price increase as real output growth.
question.q: In a long-run neutrality comparison money, nominal GDP and the price level all double. What happens to real GDP=nominal GDP/(price index/100)?
options: It remains unchanged
It doubles
It quadruples
It falls by half
question.feedback: Proportional nominal GDP and price increases cancel in the real-output ratio.

question.q: The quantity theory predicts that sustained money growth faster than real output growth can raise inflation. In the long-run neutrality framework, what should a student infer about real productive capacity?
options: Faster money growth can raise nominal prices without permanently increasing productive capacity.
Faster money growth must permanently raise productive capacity by the same percentage.
Higher inflation proves output per worker rose by the same amount.
Long-run neutrality requires inflation to be zero whenever money growth exceeds output growth.
question.commonError: Stops after predicting the price-level effect and does not separate nominal from real outcomes.
question.feedback: Use the quantity-theory result for nominal spending and prices, then apply long-run neutrality to ask which real variables need not rise permanently.

question.q: In the scarce-reserves model, which open-market operation would the Fed use to reduce the money supply?
options: Buy bonds from banks
Sell bonds to the public
Lower reserve requirements
Lower the discount rate
question.commonError: Reversing open-market purchases and sales.
question.feedback: Selling bonds pulls reserves out of the banking system and reduces the money supply.

question.q: Which sequence correctly describes an open-market purchase?
options: Fed buys bonds, reserves rise, money supply can expand
Fed sells bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Fed buys bonds, reserves fall, money supply contracts
Fed sells bonds, reserves fall, money demand vanishes
question.commonError: Breaking the reserves-to-money-supply chain.
question.feedback: A Fed bond purchase adds reserves and can support money supply expansion.

question.q: How does a higher interest rate on reserves directly affect banks’ incentive to hold reserves?
options: Hold more reserves
Hold fewer reserves
Ignore the Fed
Create commodity money
question.commonError: Thinking interest on reserves always increases lending.
question.feedback: Paying more on reserves makes holding reserves more attractive to banks.

question.q: The Fed wants to increase the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Buy government bonds from the public.
Sell government bonds to the public.
Raise taxes on households.
Reduce government purchases.
question.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases remove money from circulation
question.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it pays money into the economy, increasing the money supply.

question.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Sell government bonds to the public.
Buy government bonds from the public.
Cut the discount rate.
Lower reserve requirements.
question.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales inject money
question.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, the public pays money to the Fed, reducing the money supply.

question.q: If the Fed lowers the discount rate, which effect is most likely?
options: Banks find it cheaper to borrow from the Fed.
Banks are required to hold more reserves.
The money supply must fall.
Currency becomes commodity money.
question.commonError: thinking a lower discount rate discourages borrowing
question.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper for banks.

question.q: In a banking model with binding reserve requirements, how does a higher required reserve ratio affect deposit creation?
options: Decreases
Increases
Becomes unlimited
Does not depend on deposits anymore
question.commonError: thinking higher required reserves create more lending
question.feedback: Higher reserve requirements force banks to hold more reserves and lend less, reducing money creation.

question.q: How might banks respond to a higher interest rate paid on reserves?
options: Holding more reserves and lending less
Holding fewer reserves and lending more
Creating commodity money
Eliminating demand deposits
question.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending
question.feedback: Higher interest on reserves can make banks more willing to hold reserves instead of lending.

question.q: The central bank raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. What response is most likely, other things equal?
options: Banks are more willing to hold reserves and less willing to expand lending.
Banks reduce reserve holdings and expand lending because reserves now pay more.
Households move currency directly into government spending when reserves earn more.
The required reserve ratio automatically falls when reserve interest increases.
question.commonError: Reversing the incentive effect of higher interest paid on reserves.
question.feedback: A higher return on reserve balances makes reserve holding more attractive and tends to restrain lending and money creation.

question.q: If the Fed buys $40 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 4, what is the maximum possible increase in the money supply?
options: $160 million
$40 million
$10 million
$44 million
question.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
question.feedback: A bond purchase injects reserves. Maximum money expansion is $40 million x 4 = $160 million.

question.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply by exactly $120 million and the money multiplier is 6, how many bonds should it sell?
options: $20 million
$120 million
$720 million
$6 million
question.commonError: multiplying target money change by the multiplier instead of dividing
question.feedback: To reduce money by $120 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $20 million in bonds.

question.q: A central bank adds $240 to bank reserves and raises the interest paid on reserves. What can be concluded about bank lending?
options: Banks have more reserves and a stronger reason to hold them, so both changes encourage lending.
Banks have fewer reserves and a stronger reason to hold them, so both changes discourage lending.
Banks have more reserves, so a fixed multiplier determines lending regardless of interest on reserves.
Banks have more reserves but a stronger reason to hold them, so the net effect on lending is uncertain.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
question.feedback: Reserve availability and the incentive to hold reserves are different margins. Their combination does not determine lending without the relevant behavior, risk, demand and magnitudes.

question.q: In an explicitly simplified scarce-reserves model, a central bank buys $260 of securities from banks while the required ratio is unchanged. Which balance-sheet change begins the expansionary transmission?
options: Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes
Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected
Bank securities fall and reserves rise; easier reserve conditions can support lower short-term rates and lending
Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes” in this monetary policy tools task.
question.feedback: The purchase exchanges securities for reserve balances on bank balance sheets. Under the stated scarce-reserves model, greater reserve availability eases money-market conditions; it is not a fiscal tax cut or automatic equity gain.

question.q: A central bank wants to reduce bank deposits by $1120. The estimated actual deposit multiplier is 4 rather than the theoretical maximum of 10. How should it change reserves to achieve that reduction using the estimated multiplier?
options: Remove $4480 of reserves; multiply the desired deposit change by the actual multiplier
Remove $280 of reserves; using the maximum multiplier would understate the required removal
Add $280 of reserves; a purchase is needed for contraction
Remove $112 of reserves; the maximum must be used even when actual behavior differs
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Remove $4480 of reserves; multiply the desired deposit change by the actual multiplier” in this monetary policy tools task.
question.feedback: Using the stated actual multiplier, ΔR=ΔD/m = −1120/4 = −280. A maximum that overstates the actual multiplier would imply too small a reserve operation.

question.q: Use the money-market graph. What kind of policy is the Fed pursuing when it moves money supply from MS1 to MS2?
options: Expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal policy
A positive supply shock
question.commonError: Reversing leftward money-supply shifts.
question.feedback: MS2 is left of MS1, so the money supply falls and interest rates rise.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
question.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

question.q: Use the money-market and aggregate-demand graph. How does the move from MS1 to MS2 affect the interest rate and aggregate demand?
options: Interest rates fall and aggregate demand increases.
Interest rates rise and aggregate demand decreases.
Interest rates rise and aggregate demand increases.
Interest rates fall and aggregate demand decreases.
question.commonError: Breaking the interest-rate to AD chain.
question.feedback: A lower money supply raises r, reducing investment and shifting AD left.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
question.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

question.q: In the scarce-reserves model, how does an increase in the money supply usually affect interest rates, investment, and aggregate demand in the short run?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, and aggregate demand shifts right.
Interest rates rise, investment falls, and aggregate demand shifts left.
Interest rates fall, investment falls, and aggregate demand shifts left.
Interest rates rise, investment rises, and aggregate demand shifts right.
question.commonError: reversing the interest-rate effect
question.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

question.q: In the scarce-reserves model, how does an initial decrease in the money supply usually affect interest rates, investment, and aggregate demand in the short run?
options: Interest rates rise, investment falls, and aggregate demand shifts left.
Interest rates fall, investment rises, and aggregate demand shifts right.
Interest rates rise, investment rises, and aggregate demand shifts right.
Interest rates fall, investment falls, and aggregate demand shifts left.
question.commonError: thinking tighter money lowers interest rates
question.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy raises interest rates, reduces investment, and shifts AD left.

question.q: Which variables belong in the money-market model used to explain monetary-policy transmission?
options: Money supply, money demand and the nominal interest rate.
Aggregate demand, short-run supply and real output.
Government purchases, tax revenue and the budget deficit.
Capital per worker, productivity and technological progress.
question.commonError: confusing the money market graph with the AD graph
question.feedback: The money market relates desired money holdings to the supplied quantity at different nominal interest rates. Its equilibrium rate affects interest-sensitive spending in the aggregate-demand model.

question.q: Through the usual monetary-policy transmission mechanism, which spending change follows most directly from a lower interest rate?
options: Higher investment spending
Lower investment spending
Lower government spending automatically
A smaller money supply automatically
question.commonError: thinking lower borrowing costs reduce investment
question.feedback: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, so investment spending rises.

question.q: In the standard scarce-reserves model, how does an increase in the money supply affect aggregate demand?
options: Shift right
Shift left
Become vertical
Turn into money demand
question.commonError: confusing movement along AD with a shift of AD
question.feedback: More money lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

question.q: Why can a liquidity trap limit the effect of conventional monetary policy?
options: Nominal interest rates cannot be pushed much below zero
Money demand is always zero
Government spending cannot change
Banks cannot hold reserves
question.commonError: thinking the Fed can always lower nominal rates without limit
question.feedback: When nominal rates are near zero, the Fed has less room to stimulate spending through further rate cuts.

question.q: If the economy is weak and the Fed wants to stimulate aggregate demand, which action fits the goal?
options: Increase the money supply to lower interest rates.
Decrease the money supply to raise interest rates.
Raise taxes to reduce consumption.
Lower government spending to reduce aggregate demand.
question.commonError: choosing contractionary money during weak demand
question.feedback: To stimulate AD, the Fed can increase the money supply, lower interest rates, and encourage investment.

question.q: If inflation pressure is high because aggregate demand is too strong, which Fed action fits the goal?
options: Decrease the money supply to raise interest rates.
Increase the money supply to lower interest rates.
Buy bonds to increase investment.
Cut interest rates to shift aggregate demand right.
question.commonError: using expansionary monetary policy when AD is already too high
question.feedback: To cool AD, the Fed can reduce the money supply, raise interest rates, and reduce investment.

question.q: How does interest-sensitive spending connect the two panels' move from A to B?
options: Spending rises as borrowing costs fall; output reaches 150 and the price level 60 on the new aggregate demand curve.
Spending rises as borrowing costs fall; output 125 and price 56.25 are reached by a movement along unchanged aggregate demand.
Output 125 and price 56.25 result from lower production costs shifting short-run aggregate supply, with planned spending unchanged.
Spending rises as borrowing costs fall; output reaches 125 and the price level 56.25 on the new aggregate demand curve.
question.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
question.feedback: The rate falls from 6% to 4%, encouraging spending. The right-panel B is at output 125 and price 56.25 where higher AD intersects unchanged SRAS. A borrowing-cost change shifts spending plans rather than merely changing the price level along AD.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
question.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (100,6) and dashed MS1 at B (150,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and upper dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (100,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (125,56.25). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

question.q: In the expansionary two-panel diagram, how many units does real GDP rise from A to B?
question.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
question.feedback: Read real GDP at A and B: 125 − 100 = 25 units.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
question.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (100,6) and dashed MS1 at B (150,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and upper dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (100,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (125,56.25). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

question.q: Which output-market response matches the monetary change shown across the panels?
options: Borrowing costs restrain spending; aggregate demand shifts left to an equilibrium at output 105 and price level 40.
Borrowing costs restrain spending; aggregate demand shifts left to an equilibrium at output 100 and price level 45.
Borrowing costs lower production costs; short-run aggregate supply shifts right to output 100 and price level 45.
Output 100 and price level 45 result from moving along unchanged aggregate demand when money supply falls.
question.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
question.feedback: The rate rises as money supply contracts. Interest-sensitive spending falls, shifting AD left; the right-panel B is output 100, price 45, on unchanged SRAS.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
question.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (125,2.75) and dashed MS1 at B (100,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (125,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (100,45). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

question.q: In the contractionary two-panel diagram, how many units does real GDP fall from A to B?
question.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
question.feedback: Read real GDP at A and B: 125 − 100 = 25 units.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
question.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (125,2.75) and dashed MS1 at B (100,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (125,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (100,45). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

question.q: Refer to the money-market graph. Which movement shows contractionary monetary policy with MD1 unchanged?
options: g to e
e to g
a to d
d to a
question.commonError: Reversing a leftward money supply shift.
question.feedback: Contractionary policy shifts MS left from MS2 to MS1, moving from g to e on MD1.
question.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
question.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

question.q: Read the policy path in reverse, from MS2 to MS1. Which mechanism explains the associated aggregate-demand change?
options: The money supply expands, the rate falls, and investment raises aggregate demand from AD2 toward AD1.
The money supply contracts, the rate rises, and investment lowers aggregate demand from AD2 toward AD1.
The money supply expands and the rate falls, but the resulting aggregate demand change is a movement along a fixed demand curve.
Money demand falls rather than money supply changing, so investment raises aggregate demand from AD2 toward AD1.
question.commonError: Breaking the r-to-AD link.
question.feedback: MS1 is right of MS2, with a lower interest rate r 1. The expansion stimulates investment and shifts AD from the leftward AD2 toward AD1. The graph distinguishes the policy supply change from a demand change in the money market.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
question.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

question.q: Why might monetary policy be weak in a liquidity trap?
options: Near-zero interest rates leave little room for traditional cuts.
Money demand is always upward sloping.
Fiscal policy stops affecting aggregate demand.
The money supply cannot be changed by any central bank.
question.commonError: thinking central banks can always lower nominal rates without limit
question.feedback: When nominal rates are near zero, the usual interest-rate channel has less room to operate.

question.q: The Fed shifts MS left while the economy is already below potential. What is the likely policy risk?
options: Interest rates rise, aggregate demand falls, and the recessionary gap worsens.
Interest rates fall, aggregate demand rises, and inflation disappears cleanly.
Interest rates rise, short-run aggregate supply shifts right, and output returns to potential.
Interest rates fall, long-run aggregate supply shifts left, and unemployment returns to natural.
question.commonError: Missing the danger of tightening into weak demand.
question.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates and shifts AD left, which can worsen a recessionary gap.

question.q: Refer to the graph. At price level P1, what happens when AD moves from AD1 to AD2?
options: Output falls from Y1 to Y2.
Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
Output stays at Y1.
The graph shows only an interest-rate change and no output change.
question.commonError: missing the output movement from AD1 to AD2 at P1
question.feedback: At P1, the leftward AD shift moves output from Y1 to Y2.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
question.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

question.q: Refer to the graph. Which graph feature shows that the monetary policy is contractionary rather than expansionary?
options: MS moves left from MS1 to MS2 and aggregate demand moves left from AD1 to AD2.
MS moves right from MS2 to MS1 and aggregate demand moves right from AD2 to AD1.
Money demand moves left and aggregate demand stays fixed.
The price level falls along AD1.
question.commonError: not using the labels MS1, MS2, AD1, and AD2 to identify policy direction
question.feedback: The key evidence is MS1 to MS2 and AD1 to AD2, both leftward shifts.
question.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
question.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

question.q: A student says expansionary monetary policy raises aggregate demand by directly increasing government purchases. What is the best correction?
options: Monetary policy works mainly through money supply, interest rates, and investment.
Monetary policy works by changing G before interest rates can move.
Monetary policy works only by shifting long-run aggregate supply through technology.
Monetary policy works by raising taxes and lowering consumption.
question.commonError: Confusing monetary and fiscal policy channels.
question.feedback: Monetary policy affects AD primarily through money supply, interest rates, and investment spending.

question.q: A central bank adds $80 to bank reserves, but banks hold the added balances and qualified borrowers do not expand borrowing. What happened to reserves, credit and spending?
options: Reserves stayed fixed; weak borrowing proves no injection occurred.
Reserves rose; aggregate demand rises by the same amount.
Reserves rose; credit and spending responses remain limited.
Reserves rose; the natural unemployment rate therefore falls permanently.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserves stayed fixed; weak borrowing proves no injection occurred.
question.feedback: Reserve implementation, lending behavior and expenditure are distinct stages. Weak later links can limit aggregate-demand effects without undoing the initial reserve operation.

question.q: Tighter monetary policy raises interest rates and reduces investment by $90. Export demand rises independently. Without knowing the size of that increase or subsequent spending effects, what can be concluded about total aggregate demand?
options: It must fall because monetary policy reduces investment.
Its net change depends on the relative effects of lower investment and higher exports.
It must rise because export demand increases.
It stays unchanged because the two effects move in opposite directions.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; monetary policy establishes a net decline.
question.feedback: A correct sign for one transmission chain is not a complete net forecast under a second shock. Compare the final contributions before assigning the total AD direction.

question.q: In the standard short-run model, monetary easing lowers interest rates, making $100 in investment more attractive. However, weaker expected sales offset that incentive. Why might aggregate demand respond only weakly to the monetary easing?
options: Weaker expected sales can reduce investment despite lower interest rates.
Monetary easing failed to lower interest rates, despite the observed decline.
Investment cannot affect aggregate demand because capital spending is excluded from it.
An unreported increase in reserve requirements restricted lending despite the monetary easing.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Policy-to-rate transmission failed despite the observed interest-rate decline.
question.feedback: Lower interest rates affect aggregate demand only if spending responds. Weaker expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing becomes cheaper.

question.q: In the scarce-reserves model, monetary expansion lowers interest rates, but firms do not increase investment. Which usual effect of the policy is weakened?
options: The investment-driven rise in aggregate demand
The already-observed fall in interest
The definition of required reserves
The classification of currency in money
question.feedback: The chain from rates to investment fails to deliver the usual spending increase, so the investment contribution to AD is weaker.
question.commonError: Assumes an observed rate cut guarantees a spending increase.
Reverses the direction of expansionary monetary transmission.
question.q: In a scarce-reserves model, monetary expansion lowers rates and investment rises $10. With spending multiplier 2 and no other spending change, what aggregate demand effect follows?
options: A $20 decrease
A $20 increase
A $10 decrease
A $5 increase
question.feedback: The autonomous investment increase 10 is multiplied by 2, raising AD20.

question.commonError: Reverses the direction of contractionary monetary transmission.
question.q: In a scarce-reserves model, monetary contraction raises rates and reduces investment $15. With spending multiplier 2 and no other spending change, what AD effect follows?
options: A $30 increase
A $30 decrease
A $15 increase
A $7.5 decrease
question.feedback: The autonomous investment reduction 15 produces a total demand reduction 30.

question.q: A student says credit card balances should be counted in M1 because people use cards to buy goods. What is the best correction?
options: Credit cards are borrowing, not money balances
Credit cards are currency held by the public
Credit cards are checkable deposits
Credit cards are savings deposits
question.commonError: Counting credit cards as money.
question.feedback: Credit cards allow borrowing. They are not money balances like currency or checkable deposits.

question.q: A household keeps cash because it wants to make purchases quickly, compare prices, and save some value for later. Which answer matches all three functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, fiat money
Unit of account, leverage, discount rate
Medium of exchange, multiplier, bank capital
question.commonError: Mixing money functions with banking tools.
question.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and can transfer purchasing power into the future.

question.q: A student says, 'Money is valuable because the dollar bill itself has valuable paper.' What is the best correction?
options: Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
Fiat money has value because its paper is worth more than its face value.
Commodity money and fiat money are the same thing.
Money only has value if it can be exchanged for gold.
question.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
question.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. Its value comes from general acceptance and government backing.

question.q: A grocery store lists apples at $2 per pound. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Fractional reserve
question.commonError: choosing medium of exchange whenever prices involve money
question.feedback: The price tag uses money to measure value, so money is acting as a unit of account.

question.q: A person keeps $500 in cash for emergencies. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Store of value
Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
question.commonError: thinking money only matters when it is spent immediately
question.feedback: The cash is preserving purchasing power for later, so it is serving as a store of value.

question.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item would be counted in M2 but not in M1?
options: A savings deposit
Currency in your wallet
A checking account deposit
A traveler's check
question.commonError: putting all liquid assets into M1
question.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies. They belong in M2, not M1.

question.q: Why does money make specialization easier?
options: It removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
It makes all goods cost the same amount.
It prevents prices from changing.
It eliminates scarcity.
question.commonError: thinking money eliminates scarcity rather than reducing transaction costs
question.feedback: Money reduces transaction costs because people no longer need to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.

question.q: Which statement best explains why currency held by a bank does not count the same way as currency held by the public?
options: Bank-held currency is reserves; public-held currency is circulating money.
Currency held by banks is automatically counted twice in M1.
Currency held by banks is commodity money.
Currency held by banks is never money.
question.commonError: double-counting currency held inside banks
question.feedback: Currency held by banks is treated as reserves. Currency in the money supply refers to currency held by the public.

question.q: A household moves $4,000 from a checking account into a retail money-market mutual fund. What happens?
options: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.
question.commonError: Treating movement between M1 and non-M1 M2 assets as a change in total M2.
question.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.

question.q: A payment app transfers balances instantly from users’ checking accounts but holds no separate monetary balance. How should the app affect measured money?
options: Every transfer through the app permanently increases the measured M1 stock.
The app balance enters M2 even though no separate monetary balance exists.
It changes payment convenience without creating a new money balance.
Using the app removes the linked checking deposits from measured money.
question.commonError: Counting a payment method as a separate stock of money when it only accesses an existing deposit.
question.feedback: A payment platform that merely accesses checking deposits changes how money is used, not how much money exists.

question.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $3,000, savings deposits are $2,500, small time deposits are $1,200, retail money market funds are $800, and large time deposits are $900. If large time deposits are not counted in M2, what is M2?
question.commonError: including large time deposits when the course definition excludes them
question.feedback: M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $3,000 + $2,500 + $1,200 + $800 = $7,500.

question.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A household moves $10,000 from a checking account to a savings account. What happens to M1 and M2, using standard course definitions?
options: M1 falls, while M2 is unchanged.
Both M1 and M2 fall.
M1 is unchanged, while M2 rises.
Both M1 and M2 rise.
question.commonError: thinking every movement between accounts changes M2
question.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2; savings deposits are in M2 but not M1. Moving funds to savings lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

question.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks lend more, and the public redeposits most loan proceeds. Which money measures are most likely affected first?
options: New lending creates deposits, raising M1 and contributing to broader money measures.
Bond purchases turn financial assets into physical commodity money.
Lending immediately raises real GDP without changing deposits.
New lending reduces the checking deposits held by households and businesses.
question.commonError: thinking bank-created deposits are not part of money measures
question.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits, and checkable deposits are part of M1. M2 can also be affected depending on where funds are held.

question.q: A farmer accepts dollars for corn, uses dollars to compare seed prices, and saves some dollars for next month. Which answer correctly matches the three functions of money?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, medium of exchange, unit of account
Unit of account, store of value, medium of exchange
Money multiplier, reserve requirement, federal funds rate
question.commonError: mixing up using money to buy with using money to measure value
question.feedback: Buying uses money as a medium of exchange, comparing prices uses it as a unit of account, and saving it uses it as a store of value.

question.q: Currency held by the public is $800 billion and checkable deposits are $1,200 billion. Assume these are the only M1 components with nonzero balances. What is M1?
options: $2,000 billion
$1,200 billion
$800 billion
$400 billion
question.commonError: leaving out either currency or checkable deposits
question.feedback: M1 includes currency plus checkable deposits: $800 billion + $1,200 billion = $2,000 billion.

question.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions from before May 2020. M1 is $2,000 billion, savings deposits are $900 billion, small time deposits are $300 billion, and retail money market mutual funds are $200 billion. What is M2?
options: $3,400 billion
$2,000 billion
$1,400 billion
$2,300 billion
question.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
question.feedback: M2 equals M1 plus near monies: $2,000 + $900 + $300 + $200 = $3,400 billion.

question.q: A store prices an item at $140. A student pays with a debit card that transfers dollars from a deposit account, then calls the card a fourth function of money. Which explanation is correct?
options: Dollars measure the price and the deposit pays for the item; the card transfers the funds.
Dollars store value in the price quote, while the card provides the unit of account.
The deposit measures the price, while the card creates new money to pay for the item.
Dollars measure the price, but the deposit is not money and the card is commodity money.
question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Quote: store of value; deposit: transfer instrument; card: unit of account.
question.feedback: Distinguish the monetary unit and balances from the technology used to access them. Quoting prices uses a unit of account; paying transfers money through the card system.

question.q: An economy has currency $160, checking $320, savings $480, and small time deposits $160. Using current U.S. definitions, what are M1 and M2?
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “M1 = $960; M2 = $1600” in this money functions and measures task.
question.feedback: M1 = 160+320+480 = 960. M2 adds the time deposit once: 960+160 = 1120. Savings already inside M1 must not be added again.

question.q: A customer deposits $180 of currency into checking. A bank later makes a separate loan by crediting a borrower's checking account. Which comparison correctly separates the two events?
options: Neither event can change M1 because every bank deposit merely replaces currency
The currency deposit creates new M1; lending changes only the ownership of existing currency
The currency deposit changes M1 composition; the later loan can create a new deposit and raise M1
Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Neither event can change M1 because every bank deposit merely replaces currency” in this money functions and measures task.
question.feedback: In the first event, public currency falls as checking rises; in the second, a loan asset and deposit liability are created together. The initial transfer and subsequent credit creation must not be conflated.

question.q: In monopolistic competition, a new cluster of coffee shops opens near an established café. Which immediate effect is most likely for the café?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic
Its demand shifts right and becomes less elastic
Its marginal cost curve shifts down automatically
Its average total cost becomes zero
question.commonError: shifts_existing_firm_demand_right
question.feedback: Entry creates more close substitutes.

question.q: In monopolistic competition, several boutique gyms close after sustained losses. Which effect is most likely for a surviving gym?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic because fewer alternatives remain available
Its demand shifts right and may become less elastic
Its marginal revenue becomes horizontal at zero
Its fixed cost disappears
question.commonError: shifts_existing_firm_demand_left
question.feedback: Exit removes substitutes and can strengthen surviving demand.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm charges $42 per unit. At its chosen output, marginal cost is $31 and average total cost is $42. What are its economic profit and markup per unit?
options: The firm earns an $11 profit per unit because price exceeds marginal cost by $11
The firm is allocatively efficient
The firm earns zero economic profit but has an $11 markup
The firm must exit
question.commonError: equates_markup_with_profit
question.feedback: Price equals ATC, so profit is zero; price minus MC is the markup.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 24 units in long-run equilibrium, while average total cost is minimized at 36 units. What is its excess capacity?
options: 24 units
36 units
60 units
12 units
question.commonError: defines_as_idle_physical_capital
question.feedback: Excess capacity is minimum-ATC output minus equilibrium output.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm pays a fixed advertising fee that leaves demand unchanged. How does this affect the short-run output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost?
options: It remains unchanged
It rises because average total cost rises
It falls because fixed cost raises marginal cost
It becomes the minimum average total cost output
question.commonError: misclassifies_fixed_and_per_unit_cost
question.feedback: A pure fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MR or MC.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm pays a promotional fee on every unit sold. Which cost curves rise directly?
options: Only average total cost
Marginal cost, average variable cost, and average total cost
Only fixed cost and average fixed cost
Demand and marginal revenue only
question.commonError: misclassifies_fixed_and_per_unit_cost
question.feedback: A per-unit selling cost is a variable cost.

question.q: In monopolistic competition, a brand campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rivals. What is the most direct demand effect?
options: Demand becomes perfectly elastic
Demand shifts only because the campaign lowers marginal cost and average variable cost
The firm’s demand becomes less elastic
Marginal revenue equals price at every quantity
question.commonError: confuses_shift_and_rotation
question.feedback: Greater loyalty reduces responsiveness to price.

question.q: In monopolistic competition, a comparison website makes prices and features easier to compare across brands. What is the likely effect?
options: Firm demand becomes vertical
Every seller becomes a monopoly because buyers can now compare all products directly
Entry becomes impossible
Firm demand becomes more elastic
question.commonError: treats_all_ads_as_persuasion
question.feedback: Lower search costs make switching easier.

question.q: Lumen Bistro operates in monopolistic competition and faces demand P = 92 − 1.5Q, where P is price in dollars and Q is quantity. At an output of approximately 22.09 units, which price is closest to the price it charges?
question.commonError: reads_price_from_mr
question.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 20 units in long-run equilibrium. It would minimize average total cost at 36.67 units. What is its excess capacity?
options: 20 units
36.67 units
16.67 units
question.commonError: defines_as_idle_physical_capital
question.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm charges $70 in long-run equilibrium, with marginal cost of $50. What is its markup per unit?
question.commonError: equates_markup_with_profit
question.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 24 units in long-run equilibrium. It would minimize average total cost at 39.71 units. What is its excess capacity?
options: 15.71 units
24 units
39.71 units
question.commonError: defines_as_idle_physical_capital
question.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm charges $76 in long-run equilibrium, with marginal cost of $49.60. What is its markup per unit?
question.commonError: equates_markup_with_profit
question.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm charges $64 in long-run equilibrium, with marginal cost of $47.80. What is its markup per unit?
question.commonError: equates_markup_with_profit
question.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

question.q: Use the graph of a monopolistically competitive firm. What is the firm’s economic profit per unit at Q = 50?
question.commonError: uses_price_minus_mc
question.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC: $37 − $33 = $4.

question.q: Use the graph of a monopolistically competitive firm. What is total economic profit at the profit-maximizing output?
question.commonError: forgets_multiply_by_quantity
question.feedback: Total profit is ($37 − $33) × 50 = $200.

question.q: In monopolistic competition, a comparison website makes it easier for buyers to compare nearly identical local services. What effect is most likely on each firm’s demand?
options: Demand becomes more elastic
Demand becomes less elastic
Demand becomes vertical
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
question.commonError: treats_all_ads_as_persuasion
question.feedback: Better comparison makes substitution easier, increasing buyers’ responsiveness to one firm’s price.

question.q: A monopolistically competitive firm pays a $3 promotional fee for every unit sold, and demand is unchanged. What is the most direct short-run effect?
options: Only fixed cost rises, so output cannot change
Demand shifts right by $3 at every quantity
Average total cost falls because advertising spreads fixed cost
MC rises, so the MR=MC output tends to fall
question.commonError: misclassifies_fixed_and_per_unit_cost
question.feedback: A per-unit selling cost raises marginal cost and tends to reduce the profit-maximizing output when demand is unchanged.

question.q: A restaurant operating in monopolistic competition improves food quality. Customers are willing to pay more, but marginal production cost also rises. What determines the new profit-maximizing output?
options: The cost increase alone
The old output because quality is nonprice competition
The new marginal revenue and marginal cost curves together
The demand shift alone
question.commonError: confuses_quality_with_image
question.feedback: Quality improvement can affect both willingness to pay and cost, so the new optimum still requires comparing MR and MC.

question.q: In monopolistic competition, a policy causes several niche brands to exit. Average production cost falls, but consumers lose valued variety. What is the correct welfare conclusion?
options: Welfare must rise because average cost fell
Welfare must fall because the number of brands fell
The change is irrelevant because firms earn zero economic profit
The net effect is ambiguous without comparing cost savings with lost variety benefits
question.commonError: uses_one_sided_efficiency_claim
question.feedback: Efficiency analysis must weigh resource savings against the consumer value of differentiation and variety.

question.q: An industry is classified as monopolistically competitive because it has many differentiated sellers. In one rural town, however, only two sellers actually serve customers. What is the best caution?
options: Two local sellers guarantee a natural monopoly
Differentiation becomes irrelevant whenever geography matters
The local market may display strategic interdependence that the broad model misses
The market must still be perfectly competitive locally
question.commonError: classifies_from_one_feature
question.feedback: Market boundaries matter. A broad national description can hide a much more concentrated local competitive environment.

question.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit but charges a price above marginal cost. What does this show?
options: The firm is producing at minimum average total cost
Zero economic profit does not imply allocative efficiency
The firm must be earning an accounting loss
Entry must eliminate all market power, so this firm cannot be in long-run equilibrium.
question.commonError: claims_price_equals_mc
question.feedback: Entry can eliminate economic profit while differentiation leaves a markup and P above MC.

question.q: Atlas Coffee operates in monopolistic competition and publishes verified wait times and prices. How does this advertising help customers choose among cafés?
options: It gives customers information that can reduce their search costs.
It builds prestige without giving customers verifiable information.
It improves the coffee itself without changing what customers know.
It lowers production costs by increasing the scale of each café.
question.commonError: treats_all_ads_as_persuasion
question.feedback: Verified prices and wait times provide product information buyers can use before purchasing. This is informational advertising rather than a claim that the firm is a price taker.

question.q: Bloom Cosmetics operates in monopolistic competition and advertises prestige without measurable performance claims. How is it trying to distinguish its product?
options: It demonstrates a measurable improvement in the product’s performance.
It helps buyers compare verified prices across rival brands.
It reduces marginal production cost without affecting buyers’ preferences.
It builds a brand image that may increase willingness to pay without demonstrating better performance.
question.commonError: treats_all_ads_as_information
question.feedback: Associating the brand with prestige seeks to change preferences or perceived differentiation without documenting a physical performance improvement.

question.q: Crown Dental operates in monopolistic competition and offers a warranty that would be costly to honor if its work were poor. What can customers infer from that commitment?
options: The warranty proves that its prices must equal marginal cost.
The warranty guarantees that every rival provides the same quality.
The warranty can signal confidence in the quality of its work.
The warranty matters only as a price discount, regardless of the cost of honoring it.
question.commonError: ignores_quality_signal
question.feedback: A costly warranty commits the seller to consequences if quality disappoints. That commitment can convey information about quality, rather than simply describe the market’s cost structure.

question.q: Dahlia Delivery operates in monopolistic competition and buys an annual sponsorship unrelated to delivery volume. How should the sponsorship cost be treated?
options: It is a variable selling cost that rises with every delivery.
It is a fixed selling cost that does not rise with the next delivery.
It is a marginal production cost charged for each delivery.
It lowers total fixed cost because advertising is outside production.
question.commonError: misclassifies_fixed_and_per_unit_cost
question.feedback: The annual sponsorship payment does not vary with orders, making it a fixed selling cost rather than a per-unit cost.

question.q: Flint Apparel operates in monopolistic competition and uses more durable fabric and better construction. Why might buyers be willing to pay more?
options: A new brand image alone changes buyers’ beliefs without changing performance.
The changes make every seller’s products identical and eliminate differentiation.
Better construction necessarily lowers buyers’ willingness to pay.
The changes improve the product’s performance and distinguish it from alternatives.
question.commonError: confuses_quality_with_image
